The Jñānārṇavatantra proclaimed by Īśvara; now, the first chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of the Gaṇas, who are surrounded by Gaṇeśa, Nandin, Caṇḍeśa, and Surendra;
O one worthy of universal veneration, what is it that you constantly recite? || 1.1 ||
"What indeed is this 'Akṣamālā'? A doubt remains within my heart.
You alone are the knower of the ultimate truth—that Supreme Brahman which transcends all words. || 1-2 ||
"O Ānanda, [I speak] from the firm resolve of a mind thick with the flow of nectar.
The Lord said: 'O lady of beautiful hips, I shall tell that which is always recited by me.'"
The Mātṛkā, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa', has the form of the sacred seats (pīṭha);
she is endowed with the fourteen vowels and adorned with the three points (bindus). || 1-4 ||
O Goddess of gods, she is adorned with the *anusvāra* and embellished by a single *bindu*;
she is made radiant by the *visarga* joined with two *bindus*. (1–5)
O Maheśvarī, the circle of the Kalās has been described as the form of Śakti;
the letters from *ka* to *kṣa* are indeed the very form of Śiva. (1–6)
Because it possesses the nature of a consonant (*vyañjana*), it is always accompanied by bliss (*ānanda*) and joined with emission (*uccāra*).
Therefore, O Goddess, one should utter [the mantra] conjoined with the vowels; of this there is no doubt. (1–7)
O virtuous lady, the entity known as sound exists in the form of fifty phonemes;
O Goddess, the letter *a* is held to be the first, and the letter *kṣa* is the last.
Renowned as the Akṣamālā, she is the Mātṛkā whose form consists of the phonemes;
though her nature is the Śabdabrahman, she is recited as that which transcends sound. || 1-9 ||
Know that the supreme abode, which transcends sound, is eternally beyond calculation; it is the very nature of the Self, for the *haṃsa* is indeed the Supreme Lord. || 1-10 ||
In this very supreme reality, adorned with the three points (bindus), it exists as encapsulated by the Mātṛkā and has attained manifestation. || 1-11 ||
O fair-faced one, I shall explain the three drops in the form of seed-syllables.
Know, O Pārvatī, that the letter *ha* in the form of a drop is Brahmā. (1–12)
O Goddess of the Gods, I am Hari, together with the letter *sa*, the *sarga* (visarga), and the *bindu*.
Because they exist in an inseparable state, they are known in the world as Hari and Hara.
O Maheśānī, Brahmabindu is called Vāmā Śakti; because she vomits forth the universe, she is celebrated as Vāmā. || 1-14 ||
Jyeṣṭhā is indeed the power of Viṣṇu, protecting the three worlds;
thereafter, the Supreme Goddess Raudrī devours them in due order.
In this way, know that there are three *bindus*, adorned by the three qualities (*guṇas*).
Although the word *bindu* signifies emptiness (*śūnya*), it likewise indicates the qualities. (1.16)

Know, O Beloved, that which consists of will, knowledge, and action; whose nature is *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*; which is the essence of the three cities, and is composed of the three principles. || 1-17 ||
O Maheśānī, all this is established within the three *bindus*;
O Goddess, the succession of the three qualities [is established] by means of Ambikā and the *bindus*. (1.18)
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep arise from the three *bindus* within Śiva;
waking should be known as characterized by the quality of *sattva*, consisting solely of the nature of power (*śakti*). (1.19)
The expansion of the withdrawal of the mind desires the defects of suffering;
deep sleep, however, which is of the nature of Śiva, carries away all such withdrawals.
Having completely abandoned the attributes of the body, she is the very nature of the principle of Śiva;
consisting of the quality of *tamas*, she devours karma and is the embodiment of liberation. || 1-21 ||
The dream state, consisting of rajas, occurs at the end of deep sleep and at the beginning of waking;
it is characterized by the features of both [sleep and waking] and is marked by the characteristic of craving. (1.22)
These three states have been described as arising from the *bindu*.
O beloved, when this state of the *bindu* is known, hear now about the fourth state.
The state characterized by mere vibration at the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking,
having attained fullness, is the supreme fourth state (turyāvasthā), the highest digit.

When this very [state], which is free from existence and non-existence, beyond the qualities (guṇa), and perfectly steady, is always attained by the mind, O Goddess, [then one is liberated]. || 1-25 ||
Named Unmanī, she is the true form, the creeper of knowledge whose essence is consciousness;
she has issued forth from the three points and the resonance (nāda) as the embodiment of bliss.
Through the union of the three drops, she is named Tripurā and is formless;
though beyond all phonemes, she is yet possessed of phonemes, being solely the digit of consciousness-knowledge.
"O beloved, having fully propitiated this knowledge (*vidyā*), omniscience has been attained by me.
O Goddess, Tripurā is worshipped by me with a rosary of *akṣa* seeds. (1.28)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Mere Object of Knowledge as Essential Nature," in the glorious Jñānārṇava, the Tantra of the Nityās. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
The venerable Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, Tripurā has been indicated by way of knowledge."
Tell me in its true form, if I am dear to you.
What is the nature of Tripurā, and what are the various types of her mantras? I wish to hear all of this, so that I may attain good fortune. (2.2)
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, Tripurā is threefold; first, hear concerning Bālā, by the knowledge of whom, O Goddess, one becomes the Guru of the gods in person. (2–3)
Having uttered the fourth vowel (Ū), endowed with the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā;
[and] the end of the vowels (AU) joined with Earth (L) and adorned with the fourth vowel (Ū). || 2-4 ||
Overcome by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, the imperishable Bhṛgu is possessed of creation;
endowed with the letter *śa* and the vowel *ra*, this is considered the three-syllabled Vidyā. (2-5)
Bestowing eloquence like the surging waves of the Gaṅgā,
she is the progenitor of great good fortune and the bestower of supreme Sarasvatī.
Possessing great beauty and grace, she is the destroyer of great death;
she is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other gods, and she is the remover of sins.
The Goddess, who embodies all sacred fords, bestows gold, jewels, and other riches;
she is composed of all the worlds and brings all the worlds under her control.
The Goddess consists of all fields; she is the accomplisher of all purposes and goals.
She bestows great liberation, she is peaceful, and she grants supreme emancipation. (2-9)
Even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues,
this supreme three-syllable vidyā could never be fully described.
Even with five faces and five tongues, it cannot be [uttered];
through the Vāgbhava syllable, which possesses the splendor of the moon, she bestows the state of Lord of Speech.
O virtuous lady, she deludes the three worlds with the seed-syllable of Kāmarāja, which possesses the shimmering luster of a *śakragopa* insect, and with the seed-syllable of Śakti.
Good fortune resides in his house, who possesses a complexion like shimmering gold.
O Goddess, I shall now describe her sādhana in brief. (2-13)
Having risen at dawn, O Goddess of Gods, and having remembered one's own Guru in the *brahmarandhra*, one becomes identical with the Goddess, purified by the stainless mass of her radiance.
Then the wise one should perform the rite of bathing while recollecting the root mantra;
having consecrated water three times in his joined palms, he should pour it over his head.
O Supreme Goddess, one should cast [the water] away, perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) three times, and offer libations (tarpaṇa).
One should sprinkle the body three times and present the arghya offering to the Sun.
O Goddess of gods, O beloved, [one should worship] with the root mantra or with the mantra of the Sun;
[the seed-syllable of Śiva] situated in fire and adorned with the left eye. (2-17)
One should then utter the word *haṃsa* joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*;
O Goddess, with this mantra one should present the water offering (*arghya*) to the Sun.
One should recite the mantra of the Supreme Goddess Gāyatrī according to one's capacity, having first uttered the root-vidyā and [the words]: "O Vāgīśvarī, we know thee... (2.19).
Having uttered the second seed-syllable, [one says] "and may we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī";
having uttered the third seed-syllable, [one says] "may that Śakti impel us. (2.20)
After reciting [the mantra] according to one's ability, one should then enter the sacrificial pavilion.
[One should also worship] Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, as well as Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Having worshipped the Door-Glory (Dvāraśrī), the Threshold (Dehalī), and the Person known as Vāstu, O Supreme Goddess, the wise one should then worship the Seat (Āsana). || 2-22 ||
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Parā, and then preceded by the Support (Ādhāra),
one should write the word "Śakti" and then write "Kamalāsana."
O Dear One, having placed the word "namaḥ" at the end [of the mantra] as the mantra for the seat,
the wise one, O Goddess, should then sit down and cause the spirits to tremble.

One should perform the rite of elemental purification (bhūtaśuddhi) by means of three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), having uttered the great seed-syllable of Vāyu which has emerged from the hexagon. || 2-25 ||
O Maheśānī, one should dry up the body of sin that is black in color;
sitting properly upon the seat, one should fill the abdomen with the left [nostril]. || 2-26 ||
Having performed the retention (kumbhaka) three times, one should exhale through the right [nostril];
this is the closing of the nostril using the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb. (2-27)
That is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*, performed without the index and middle fingers;
[one should visualize] the personification of sin, with the luster of lampblack, situated in the left side of the abdomen. || 2-28 ||
The murder of a Brahmin is his head; the theft of gold is his two arms; the drinking of liquor is joined with his heart; and violating the teacher’s bed is his two hips. (2.29)
The contact with him was a pair of calamities for his limbs and minor members;
he had hair on his body like minor offenses, and his beard and eyes were black.
One should visualize the sinner in the belly as being enraged and bearing a sword and shield;
O Supreme Goddess, one should dry up his body with the seed-syllable of wind (YAM).
Having made it dry by associating it with sin, and having burnt it by that sequence using the seed-syllable of fire, O Śivā, together with the sin.
Afterwards, one should wash it, freed from evil, with the water of immortality;
by means of the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra, one should establish the life-force within the body.
Having uttered the *mukhavṛtta*, one should then utter the *haṃsa* in reverse; O Supreme Goddess, this is the three-syllabled *vidyā*.
This mantra for the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) shall accomplish all rites;
by that very procedure, O Goddess, one should stabilize one's own body. (2-35)
O Goddess of the gods, having purified one's body, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with a concentrated mind.
O Great Goddess, the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
One should place [the syllables] on the head because they are worthy of worship; O Dear One, the *paṅkti* meter is placed in the mouth.
The deity is Bālā Tripurā Parameśvarī, who resides in the heart. (2-37)
The seed-syllable is Vāgbhava, Śakti is the third, and likewise Kīlaka;
O Maheśānī, Kāmarāja is declared to be the metre for the ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should sequentially assign the three syllables from the navel to the feet, from the throat to the navel, and from the head to the throat. (2–39)
On the palm of the left hand and likewise on the palm of the right hand,
O beloved, one should place the Vidyā consisting of three seed-syllables within the hollow formed by joining both palms.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the five arrows in sequence upon the fingers of the hand,
starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger.
Having written the two final letters of the series [tha and pha], they are indeed situated in fire (ra) in sequence;
it is then encircled by the mouth-circle, the eye, and the left [hand]. || 2-42 ||
These two arrows are declared to be the Mādana, situated upon the earth;
O fair-faced one, it has the form of the letter 'na' enriched by the fourth vowel and the bindu.
The letter *pha* joined with the sequence, adorned with the left ear [the vowel *u*], conjoined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, and possessing the *sarga* (visarga), is the Moon, O Dear One. (2.44)
O Maheśānī, O Pārvatī, listen to the names of the five arrows:
Kṣobhaṇa, Drāvaṇa, O Goddess, and likewise the one known as Karṣaṇa.
O Supreme Goddess, the names of Vaśya and Unmāda follow in sequence; know that Kāmas reside in those very places—now hear their seed-syllables. || 2-46 ||
The seed-syllable of Parā, the middle Bāṇa, and Vāgbhava, O Supreme Goddess; then the fourth Bāṇa and the seed-syllable of Strī, O Beloved, in due order. (2–47)
O Goddess, my beloved, hear these five names:
Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makaradhvaja, and Saṃjñaka. (2.48)
O Maheśānī, the fifth is proclaimed as Mīnaketu.
Having placed these [syllables], O Queen of the Gods, one should thereafter perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands.
Having repeated the root mantra twice, one should then place the Mātṛkā upon all the surfaces of the fingers according to the sequence of the six-limbed ritual.
O Goddess of gods, hear the Mātṛkā, which destroys sins through its ritual placement (nyāsa).
Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra, and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas). || 2-51 ||
O Goddess, the deities are the Mātṛkās; the seed-syllables are the collection of consonants, while the powers are the vowels. One should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Between *aṃ* and *āṃ* is the *ka*-group; between *iṃ* and *ī* is the *ca*-group;
between *uṃ* and *ūṃ* is the *ṭa*-group; and between *eṃ* and *aiṃ* is the *ta*-group. (2.53)
Oṃ au, in the middle, the labial class (pavarga) in sequence, O Supreme Goddess;
at the end of the anusvāra and visarga, the palatal (ya-varga) and dental (śa-varga) classes, together with their markers. || 2-54 ||

O Goddess, one should then assign the heart, the head, the crest, and the armor; thereafter, one should assign the eye and the weapon, ending with the syllable *ṅ*, according to the sequence of *namaḥ* and *svāhā*.
O Dear One, one should employ [the mantras] ending in *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*;
this six-limbed [mantra] of Mātṛkā is remembered as the remover of all sins. (2.56)
One should place the sixteen vowels upon the lotus of the throat with its sixteen petals;
one should place the twelve letters beginning with *ka* upon the twelve-petaled lotus of the heart.
One should place the ten [vowels] beginning with *ḍa* upon the ten-petaled lotus at the navel;
and one should place the six [vowels] beginning with *ba* upon the six-petaled [lotus] situated at the genitals. (2.58)
One should place the four classes [of consonants] upon the support (ādhāra), and the four vowels upon the four petals;
O Dear One, one should install the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa* upon the two-petalled lotus situated between the eyebrows.
Having thus performed the internal placement of the *mātṛkā*, one should perform the placement on all the limbs:
on the head, around the mouth, and on the eyes and ears, O Pārvatī.
O Dear One, one should place [the mantras] in sequence upon the nose, cheeks, lips, teeth, head, and face, as well as at the ends and joints of the pair of hands and feet.
O Goddess, one should then sequentially place the letters beginning with *ya*, together with their respective elements, upon the two sides, the back, the navel, and the abdomen.
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituents (dhātavaḥ).
One should also install the vital self (prāṇātmā), the individual self (jīvātmā), and the supreme self (paramātmā).
In the heart, at the base of the arms, and likewise at the back of the neck, O beloved; in the armpits, at the edge of the chest, and likewise in the pair of hands and feet. (2.64)
O Goddess, one should sequentially place [the letters] pervading the belly and the face;
she who has the form of the fifty letters and is adorned by Kandarpa and the Moon.
Resembling pure crystal, adorned with pure silk,
and decorated with shimmering ornaments of pearls and diamonds, [she holds] a rosary and a water-pot.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Goddess, who bears a book and a boon-granting gesture, one should thereafter perform the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsa), O Mistress of the Gods.
O Dear One, one should perform the donning of the armor of the body with the three seed-syllables in sequence;
first, one should place them on the two hands—at the wrists, the palms, and the nails.
Having placed [the hands] on the right and left armpits, elbows, and palms,
one should likewise place them again on the right and left feet.
O Goddess, one should then place [the mantras] at the feet, the heart, and the genitals;
O Mistress of the Gods, one should place them upon these limbs according to the sequence of withdrawal.
O Supreme Goddess, know the Vidyā according to the very sequence of emanation; then, O Great Goddess, one should install that which is named and marked by the nine yonis.
Furthermore, [one should touch] the ears, the chin, the temples, and the region of the face; the eyes, the nose, the pair of arms, and the heart, O beloved.

Likewise, O Goddess, one should place [the hands] on the two elbows, the navel, the two knees, and the secret organ; then on the two feet, the private parts, the two sides, the heart, and the two breasts.
And one should place upon the throat that which is called the nine-yoni, consisting of the three seed-syllables;
O Goddess, one should perform the six-limbed rite by repeating [the mantra] twice in due order.
O Goddess, on the mountain-born [linga], one should again place the arrows and the Kāmas according to the count of three, two, one, ten, three, and two for the fingers. (2.75)

Having performed the pervasive placement [of the mantra] upon the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the root support (mūlādhāra) in due order by means of the root mantra, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of Bālā," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now begins the third chapter. The Lord said:
Having thus performed the ritual placement upon the body, one should then remain with a concentrated mind.
O Dear One, one should perform the rite of the inner sacrifice, which is directly composed of Brahman.

In the *mūlādhāra*, [one should contemplate] the Root-Vidyā, whose radiance is equal to ten million flashes of lightning, O Beloved, resembling ten million suns and as liquid as ten million moons. (3-2)
O Dear One, O lady of excellent countenance, that [energy] has the nature of a spider's thread, possesses three circles of bindus,
and arises through the innate descent of the upward power.
Through the firmness of the root power and by means of awakening the central seed-syllable, one should contemplate the Supreme Goddess, who is blissful with the mass of supreme bliss. || 3-4 ||
Having thus performed the internal sacrifice, one should perform the external worship;
there, seated facing the east, one should perform the drawing of the mandala.
On a clean site, in an auspicious place, one should write this unsurpassed yantra on a cloth.
One should draw straight lines from the northeast (īśāna) to the southeast (agni). || 3-6 ||
Drawing two lines from the northeast toward the southeast, the preceptor unites them at the western point; this is the supreme Śakti-line, O beloved.
This [maṇḍala] has the form of a triangle; upon it, one should draw two Śaktis. || 3-8 ||
O Supreme Goddess, one should draw a line like a measuring rod from the tip of the eastern power-line toward the corners of the wind and the rākṣasa (southwest).
Then, following the sequence of breaking the joints of those two powers,
draw the two lines from the corners toward their tips, making them extend forward.
This is the fire-maṇḍala, O Goddess praised by heroes, with its apex pointing east;
it is formed, O Beloved, by one fire and two śaktis. (3-11)
O Dear One, this sovereign wheel (cakrarāja), enriched by the splendor of the nine wombs (navayoni), generates all good fortune and bestows all sovereignty. (3-12)
It bestows all accomplishments, removes disease, and grants wealth; this [mandala], resembling the full moon, should be drawn outside [the central circle]. || 3-13 ||
One should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with its center as the ascendant, joined by eight knots;
these knots should be formed by enclosing [the syllables] between two *praṇavas*.
O lady of excellent vows, the knots should be known as vajras by means of the *praṇavas* alone;
having drawn the eight tridents, one should then draw a square, O beloved. (3.15)
O beautiful woman, having written the syllables *ha* and *sauḥ* within a triangle, [which is] richly adorned with the beauty of four gates and likewise brings joy to all; || 3-16 ||
One should write the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) in the center, and the sixteen vowels, O Goddess of Gods, in pairs within the eight corners without distinction.
Having inscribed [the letters] on the eight petals, starting from the west and proceeding clockwise,
O Supreme Goddess, [one should place] the groups of consonants beginning with 'ka' at the locations of the knots.
O Dear One, one should write the first syllable of each of the seven names in sequence;
the letter *kṣa* should be joined as the eighth, and the remaining letters should be arranged in their proper order.
Having inscribed [the syllables] on the points of the tridents in the sequence starting from the west, O Supreme Goddess, one should then draw a circle of the Mātṛkā outside of that. || 3-20 ||

O Great Goddess, having inscribed the Mātṛkā, which is the source of all desires, within a square [mandala], one should worship the yantra upon a plate made of gold, silver, or other materials. (3.21)
Or on copper, or on a mirror, or on a slate, or even on one produced from Kashmir;
or on the ground smeared with sandalwood and other substances, or again with saffron. (3.22)
Or else, it may be fashioned on birch bark using vermilion powder, musk, saffron, and camphor,
or with substances such as yellow orpiment, or even mentally.
Having inscribed the yantra with a pen of gold and jewels, O Goddess of Gods, one should worship it with the materials for ritual offerings, which accomplishes all purposes and goals.
Having meditated upon her, who causes the expansion of Brahman, according to the very sequence of the family tradition (kulāgama),
[extending] from the root-center to the aperture of Brahma, as slender as a lotus fiber.
For the pacification of inauspiciousness, one should meditate upon her, radiant as the rising sun, with a mass of hair dark as wandering bees and adorned with pure flowers. (3.26)
She was resplendent with a line of pearls shimmering like bees at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
adorned with a tilaka of radiant jewels upon her pearl-like brow, and blazing with a crown.
She is enriched with pure pearls and jewels, wears a crown adorned with a crescent moon,
and is graced by a row of three eyes that have the dark luster of wandering bees.
She is supreme, adorned with great jeweled earrings as radiant as the sun,
and embellished with necklaces of pearls shimmering with the luster of Venus.
She was resplendent with the shimmering luster of pearls from her necklaces and armlets,
and she shone in garments as white as the spray of the Ganges and camphor.
She was resplendent with vine-like arms resembling śrīkhaṇḍa creepers,
adorned with shining ornaments such as bracelets, and radiant with the luster of her wrists.
She is resplendent with hands like young sprouts of coral, and she possesses a girdle of diamonds, lapis lazuli, and pearls, which is of stainless luster. || 3.32 ||
Adorned with sprouting feet shaped like the petals of a red lotus,
and decorated with pearl anklets resembling a garland of stars.
With one left hand she holds a book, and with the other,
O fair-faced one, she bestows the gesture of fearlessness upon the practitioner.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, who bestows subjugation, good fortune, and eloquence, holding a rosary and the gesture of granting boons with her two right hands. || 3.35 ||
O beloved, one should meditate upon her who is as white as milk, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and who is serene.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Meditation on Tripureśvarī," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"The circle of the wheel has been described, but no worship was mentioned for that mandala."
O Supreme Lord, it has been told; I wish to hear it according to its true nature.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the supreme *pūjā-maṇḍala*;
first, one should perform the worship of the seat (*pīṭha-pūjā*), which is adorned by the Sun and the Goddess. (4.2)
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā; after that, Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, Kubjikā, Ṛddhi, and Viṣaghnikā. || 4-3 ||
Dūtarī and Ānandā—O Goddess, these are the twelve Śaktis. [They hold] a moon-bright parasol shimmering with pearls and pure gems. || 4-4 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, [he held] two chowries white as the waves of the Ganges, and a casket for betel-leaf shining with the brilliance of the nine gems. || 4-5 ||
With garlands of *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *śatapatra*, and other flowers;
likewise, a vessel made of jewels filled [with them], as well as one filled with ornaments. || 4-6 ||
A casket and a pair of fans, adorned with the nine precious gems,
as well as [ornaments] with the feathers of a blue-necked peacock and graced with usīra grass.
A golden cup enriched with camphor and musk and adorned with powdered saffron; a comb resplendent with diamonds. || 4-8 ||
O Supreme Goddess, the Śaktis established upon the sacred seats (pīṭhas) bear a collyrium stick and a casket filled with moonlight.
O fair-faced one, the [deities] numbering as many as the sun (twelve) are to be worshipped all around, starting from the east;
having worshipped them, O Goddess of gods, one should worship the Pretasiṃhāsana in the center.
It has the expansive form of jewel-gold, radiant, pure, and imperishable;
it is the actual bestower of liberation upon the five corpses as a seat—of this there is no doubt.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Maheśāna, tell me of the five *pretas* and their cause; how is it, O All-pervading Lord, that they are lifeless, indestructible, and of eternal form? || 4-12 ||
"In that which is devoid of a living soul, there is only destruction; how then have they attained permanence?
The Lord said:
"O blessed lady, you have asked well: how is it that [the body] consists of the five *pretas*? (4.13)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these five, O lady of beautiful hips, are always present as the immobile *pretas*. (4.14)
O Supreme Goddess, the motherhood of Brahmā consists of the form of emanation;
this is to be understood as the power of Vāmā, for Brahmā is a preta—of this there is no doubt. (4.15)
Śiva has no instrument; however, Śakti always possesses an instrument.
O beloved, the creation of hundreds of thousands of cosmic eggs arises from Śakti.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, Śiva is undoubtedly a ghost;
likewise, there is no protection in Viṣṇu, for it is the supreme Śivā who protects. (4-17)
O Great Goddess, she who is named Jyeṣṭhā is indeed declared to be Viṣṇu;
but Viṣṇu, O Goddess, is motionless, while Vaiṣṇavī is that which effects pervasion. || 4-18 ||
Protecting the entire world, she is the author of the drama of the universe;
for this very reason, O Great Goddess, Viṣṇu is a ghost, without a doubt.
Rudra, however, is the supreme reality; indeed, Śiva is utterly immovable.
But Rudra’s power, O fair-faced one, which has the nature of darkness, is that which devours.
The three qualities do not exist in Śiva; the Supreme Lord transcends all qualities.
O fair-faced one, how can there be a devouring of that which is quality-less and immovable?
The power of Rudra devours the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving;
O beloved, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are always beyond the guṇas.
O Supreme Goddess, they possess attributes and consist of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
O Varārohā, even Īśvara is always a great preta, O sinless one.
O Śivā, why would there be immobility, and how could there be lordship, O beloved? (4.23)
He who is himself the agent and the remover is the Lord; it cannot be otherwise.
O beautiful one, the pair of being the agent and the remover does not exist in the Immutable.
Sovereignty belongs to Śivā alone, and not to Śiva, O Supreme Goddess;
for this very reason, the Great Preta is the Lord, and not otherwise. (4.25)
O beloved, Sadāśiva is the great preta, entirely motionless;
he is the unmanifest supreme bliss, and Śivā consists of the bliss of Brahman. || 4-26 ||
O Goddess Śivā, without Śakti, no latent impression (vāsanā) arises;
for this very reason, O Great Mistress, one should worship the seat of the Great Preta.

The seed-syllable situated in the center of the wheel is the great state of Sadāśiva; ending with the letter *ṅa* and seated upon the lotus-throne of the preta, it is declared to be the Heart-mantra. (4.28)
O Supreme Goddess, this mantra of the Mahāsana consists of the syllable *kalā*;
having worshipped the Lion Throne (Siṃhāsana), perform the invocation thereafter. (4.29)

O Supreme Goddess, by means of the sequence of the channels (nāḍīs), one should [perceive] the digit of consciousness (saṃvitkalā) residing from the root center up to the aperture of Brahmā—the omniscient Kulasundarī. || 4.30 ||
Having invoked her into the center of the wheel, one should satisfy Kulasundarī;
O sinless one, I shall now describe to you the mudrās for invocation and the other rites.
One should turn the upward-facing añjali downwards; this becomes the invocation (āvāhanī). But when it is reversed, it is considered the installation (sthāpanī).
The two fists joined together constitute the form of *saṃnidhāpana*;
with the thumbs tucked inside the fists, it constitutes the form of *saṃnirodhana*.
When the two index fingers of this very same mudrā are straightened and rotated clockwise and counter-clockwise, it is the Avaguṇṭhanī mudrā.
O Goddess, the most excellent practitioner should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs of the Goddess using the limb-mantras;
this is the mudrā called Saṃkalīkaraṇa, which effects pervasion.
O Dear One, having joined the two hands together, one should bind the two thumbs;
this is the mudrā known as Paramīkaraṇa, which follows thereafter. || 4-36 ||
After turning the two hands back, join the pair of the index and middle fingers;
then, join the pair of the little and ring fingers together.
This is declared to be the Dhenu-mudrā; it effects the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*). After displaying these common mudrās, thereafter— || 4-38 ||
O Beloved, she displays the mudrās of granting boons and fearlessness;
O Beloved, her left hand should be made level like a book.
This mudrā, called the Book, bestows the play of speech;
it is formed by joining the index finger and the thumb on the right hand, O Pārvatī.
This mudrā, known as the *akṣamālā*, indeed becomes the *jñānamudrā* when one forms a fist with the right hand and the index finger takes the form of a goad. (4.41)
The great mudrā called the Hook (Aṅkuśa) becomes the attractor of the three worlds;
O Goddess, the pair of index fingers [joined] on the left shoulder takes the form of a chain. (4.42)
The noose mudrā is fully described as capable of attracting the three worlds;
O beloved, make your hand like a bow held in the grasp.
This is declared to be the mudrā of the bow, positioned in the left hand;
O beloved, make your hand like a bow with an arrow held in it. (4.44)
This is declared to be the Bāṇamudrā, which cuts down the host of enemies.
O Goddess, one should form the palm of the left hand into the shape of a skull.
O Queen of the Gods, the *kapāla-mudrā* always brings bliss to the Goddess.
When the two hands are formed into the shape of a lotus, that becomes the *kamala-mudrā*. (4.46)
This is the lotus mudrā, considered to bring about the increase of prosperity;
thus, O fair-faced one, having displayed these weapon-mudrās.
Accompanied by his wife, he should always offer perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth; he should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with ritual services and ornaments.
One should fashion the limbs of absorption within the body and properly satisfy Śivā;
O Dear One, the worship of the retinue follows after first performing the form of the limbs.
After the worship of the Guru, one should first worship the Guru; one should worship one's own Guru in the middle of the eastern womb and the central womb. || 4-50 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, one should display the Viśeṣamudrā for the sake of all accomplishments.
Having properly crossed the two hands, the index fingers and the little fingers should be made equal. (4-51)
One should place the middle fingers together, and immediately after that, join them at their centers; O Goddess, the ring fingers and the little fingers should likewise remain as they naturally are.
By joining the two thumbs in the shape of a vulva, one should form this gesture;
it is called the Yoni-mudrā, the supreme mother of the three worlds.
This very [power], when cast into the heart, becomes the agitator of the three worlds;
the Supreme Goddess, when situated in the mouth, is named the Dissolver of the Three Worlds.
The Great Goddess, stationed between the eyebrows, becomes the attractor of the three worlds.
Stationed on the forehead, O Great Goddess, she is the subjugator of the three worlds.
O Goddess, residing in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), you cause the three worlds to go mad;
one should display the seal consisting of the five mudrās and the yoni-mudrā.
Then, O Adrijā, one should worship the enclosure of the six limbs all around the pedestal, in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, in the center, and in the cardinal directions. (4-57)
Having worshipped Rati in the eastern corner and Prīti in the northern corner,
one should then worship Manobhavā in the southern corner and thereafter worship the arrows.
O Goddess, one should worship two arrows in the north, two in the southern direction, and one at the front; thus, O Adrijā, one should worship the five arrows in due order.
O Goddess, one should likewise worship the five arrows;
O Goddess, [one should worship] Anaṅgakusumā and likewise Anaṅgādimēkhalā.
Anaṅgamadanā, and after her Anaṅgamadanāturā;
O Goddess, [worship] Subhagā, Pañcamī, Bhagā, and Bhagasapīṇī. || 4-61 ||
O Great Goddess, one should worship Bhagamālā in the sequence starting from the east within the eight wombs; O Mistress of the Gods, one should then worship Brāhmī and the others.
O fair-faced one, by means of the division into pairs of pairs, [one should worship] on the eight-petaled [lotus]:
Asitāṅga and Brāhmī, Ruru and Māheśvarī, O beloved. (4–63)
Caṇḍa and Kaumārikā, Krodha and the deity Vaiṣṇava; Unmatta and Vārāhī, and Māhendrī and Kapālin.
One should worship Bhīṣaṇa, Cāmuṇḍā, and Saṃhāra as the eighth;
one should fully honor the pairs, O Great Goddess Mahālakṣmī.
Then, one should worship the eight sacred seats (pīṭhas) according to the sequence starting from the west:
Kāmarūpa, Malaya, and likewise Kaulagiri.
Kulāntaka, Cauhāra, and beyond that Jālandhara;
Uḍḍīyāna and Devakūṭa—this is the sequence of the eight sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 4-67 ||
O Goddess, having worshipped at the locations of the knots in the order starting from the west,
[one should worship] the trident all around within the circular maṇḍala of the Mātṛkās.
O Dear One, the ten Bhairavas are to be worshipped starting from the west in successive order:
Hetuka, Vetāla, and Tripurāntaka in their midst.
Agnijihva, Kālānta, and likewise Kapālin; Ekapāda of fearsome form, Malaya, and Hāṭakeśvara.
O Great Goddess, having worshipped the ten Bhairavas in the circle of the Mothers, O Maheśānī, one should worship the eight guardians of the world within the square. (4.71)
One should worship Indra, Agni, Yama, the goddess, Rākṣasa, and likewise Varuṇa,
Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna, according to the sequence starting from the east.
One should worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu in ascending and descending order respectively; having uttered the seed-syllable "Vāṃ," one should write "Salutation to Baṭuka."
Having uttered the seed-syllable *yāṃ*, one should likewise say "Homage to the Yoginīs";
having uttered the seed-syllable *kṣāṃ*, one should indeed say "Homage to Kṣetrapāla."
Having uttered the seed-syllable *gāṃ*, one should then write *gaṇapati*;
ending with *ṅe* and followed by *namaḥ*, [the deities] are to be worshipped in sequence in the directions starting from the west.
O Parameśvarī, in the square, one should worship in the intermediate directions according to the sequence beginning with Vāyu, as will be described, O Maheśvarī. (4–76)
O beloved, one should worship the Vasus, the twelve Ādityas, and the Rudras, as well as all the beings, in their proper order, O lady of excellent hips. (4.77)
Having performed the preliminary worship, one should worship the Goddess with the ritual offerings;
when one worships the Cakra, one should be facing north.
Then, O Goddess, the northern direction becomes established as the eastern direction;
when one worships the wheel facing the western direction, O Goddess, [the directions are thus transposed]. (4.79)
Then, O Goddess, the western direction is established as the eastern direction;
at that time, O Goddess, one should worship the Cakra facing the southern direction.
Then, O Goddess, the southern direction is indeed the eastern direction; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Sequence of Worship of Tripureśvarī," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The Śrī Devī said:
The sequence of the Kumārīs has been declared, together with the mudrās and the postures (āsanas).
Now, O Lord, I wish to hear about the offering of oblations and other such rites.
Īśvara said:
One should properly diffuse the incense while remembering the root mantra in one's heart:
"This excellent incense, rich in fragrance, is produced from the essence of the trees. (5-2)
"May this incense, to be smelled by all the gods, be accepted. With this mantra, O Goddess, one should offer incense to the Goddess. (5.3)
A brilliantly shining great lamp, dispelling darkness everywhere—may this lamp, a light both internal and external, be accepted. (5.4)
In the same way, O Supreme Goddess, this lamp-mantra is at the end of the Vidyā;
then one should perform the Ārātrika rite for the sake of accomplishing all purposes. (5.5)
O Supreme Goddess, one should draw a beautiful eight-petaled lotus with saffron upon a vessel made of gold, silver, or bell-metal.
Having prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru) in the form of the moon, one should place a single lamp upon its center at the head of Śivā, and eight lamps upon the eight petals.
[He should offer] vessels filled with ghee, adorned with seals and accompanied by goblets, containing sugar and made from barley, wheat, mung beans, and other grains. || 5-8 ||
Having consecrated it with the mantra of Ratneśvarī, O Great Goddess, thereafter, O lady of excellent complexion, one should inscribe the Śrī-bīja and the Parā-bīja. (5–9)
O Dear One, the letters *ga*, *sa*, and *au* are followed by *ma*, *pa*, *na*, and *indra* (the letter *i*) in sequence;
they are joined with the left ear (*vāmakarṇa*), that is, the letter *u*, and adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*. (5–10)
These five seed-syllables, O beautiful one, are the five jewels;
when the first seed-syllable is reversed, this becomes the nine-syllable Ratneśī.
Having worshipped with the root mantra, one should then perform the ārātrika rite;
lifting the vessel, one should move it repeatedly up to the head. (5.12)
O Great Goddess, one should then perform the lustration rite nine times:
"O Goddess, Navātmanī, who are joined with all the wheels and the mistresses of the wheels! (5.13)
"O Goddess, accept this *ārātīka* for my success.
O Goddess, the mantra for the *nīrājana* rite is revealed at the end of the *vidyā*. (5-14)
O Maheśānī, the Cakramudrā is established as follows:
one should insert the right little finger into the hollow of the thumb of the left hand. (5-15)
One should place the right thumb into the hollow of the left little finger;
O Goddess, this is declared to be the *cakramudrā* formed by the two hands joined together.
Having performed the rite for the removal of obstacles, one should then present the food offering (*naivedya*).
[He is] like pure crystal, with a radiance equal to the rays of the moon. (5.17)
O Goddess, O Beloved, the rice cooked from fine grains is lovely and soft; it is made delicious, O Beloved, by being enriched with asafoetida, cumin, black pepper, and fresh ginger. || 5-18 ||
The *vaṭaka* has the appearance of saffron, and the *pāyasa* resembles gold;
it is deep and beautiful with milk, and filled with an abundance of sugar. || 5-19 ||
O beloved, pancakes made from birch bark mixed with the ghee of a tawny cow, O Goddess, should be served; likewise, soup made from mung beans mixed with sugar. || 5.20 ||
The wise one should prepare various kinds of drinks and many types of side dishes—food endowed with such flavors—as an offering. || 5.21 ||
Or one may offer to Tripurā a form mentally constructed,
such as divine, well-prepared *paramānna* (milk-rice) placed within a golden vessel.
"O Supreme Goddess, accept [this offering] fivefold and endowed with the six flavors.
At the end of the Vidyā, O Supreme Sovereign, the mantra for the food offering (naivedya) has thus been proclaimed. || 5.23 ||
Then, O Goddess, having performed the circumambulatory sprinkling, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
O Mistress of the Gods, one should offer five oblations in sequence with the root mantra.
One should know this to be the essential nature of the five oblations: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.

Six oblations with the six-limbed [mantra] are declared to be this daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma). Having performed the rite of the daily fire-sacrifice, one should perform the rite of offering the bali-oblation. || 5-26 ||
O Dear One, O Goddess, there is likewise a quartet of mandalas in due order in the northeast, the southeast, the southwest, and the northwest.
O Goddess, one should draw a triangle and a void (bindu) all around the Śrīcakra;
having worshipped it with the previous mantras along with Baṭuka and the others, O Adrijā.
Come, come, O Goddess! O End of Sons! O End of Vaṭukas! And then, O Lord! O End of Kapila! O Mass of Matted Hair! O Radiant One! And O Three-eyed One! || 5-29 ||
And Jvālāmukha, at the very end, destroy, destroy all obstacles! Accept the offering together with all ritual services! [Dvidhāpada]. || 5-30 ||
The mantra of Baṭuka is declared to be accompanied by the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess, Svāhā).
O Goddess, O beloved, the offering for Baṭuka is performed according to this rite.
Whether above the cosmic egg, or in heaven,
or in the expanse of the sky, or on the surface of the earth, or in the partless [reality],
or in the netherworld, or in fire, or in water—
Wherever two winds may be situated, || 5-32 ||

May the goddesses, who have established their feet upon the sacred fields, seats, and secondary seats, and who are ever pleased by incense, lamps, and other offerings, grant us constant auspiciousness.
May those who are worshipped by the lords of heroes protect [us] according to the ritual of the bali offering.
At the end of this, O Maheśānī, one should write the seed-syllable *yām*, followed by *yoginībhyaḥ svāhā*; at the end of all the syllables, one should inscribe the word *yoginī*.
Having written the armor (*kavaca*) and the weapon (*astra*), one should again write the *vahnijāyā* (the wife of fire, i.e., the *svāhā* mantra).
O Goddess, with this mantra, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the Yoginīs. (5.35)
O Dear One, one should write the syllable *kṣa* conjoined with the six long vowels;
one should also write the place, the field, the station, the protector, and the incense, lamps, and so forth. (5.36)
Having drawn the figure of Bali together with his attendants, one should then say, "Take, take!
O beautiful one, this is the mantra of Kṣetrapāla, joined with the Vahni-jāyā (Svāhā). || 5.37 ||
O Goddess, the bali offering for the Kṣetrapāla is prescribed with this mantra;
having written "gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ" three times, one should then write Gaṇapati ending in the suffix "-ḍa".
At the end of *vara*, at the end of *varada*, and at the end of *sarva*, one should write *jana*;
having uttered "bring [him] under my control" (*me vaśam ānaya*), one should write all the subordinate terms.
Having uttered "cārānte sahitaṃ" and "baliṃ gṛhṇa," followed by two words ending in vowels and joined with the wife of fire (svāhā),
this mantra for Gaṇeśa should offer the bali.
One should offer the bali-offering to Baṭuka with the left thumb and ring finger;
one should join the index and ring fingers above the middle finger.
The offering for the Yoginīs should be made with the left hand in the shape of a vulva;
one should join the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger in the form of a vulva. (5.42)
First, having formed the left fist, extend the index finger straight;
O Goddess, by this mudrā, the offering to the Kṣetrapāla shall be accomplished.
Likewise, one should make the middle finger of the fist straight like a staff;
this is the Gajatuṇḍā Mahāmudrā, which serves as an offering to Gaṇeśa.
Alternatively, one should draw a single maṇḍala on the left side;
right there, one should perform the offering of the bali for the sake of accomplishing all aims.
Having gratified the Guru and the deity with the auspicious principles of self-knowledge,
one should, being filled with bliss, accomplish all rites.
By this rite, O Goddess, one should worship the Supreme Goddess,
who is elevated upon five lion-thrones and whose nature is supreme bliss.

One should always meditate upon the Citkalā, bound by five lion-thrones; O Dear One, one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform the fire-oblation with a tenth part of that amount.
One should likewise perform the libation (tarpaṇa), and one shall become possessed of all good fortune.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of Tripureśvarī," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The venerable Goddess said:
How is that supreme Tripurā seated upon the five lion-thrones?
Tell me, O Great Lord, how the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) comes to be.
Īśvara said:
Just as Śrī Tripurā is Bālā, so too is Tripurabhairavī; she is named Saṃpatpradā (Bestower of Prosperity). Listen to [her mantra], O you of pure mind. (6.2)
Śiva and Candra situated in Vahni; immediately after that, the Vāgbhava [bīja];
likewise, O Goddess, the Kāmarāja [bīja] followed by Śiva and Candra. (6.3)
O beloved, listen to the third [syllable], which is enriched by the Earth-seed (la), the End (ha), and Fire (ra).
O Great Goddess, one should join Śiva (ha) and Fire (ra) with the Seed of Power (hrīṃ). || 6-4 ||
O beloved, listen now to the specific [instruction] regarding that which resides in the fire within the ether;
O Supreme Goddess, having abandoned the emission of the maiden consisting of the bindu. || 6-5 ||
O beloved, the goddess Tripurā Bhairavī is the bestower of great prosperity;
a vidyā equal to this is difficult to find in the three worlds. (6.6)
She is composed of the bliss of Brahman and is the direct bestower of universal sovereignty;
O beloved, I shall now describe her meditation, which grants great prosperity. (6–7)
She possesses the radiance of a thousand copper-colored suns, with the tips of her matted locks shimmering like the moon;
her crown is adorned with jewels and variegated pearls that gleam with splendor.
Adorned with a garland of severed heads dripping with the mire of blood,
she is enriched by the beauty of her three eyes and possesses a face like the full moon.
She was radiant with strings of pearls, her full and elevated breasts were firm,
her waist was marked by the three folds, and she was adorned with various ornaments.
Clad in red garments, her form intoxicated with youth;
she holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right.
One should constantly remember her who is ever intent on bestowing boons and who grants great prosperity;
all rites such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship should be performed just as they are for Kumārī, O lady of excellent vows. || 6-12 ||
The goddess Tripurā Bhairavī is endowed with five lion-thrones.
First listen, O Mistress of the Gods, to what occurred when Brahmā was the creator of the universe. (6–13)
O Goddess of gods, O Supreme Sovereign, although he was then devoid of consciousness, by propitiating the deity of Tripura, he became the creator of the creation.
O beloved, having propitiated that Brahmā through great austerity,
he became this Śakra, the king of the gods and guardian of the eastern quarter.
Then Tripurā, seated upon the eastern lion-throne, became gracious.
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain [the mantra] as it resides upon the eastern lion-throne. (6-16)
Having uttered the seed-syllable Vāgbhava, [one should join] it with the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa);
"Sakalā Bhuvaneśānī" is the second seed-syllable extracted.

O Maheśānī, the Vidyā consisting of the *jīva*, the *prāṇa*, situated in fire (*vahni*), adorned with the vowel of Śakra (*śakra-svara*), and enriched by the *visarga*, is the Mother of the Three Worlds. (6.18)
The Goddess who deludes the three worlds, whose essence is the consciousness of the Supreme Brahman, is named Caitanyabhairavī; she is pure awareness within the undivided Śiva. (6.19)
She possesses the brilliance of a thousand rising suns, is adorned with various ornaments,
has a beautiful crescent moon shining upon her crown, and is clothed in red garments.
She is the eternal one, holding a noose and a goad, with a skull-cup in her left hand;
she is richly adorned with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and possesses full, elevated, and firm breasts.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess seated upon the eastern lion-throne;
one should perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) twice, characterized by [the visualization of] all the limbs.
O Goddess, I shall describe her yantra, which deludes the three worlds;
it consists of a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-petaled lotus, O lady of beautiful countenance.
One should draw a mandala that is square and has four gates;
there, one should invoke the Great Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, as before.
Thereafter, one should display the mudrās and perform the worship of the retinue;
O Goddess, the first enclosure consists of the six limbs as before. || 6.25 ||
Then, O Supreme Goddess, Rati and the others are to be worshipped as before;
O fair-faced one, Vāsanta is in front and Kāmadeva is on the left.
O Daughter of the Mountain, one should likewise place the bow in the southern corner and the arrows as before;
[and one should worship] Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, and Kākinī. (6.27)
O Goddess, one should worship Śākinī and Hākinī starting from the western direction in sequence;
Anaṅgakusumā is the principal [deity] on the eight petals as before.

Furthermore, one should worship the cuckoo (*parabhṛt*) and the crane (*sārasa*), as well as those called the parrot (*śuka*) and the cloud (*megha*), and also the side-glances (*apāṅga*), the play of the eyebrows (*bhrūvilāsa*), the gestures (*hāva*), and the expressions (*bhāva*). || 6.29 ||
One should worship the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, in their proper sequence.
O Goddess, praised by heroes, this has been declared for the eastern lion-throne. (6.30)
And Kāmeśvarī, among the Rudrās, is seated upon the eastern lion-throne;
the two seed-syllables of this very Vidyā have been proclaimed. (6.31)
At the end of that, O Supreme Goddess, [are the words] *nityaklinne madadrave*. O Supreme Sovereign, the third [syllable] of this very [mantra] belongs to the Rudras.
O Goddess, the worship, meditation, and so forth for Caitanyā are as before;
however, O sinless one, there is a specific distinction regarding the triangle, which I shall now tell you. (6.33)
Following the sequence of the front corners, one should worship Nityā, Klinnā, and Madadravā for the sake of attaining all siddhis, after [the worship] of the six-limbed enclosure.
In this very manner, one should worship the supreme goddess Tripurā Bhairavī, who is seated upon the eastern lion-throne.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eastern Lion Throne," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
The Lord said: "O Goddess of gods, having worshipped this Mahātripurabhairavī..."
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, Pālaka remained motionless due to his state as a preta.
O Goddess with eyes like blue lotuses, by means of that meditation, Śakti herself became his steadfast state of a preta under the guise of yogic sleep.
Having propitiated her with the Aghora face, O Goddess, Mahāviṣṇu conquered Tripura, which caused terror to the three worlds. (7.3)
Then, O Supreme Goddess, you were seated maturely upon the throne to the right;
I shall now declare her mantra, which cuts asunder the burden of enemies. (7.4)

O Dear One, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] consists of Śiva (SA), Candra (I), and Mādana (KA) at the end, followed by Vānta (HA) conjoined with Vahni (RA), pierced by Śakti (I), and enriched by Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā. || 7-5 ||
That indeed is the Kāmarāja [seed-syllable] of Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity;
it is also the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva seated upon the lion-throne.
O Great Goddess, who is capable of describing this Vidyā?
I shall now proclaim its meditation, which cuts through the burden of enemies. (7.7)
She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, has the moon as her crest-jewel, and is three-eyed;
she is beautiful with various ornaments and is the destroyer of all enemies.
Adorned with a garland of heads from which blood flows, and clad in red garments;
[holding] a trident, a hand-drum, a sword, and a shield.
O Goddess, she stands upon the throne of Śiva, holding in due order the Pināka bow and arrows, a pair of noose and goad, a book, and a rosary of beads.
Having meditated thus, O Great Goddess, one should begin the worship of the maṇḍala—a triangle, a circle, and a lotus with eight petals within a circle. (7–11)
The square [mandala], provided with a seat upon the earth—this is the Tripurayantrikā.
O fair-eyed one, it consists of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Kālī. (7–12)
One should worship Kalāḍhyā and Balāḍhyā, and Vikariṇī in the southwest;
likewise, one should invoke Balapramathinī and Sarvabhūtāntakarī.
Likewise, having recited the *damanī* mantra accompanied by the word *manonmanī*, one should worship the seat (*pīṭha*) in this manner and then worship the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*).
The form of the Aghora-vidyā indeed cuts away great sins.
O Goddess, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] is in Aghora, while Bhuvaneśvarī is in Ghora.

Having written "ghoraghoratarebhyaś ca" (O you who are most terrible among the terrible), O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should write the pair of seed-syllables of the Goddess for all [the mantras] belonging to all the Śivas. || 7.16 ||
One should perform the *namaste'stu* salutation at the feet and write "hsau" in the form of Rudra;
O Dear One, this [deity] to be meditated upon has been described as consisting of thirty-three syllables. (7–17)
O Goddess, with this mantra a wise person should worship the Lion Throne;
thereafter, one should perform the invocation and so forth, followed by the sequential worship.
O Goddess, first there is the repetition of the limbs; with a double repetition, the worship of the limbs is performed.
Having worshipped the triad beginning with Rati, one should likewise worship those beginning with Anaṅga.
Having worshipped the pair beginning with Brāhmī on the eight petals, [one should worship] the Mātṛkās on the earth-mandala,
and the world-protectors along with their weapons, O Supreme Goddess.
One should worship Rudrabhairavī, who is seated upon the second lion-throne.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Worship of Rudrabhairavī," in the second throne of the *Nityātantra*, the illustrious *Jñānārṇava*.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The Lord said: In the west is the goddess Bhairavī, the supreme sovereign consisting of six peaks.
O Goddess, by whose manifestation that Śiva becomes capable of creation and withdrawal.
O Goddess of the Gods, having extracted [the letters] from the pair of seeds of Ḍākinī and Rākinī, one should join them with the seeds of Lākinī and Kākinī, [which are] the Moon and the Sun. (8.2)
One should write the third seed-syllable, joined with the first letter *ai* and adorned with the second vowel *ī*, combined with the fourth vowel *u*. (8.3)
The third [syllable], O Daughter of the Mountain, is pervaded by the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā;
this is the Vidyā, O Great Goddess, which abides upon the Lion Throne of Rudra. (8-4)
I shall now describe her meditation, which cuts through all beings—
[the meditation on] the Goddess who has the luster of the rising sun and resembles the hibiscus flower.
She is beautiful with a garland of severed heads, her garment is like the rising sun,
and her full, elevated breasts have the shape of golden jars.
Holding a noose, a goad, a book, and a rosary—
having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess with mental offerings.
O Supreme Goddess, having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating [the mantra] twice,
O lady of excellent hips, one should draw the triangle and its enclosure for her *yantra*.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus on the outside with petals equal in number to those of the sun;
thus one should draw the mandala as a square with four gates. (8–9)
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should worship the six-limbed enclosure as before;
O Goddess, one should worship the triad beginning with Rati within the triangle.
The Ḍākinīs and others [are placed] in the hexagon; thereafter, on the eight petals, the pair beginning with Brāhmī; thereafter, on the twelve petals, [the deities] beginning with Ravi. (8–11)

O Beloved, one should worship the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) of Bālā, beginning with Vāmā, within the square; and [one should worship] the world-protectors (lokapāla) together with their weapons, O Supreme Goddess.
In this manner, one should perform the rite of worship for the attainment of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation;
by this very procedure, one should worship Bhairavī, who is known as the Eternal (Nityā).
She is the eternal bestower of all good fortune and the giver of universal sovereignty.
[One should contemplate] the six syllables of this very Vidyā as they stand in their proper sequence.
"O mature woman, speak [this] which is the opposite; this is the knowledge that bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess, she is called Nityā Bhairavī, the destroyer of the burden of enemies. (8-15)
One should perform all [the rites], such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship, for this [deity] as previously described. || 8-16 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Western Lion Throne," in the glorious Jñānārṇava, the Nityā Tantra.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, to the Great Vidyā which bestows the desired fruits when contemplated.
By the mere knowledge of which one becomes the sovereign of the world.
O Goddess of the Gods, the first [syllable] is Vāgbhava, beginning with *haṃsa*; at the end of *hasa* is the second seed-syllable, which is the Earth-seed (*bhū-bīja*), Bhuvaneśānī. (9-2)
O Maheśānī, the third seed-syllable is extracted as Śiva and Candra, adorned with the vowel of Indra (Śakra) and pervaded by Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā. (9.3)
O Maheśānī, this is the Vidyā Bhuvaneśvarabhairavī; O Deveśī, it is distinguished by the central seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels. (9.4)
Having duly assigned the six limbs [of the mantra], one should meditate upon the four-armed Goddess,
who resembles the hibiscus flower and has the luster of the pomegranate blossom.
She has the crescent moon in her matted locks, possesses three eyes, and wears red garments;
she is beautiful with various ornaments and has full, high, and firm breasts. || 9.6 ||
One should meditate upon the auspicious goddess holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
having thus visualized her, one should worship the goddess and perform the extraction of the yantra as before.
O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped the throne of Caitanyabhairavī as if it were a yantra, one should perform the worship of her retinue. || 9-8 ||
O Goddess, one should worship the six-limbed enclosure as before;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should worship Rati and the others within the triangle.
O beautiful one, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are to be worshipped right there;
likewise, the Ḍākinīs and others are to be worshipped on the eight petals thereafter. (9–10)

Then one should worship Anaṅgakusumā and the others, followed by the pair beginning with Brāhmī; then, upon the orb of the earth, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the attendants beginning with Baṭuka. || 9–11 ||
One should worship the sixty-four Yoginīs, O Goddess adored by the gods; for, O Supreme Sovereign, Kubera is the companion of Sadāśiva. || 9-12 ||
By means of that very [mantra], this goddess was propitiated; therefore, she became the Queen of Kings (Rājarāja).
By that same [mantra], the Vidyā Gaurī, who bestows white (auspicious) fruits, was propitiated.
She is named Annapūrṇeśvarī, the bestower of all prosperity upon the virtuous.
O Goddess, by means of this vidyā, Kubera became the lord of wealth. || 9-14 ||
Among all the world-protectors, there is an abundance of wealth, jewels, and so forth; likewise, by her grace, there is a constant abundance of food in that place. (9-15)
O Daughter of the Mountain, the Great Goddess Annapūrṇā is the manifest cow of plenty;
I shall proclaim her mantra, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments. (9-16)
One should write the syllable Tāra (Om), Bhuvaneśānī, the Śrībīja, and the Kāmarāja;
at the end of the word "hṛt" (heart), one should write the syllables "bhagavati" and the word "māheśvari. (9-17)
This twenty-syllable vidyā consists of "Aṇṇapūrṇe" and "agnijāyā.
There is no vidyā like this on earth that bestows such accomplishments (siddhi). || 9-18 ||
O Maheśānī, the six limbs [are assigned] by means of [the letters] differentiated by the six long vowels, following the placement of the meters (chandaḥ). || 9-19 ||
The seer of this mantra is Brahmā, its meter is Paṅkti, O fair-faced one;
the deity is proclaimed to be the Goddess Annapūrṇeśvarī. (9-20)
The seed-syllable is Bhuvaneśānī, and the Śrī-bīja is said to be the Śakti;
the Kīlaka is Kāmarāja, which follows the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 9-21 ||
Again, one by one, and once more one; two, four, four, four, and likewise two—these are the steps, O Pārvatī. (9.22)
O Goddess of gods, one should place the nine syllables at the nine gates; O lady of beautiful countenance, they should again be placed upon them from the head down to the anus.
One should place the nine steps from the anus up to the *brahmarandhra*, sequentially in the *brahmarandhra*, the mouth, the heart, and the *mūlādhāra*. (9.24)
Having placed the four seed-syllables, one should place the others in the remaining positions;
then, O Goddess, having placed the *golaka* according to the rule, O Beloved.
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and draw the worship mandala; first a triangle, then a four-petaled lotus, and after that an eight-petaled one. || 9-26 ||
One should draw the circle of the earth with its petals and four gates;
one should worship the goddesses of the pedestal all around the lion throne.

On the lion-throne to the right, the presiding goddesses of the sacred seats (pīṭhanāyikāḥ) have been described; O Supreme Goddess, one should worship those very goddesses, beginning with Vāmā, upon the seat.
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā; Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalātmikā. (9-29)
The ninth [is] Parameśānī; having invoked the Goddess who is situated near the lion-throne, one should worship her while remaining composed and performing meditation. (9.30)
She has the luster of the color of molten gold, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament;
her crown is radiant with the light of the nine jewels, and she is reddish like saffron.
Clad in variegated garments, with intoxicating eyes and three faces, her full, high, and firm breasts were shaped like golden jars. || 9.32 ||
White as the luster of cow’s milk, five-faced and three-eyed,
with a serene countenance, peaceful, and adorned by his blue throat.
Seeing him dancing with great joy, adorned with shimmering serpents as his ornaments, white as a kunda flower, she became filled with supreme bliss.
She has eyes that rise and quiver with joy, and her hips are adorned with a girdle;
she is eternally devoted to the giving of food and is graced by both the Earth and the Goddess of Prosperity.
Having meditated thus, O Goddess, one should perform the sacrifice; one should worship the enclosure of the six limbs.
The worship of the limbs is performed in the intermediate directions—namely, the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, and the center—as well as in the cardinal directions.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the worship of the triangle; [the mantra is] the Tāra, the Prāsāda-bīja, and then "Hṛcchivāya. (9.37)
O Goddess, one should worship with this seven-syllabled great vidyā;
O Sovereign of the Gods, [one should worship] the dancing Īśvara at the tip of the triangle.
Having first uttered the word "Oṃ namaḥ," then the word for the Blessed One, then for the one in the form of a boar, and likewise for the Lord of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ. || 9.39 ||
"Give me [the word] *ṅenta*, [the word] *bhūpati*, and [the phrase] 'give it to me'—this mantra of Varāha, O fair-faced one, is joined with the wife of Agni (Svāhā). || 9.40 ||
O Goddess, with this vidyā one should worship in the left corner;
having first uttered the word "oṃ namaḥ," one should write "Nārāyaṇa" ending in the letter Ṅ.
One should worship Nārāyaṇa in the southeast corner in due order;
O Supreme Goddess, Bhū and Śrī are to be worshipped on the left and right sides.
O Goddess, O sinless one, I shall tell you this by means of a single mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance! Grant me food, O Mistress of Food! (9.43)
In the same way, having written this name, cause it to be offered thereafter;
then, one should employ the mantra by enclosing [the name] with the consort of Fire (svāhā). || 9.44 ||
With the syllable *glauṃ* or with the goddess Rāmā, one should worship in sequence on the left and right petals;
thereafter, on the four-petaled lotus, they are to be worshipped in order starting from the west.
One should worship Tārā with Paravidyā, Bhuvaneśī with her own self, Kamalā with Ramā, and Subhagā with Kāma, O auspicious lady. (9.46)
O Maheśānī, on the eight petals, starting from the west, are Brāhmī and the others;
O Supreme Goddess, on the sixteen-spoked wheel, they take the form of the lunar mandala. (9.47)
The sixteen digits (kalās) are indeed to be worshipped in sequence starting from the west:
Amṛtā, Mānasī, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Prīti, and likewise Rati.
Śrī, Hrī, Svadhā, Rātri, Jyotsnā, and likewise Haimavatī;
Chāyā, Paurṇamāsī, Nityā, and Amāvāsyā as the sixteenth.
The remaining syllables, ending with the word "annapūrṇā," are to be worshipped;
one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in order within the square.
Thus, for one who has properly worshipped [the deity] and gives food and gold according to their own capacity, she indeed makes them a king of kings and a lord of wealth. (9.51)
O Beloved, you are the bestower of accomplishment, the science of accomplishment, and the giver of food even to me;
now another distinction of Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī is being told.
O Goddess of gods, she herself is Sahādyā; at that time, she is Sakaleśvarī.
O Pārvatī, meditation, worship, and all such rites belong to her alone. (9.53)
O lady of excellent hips, know that in the northern direction is this lion-throne, where Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity, resides as Kauleśabhairavī.
O Pārvatī, that Bhairavī [is associated] with the three seed-syllables beginning with *hasa*;
this one, however, begins with *saha*, and her worship, meditation, and so forth are likewise [to be performed].
In the beginning and at the end of this very vidyā, the letter *ra* is excluded;
therefore, O Supreme Goddess, she is known by the name Sakalabhairavī. (9.56)
O Dear One, Bhairavī bestows prosperity; she consists of the five lion-thrones and is Mahātripurabhairavī, whose nature is meditation, worship, and so forth.

O Dear One, having uttered the *siṃhāsana* consisting of *hasrīṃ*, which is to be honored through the vidyās of the four traditions (*caturāmnāya*), [one should utter] that which consists of *hhrīm*, O Daughter of the Mountain. (9.58)

The Śakti mantra is proclaimed as the four seed-syllables ending with *sakala* and *hrīm*. With the addition of the *Śrī* seed-syllable and the third [seed-syllable] *kuru*, it becomes the Nityā of four syllables. (9.59)
This Vidyā named Unmanī bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is the Great Vidyā of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) as it is proclaimed in the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya).
Having uttered the seed-syllable Vāgbhava, [one says] "klinne," the seed-syllable of Kāma, "madadrave," "kule," "hasrau"—this is the Vidyā Bhoginī, O Dear One. (9.61)
This vidyā of the Southern Tradition is called the Western Tradition;
it consists of Vāgbhava, Parā, Śrī, and *hasakhaphrom*, O Dear One. (9.62)
Then, O Goddess, these five Praṇavas are remembered as having their bellies bound together;
having written them out separately, O Īśvarī, O Blessed Mother. (9.63)
The fourth is the *praṇava*, and likewise *hasakaphrom*, O Dear One;
then *kubjikā* and *hasrām*, *hasrīm*, and after that *hasrau*. (9.64)
One should write "Aghore," "Ghore," and "Aghoramukhi";
[then] "Hasrāṃ Hasrīṃ Kiṇi" twice, and "Vicce"—this is the thirty-two-syllable mantra. (9.65)
O Goddess, having encased [the mantra] with the previously mentioned *praṇavas*, one should meditate upon this Kubjikā, the Great Vidyā, the deity of the Western Tradition. (9.66)
Having uttered *khaphreṃ*, one should write the word *mahācaṇḍa*;
thereafter, the word *yogeśvarī*—this is the Vidyā of Kālikā, O Dear One. (9.67)
This is the knowledge of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), renowned by the name Kālī;
O Supreme Goddess, the Lion Throne is always to be worshipped with these [mantras].
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for the Siṃhāsana-vidyā," in the Śrīmajjñānārṇava, the Nityā-tantra.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
The venerable Goddess said:
"O God, you have revealed that Tripurā is of two kinds."
O Śaṅkara, reveal that which was spoken as being threefold.
Īśvara said: O sinless one, I shall describe to you that which is the supreme nature of Brahman, consisting of the threefold Nāda and Bindu, and composed of Śiva and Śakti.
O Supreme Goddess, she remains pervading the universe and Śiva;
she was previously described by means of the qualities—now hear that which consists of the nature of Śiva and Śakti.
The imperishable power is the Mātṛkā, beginning with the letter *ha* and ending with the letter *sa*.
O Supreme Goddess, the letter *ha* alone is said to be Śiva. (10.4)
Then, by virtue of being the first and last syllables, I am the soul of all;
O Goddess, everything that is expressed by the letters of the alphabet is I. (10.5)
The letter *ha*, O Supreme Goddess, is of the nature of the void, eternally imperishable;
the letter *sa*, being of the nature of power (*śakti*), is the supreme speech (*parāvāc*) and possesses the visarga. (10.6)
Since it is the cause of origination, it is designated as "power" (śakti);
O beautiful one, that yoga reveals the self by means of the word "I" (ahaṃ).
Through the union of the three drops, she is Mahātripurasundarī;
that Goddess exists in the form of sound (nāda), having the nature of the half-syllable *ha*.
O Supreme Goddess, since the letter *ha* is the very form of Śiva,
the Great Power (*mahāśakti*), whose nature is the half-form of the letter *ha*, constitutes his half-body.
For this very reason, O Goddess, Mahāvidyā, Mahātripurasundarī, the supreme sovereign, is called the eternal digit of consciousness (citkalā). (10.10)
O auspicious one, by the grace of the glorious Guru, he is endowed with the lineage of the tradition.
O Queen of the Gods, having risen at dawn and bowed to the Guru with his [own] names, || 10-11 ||
O Goddess, having performed the twilight ablutions and other rites, that best of men,
adorned with all the finery of ornaments and dressed in fine attire, [anointed himself] with camphor, saffron, and other perfumes.
His limbs radiant with highly precious sandalwood and other unguents, he was reddened by saffron;
he was enriched with ornaments of the nine gems and resplendent in crimson garments.
With his face colored by betel and his mind delighted by wine,
he arrived at the sacrificial hall, which was variegated with patterns of red lac.
Abounding with many kinds of incense, filled with heaps of flowers,
smeared with cow dung, and adorned with beautiful canopies of blossoms.
Having sat upon a seat that is pleasing to the mind, soft, and smooth, one should perform the extraction of the mantra for the sake of accomplishing all goals. (10.16)
Having uttered the first, Vāgbhava, and the second, Kāmarāja, the third belongs to Kumārī; she is Tripurā, the Supreme Goddess. (10–17)
O Supreme Goddess, the first Vidyā is Karaśuddhikarī;
O Great Goddess, the second is Kumārī, who is Tripureśī. (10.18)
Having set aside the first [mantra] of Tripureśī, one should surround Bhuvaneśī;
with this, one should offer the seat for the Self and perform the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga) for Tripureśī. || 10-19 ||
O Maheśānī, when Tripureśī is established with the three seed-syllables (bījas), know her, O Goddess, as Tripuravāsinī seated upon the throne of the wheel (cakrāsana). || 10-20 ||
O Maheśānī, Tripureśī is conjoined with Śiva and Candra in the Vāgbhava and Kāmarāja [Kūṭas], while in the third [Kūṭa] she is of the nature of Śiva. || 10-21 ||
O Dear One, this Śrī Tripurā, who resides upon the seat of all mantras, becomes established upon the seat of the Self when, O Daughter of the Mountain, the third [syllable] is omitted. (10.22)
Having superimposed the nature of the *bīja*, she is seated upon the throne of the accomplishment of the goal;
she is declared to be Tripurāmālinī—now hear of the Siddhā named Tripurā. (10.23)
Bhuvaneśī is endowed with Śrī, and Kumārī is likewise most excellent; she is declared to be Mūrtividya, while Māyā is Lakṣmī, established as the supreme. (10.24)
O Goddess, one who desires the accomplishment of Tripura should worship with this vidyā.
The two seed-syllables of Māyā and Lakṣmī are the first and second, while the third is the seed-syllable of Śakti. (10.25)
Tripurā and the others are the first [seven]; this eighth is proclaimed as Tryambikā.
Bhairavī, who bestows prosperity, resides within her third seed-syllable. (10.26)
O beautiful goddess, having placed the *bindu* there, one should project the creation;
O goddess honored by the gods, one should perform the invocation with this [mantra]. (10.27)
The science of the Mūlavidyā has been fully declared; it is Māyā, the supreme Lakṣmī, who abides there.
O Goddess, with this Vidyā one should worship her, the bestower of success in Tripura. (10.28)
O beautiful goddess, hear the root-mantra (mūlavidyā), served by all the scriptures, which consists of the Siddhāmbā, Āvāhinī, Mūrti, and Vidyā. || 10-29 ||
And [I bow] to the imperishable digit of consciousness (citkalā), O beloved, who is worshipped by all philosophical systems;
[the sequence is: Earth, Moon, Śiva, Māyā, Śakti, Kṛṣṇa, Adhvan, and Mādana. || 10-30 ||
The half-moon and the bindu—these nine syllables are called Meru;
the mantras of Mahātripurasundarī originate from Meru. (10.31)
O Goddess, from the letter *la* arises the earth, complete with its mountains, forests, and groves;
it is endowed with fifty sacred seats (*pīṭha*), consisting of all holy fords (*tīrtha*), and is supreme.
O Śivā, you consist of all the Gaṅgās and consist of all sacred sites;
from the letter *sa*, you take the form of the moon, the stars, the planets, and the zodiac signs.
From the letter *ha*, she is established as the sphere of space (*vyomamaṇḍala*) in the dialogue with Śiva;
from the letter *ī*, O beloved, she is Māyā, the creator of the universe, whose nature is the fourth state (*turya*).
From the letter *e* arises the Vaiṣṇavī energy, intent upon the protection of the universe;
from the letter *ra*, she is endowed with splendor, having the nature of supreme light. (10.35)
From the letter *ka* she is the granter of desires, possessing a form at will, the throbbing and imperishable one;
by means of the half-moon, O Goddess of gods, she is proclaimed as the source of the universe. (10.36)
By means of this [Bindu], which is the form of Śiva, the form of emptiness, and the witness, there is everywhere a pervasive and unwavering state of being through its very nature. (10.37)
Thus, O lady of excellent vows, by means of this Meru which is the form of the Supreme Brahman, the mantra of Tripurā is produced from these nine constituent syllables. (10.38)
Otherwise, there is no accomplishment whatsoever in the mantra of Śrī Tripurā; nor, O Mistress of the Gods, is the Śrīcakra anything other than the form of Meru—of this there is no doubt. (10.39)
The letter *la* is the seed-syllable of the earth; by it, the circle of the earth is expressed.
O auspicious lady, the letter *sa* is the moon, consisting of sixteen digits. (10.40)
Therefore, the sixteen-petaled [lotus] is indeed the letter Ha; Śiva is said to be that.
O auspicious lady, since the eight powers (aṣṭamūrti) are ever-present, it therefore becomes the eight-petaled [lotus]. (10.41)
The letter *ī* is Mahāmāyā, who protects the fourteen worlds; therefore, O Dear One, she is *Parā*, and her position shall be in the northeast corner.
Abiding in the eleventh station, Śakti gave birth to the three worlds;
she is renowned as Viśvayoni, and Viṣṇu is her tenfold form.
O Supreme Goddess, from the letter *ra*, the Cakra expands, pervading all;
