for the letter *ra* is the imperishable light that brings about the ten-cornered [Cakra].
Fire, endowed with the ten digits (kalās), has the form of a ten-cornered figure;
O Goddess, from the letter *ka* arises Madana, who possesses the nature of Śiva in eight forms.
Then she made the womb-subjugating [mudrā], which should be marked with the sign of the eightfold womb (vasuyoni).
Since the half-mora, in the form of sound (nāda), gives birth to the qualities (guṇas), for that reason... || 10-46 ||
The womb (yoni) is triangular in form; by means of the drop (bindu), it becomes the state of the Drop (baindava).
It is the very nature of Kāmeśvara, whose essential form is the universal manifestation.
O lady of excellent hips, the Śrīcakra originates from the ocean of the Śrīvidyā;
seated there facing the east, one should draw the king of cakras.
Then, on a level and even patch of ground, one should draw a wheel upon the earth using either powdered vermilion or saffron powder.
Straight-lined, pleasing to the eye, with joints that are even and straight;
or else [made] of gold and silver, copper, or many minerals. || 10-50 ||
Having fashioned a cloth-strip from white sandalwood and red sandalwood,
O beloved, one should place it upon the cloth and draw [the design] with a golden pen.
With *rocanā* and saffron, as well as musk, sandalwood, and camphor,
one should draw straight lines from the northeast (Īśāna) to the southeast (Agni).
Drawing two lines from the northeast toward the southeast, the preceptor unites them at the western point; this, O beloved, is the supreme Śakti-line.
This [form] has the shape of a triangle; upon it, one should draw two Śaktis. (10.54)
At the tip of the eastern power-line, one should draw a line like a measuring rod,
O Supreme Goddess, extending toward the corners of the wind and the rākṣasa (southwest).
Thereafter, by means of the sequence for breaking the joints of those two powers,
draw the two lines from the corners toward their tips and extend them forward.
This fire-maṇḍala, O Goddess praised by heroes, has its tip facing east;
there, O fair-faced one, listen now to how the three wheels arise. || 10-57 ||
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, having extended the eastern line from the two corners of Pūrvaśakti and Vahni, and likewise [the western line] from Paścima and Vahni. || 10.58 ||
O Goddess, having extended a line from the northwest and southwest corners toward the west,
one should join it according to the sequence for dividing the junctions.

The lines leading to the tip of the *yoni* in the eastern direction extend sequentially from south to north; likewise, the two lines situated in the fire [southeast] extend sequentially toward the western direction. || 10.60 ||
By joining the two corner tips, there shall likewise be a ten-cornered [figure];
in the same manner, O Goddess of the gods, there is a second ten-cornered [figure]. (10.61)
Having extended the lines starting from the northeast and southeast corners to the tips of the eastern womb, one should subsequently join them in sequence toward the western direction. || 10-62 ||

O beautiful one, having extended the lines from the northwest, southeast, and northeast, O Goddess, one should likewise join them at the western end, reaching toward the direction of Indra (the east). || 10-63 ||
In one place, O Goddess of the gods, one should join the beautiful [line] so that it touches the tip of the eastern corner, such that it becomes a six-cornered [figure]. (10.64)
O Goddess of the gods, having left the four corners starting from the southeast corner, O Goddess, one should manifest two lines in the middle within the ten-cornered space. || 10-65 ||
There are two divisions on the right side and likewise two on the northern side;
then, O Goddess, according to the sequence of the division of the joints of the hexagon.
By joining the *yoni* and the fire (*vahni*), the letter *śa* is always produced;
one should join the straight-lined stroke situated between the armpits. (10.67)
The straight-formed [mandala] is as follows: O Goddess, it arises as exceedingly beautiful;
facing forward with five śaktis at its tip, it has four fires in front. (10.68)
O fair-faced one, this is the eight-spoked wheel within the triangle of the bindu;
know that the center of the wheel likewise consists of a pair of ten-spoked wheels. (10.69)
O Goddess, marked with the womb of Śakra, it should be situated between the outer and the middle;
this wheel, O Maheśānī, increases all good fortune. (10.70)
O Goddess, it bestows all sovereignty and destroys all calamities;
it is filled with many jewels, rubies, and gold.
O Goddess, it bestows great liberation and brings about the great play of speech;
outside of this, O Great Mistress, is a circle resembling the full moon.
O Mīnākṣī, fashion that beautiful eight-petaled lotus;
then, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should draw a sixteen-petaled lotus.
Outside of that, O Goddess of the lords of gods, is the Nivṛtti [circle], endowed with the Mātṛkās;
it is square and provided with four gates, O Supreme Goddess.
Sixty-four million yoginīs of great power are established within this wheel; indeed, they honor the practitioner.
It is square, adorned with the letters of the Mātṛkā for the sake of attaining success,
fashioned with pearls and rubies, and graced by level ground.
Named Trailokyamohana, it bestows the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree;
it has sixteen spokes, the form of the lunar disc, and is the abode of all.
O auspicious one, it fulfills all desires, raining down a flow of nectar;
O Great Goddess, it has eight petals and resembles the Japā flower. || 10.78 ||
Named "The Agitator of All," it fulfills all desires;
O Great Goddess, these three constitute the Wheel of Emanation which bestows happiness.
Adorned by the presiding goddess of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), it bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
O Goddess, it has fourteen spokes and possesses the luster of a pomegranate flower.
O auspicious one, it bestows infinite fruit and grants all good fortune;
O beloved, it has ten spokes, shines like molten gold, and resembles vermilion. (10.81)
The second [wheel] is also eight-cornered, resembling a hibiscus flower; it is the wheel that accomplishes all aims and always grants whatever the mind desires. || 10.82 ||
O Auspicious One, this wheel which produces all protection consists of great gnosis;
O Great Mistress, these three constitute the wheel of maintenance, which bestows happiness. (10.83)
It is to be worshipped according to the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya) and bestows desired fruits;
it has eight corners, O beautiful lady, and is as red as the rays of the rising sun. || 10-84 ||
Resembling a ruby in appearance, it always removes all diseases;
it possesses the brilliance of a thousand rising suns and the luster of the bandhūka flower. (10.85)
O Īśvarī, the wheel bestows all accomplishments and is the abode of all;
it is the triangle, the cause of the origin of everything, and the perpetual granter of prosperity. (10.86)
O lady of excellent hips, the Bindu-cakra is supreme and consists of all-bliss;
O Supreme Goddess, it is the leader of the cakras and is composed of Sadāśiva. || 10-87 ||
This wheel, however, is of the nature of withdrawal, consisting eternally of Brahman;
it is to be cultivated according to the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), while the triad [of other wheels] is served by the Northern Tradition (Uttara).
In this wheel, O Goddess praised by heroes, the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) revolve;
on the petals of the wheel, O Mistress of the Gods, the path of words (padādhvan) is proclaimed.
Within the three junctions of the wheels, the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is established;
O sinless one, I shall now describe to you the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan), which has the form of the Mātṛkā.

Since the eight groups of the Mātṛkā are established in the directions in successive order, know that the sixteen-spoked [cakra] consists of the earth element, is composed of that, and is of the nature of the Kalās. (10.91)
The eight petals are marked with the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa*;
those from *ka* to *ḍha*, which are the letters of Indra, are situated in the corners of Indra (the east).
The ten syllables beginning with *ṇa* and ending with *bha* are in the first ten-spoked wheel;
those beginning with *ma* and ending with *śa* are in the second ten-spoked wheel as well. (10.93)
I shall describe to you the eight syllables in the eight corners and those in the triangle; the pair *ha* and *kṣa* located in the center, from *a* and *ka* up to the end of the triangle. (10.94)
O Goddess, the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) has been described as having the form of the seat of the Mātṛkās;
it is a wheel filled with the thirty-six principles, according to the root [tradition]. || 10.95 ||
The path of the principles (tattvādhvan) has been described, O Goddess, as having the nature of the principles, O fair-faced one;
the path of the kalās is elevated by the five lion-thrones through the authority of the wheel. || 10.96 ||
Accompanied by the Child (Bālā) and joined with Bhairavī, Mahātripurasundarī—Tripurā, enriched by Tryambikā—manifests fully upon attaining the Cakra. || 10.97 ||
This is declared to be the path of mantra, O sinless one, as a certainty at all times.
Thus, one should contemplate the Śrīcakra, which is pure through the six paths. (10.98)
O Goddess, when one raises the wheel while facing the northern direction,
then, O Goddess, that northern direction is said to be the eastern direction.
O Goddess of gods, when the practitioner facing the western direction raises the wheel, then the northeast becomes the southeast; of this there is no doubt. (10.100)
Then the western direction should be known as the eastern direction; of this there is no doubt.
Then the northwest, the southeast, the northeast, and the southwest shall likewise be so. (10.101)
When the practitioner facing south raises up the wheel,
then that direction is indeed the east, while the rakṣasa-corner is like the southeast.
This wheel, which has the form of Meru, has been extracted from the syllables of the Śrīvidyā;
it consists of all the Āgamas, O Goddess, as has been told, O you who are worshipped by heroes. (10.103)

Thus ends the exposition on the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), the knowledge of the four seats (*caturāsanavidyā*), the knowledge of the invocation (*vāhanavidyā*), the knowledge of the sacrifice (*yajana-vidyā*), the nature of the Meru, and the extraction of the *Śrīcakra* within the *Nityātantra*, the illustrious *Jñānārṇava*.
The tenth chapter, named [the Nāma], ends here. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The Lord said: "O Goddess of gods, Tripurā is now described by means of these syllables."
This nine-syllabled Great Meru is the spherical egg of Brahmā.
The square is the bow, the triangle is its cavity, and that is the mouth;
this mandala of the universe has been described to you as being without support. (11.2)
The letter *la* is a square, O Dear One, by virtue of being the seed-syllable of the Earth;
the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), however, is the bow, showering down flowing nectar.
Fire takes the form of a triangle; because of its triangular nature, the supreme Śivā is [also] a triangle.
The letter *e*, the letter *ra*, and the letter *ī*—these three constitute it. (11.4)
In the form of the transformation of Māyā, she has the form of resting upon a hexagon;
the letter *ha* is of the nature of space, and the *bindu* is in the circle of the face. (11.5)
O Supreme Goddess, desire exists everywhere in the form of will;
therefore, this Meru-maṇḍala is indeed explained as Mādana.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the seed-syllable (bīja) according to the Kāmeśvarī doctrine;
it is the most excellent seed-syllable of Kāmeśī, [consisting of] *sakalā* and *bhuvaneśāni*. (11.7)
By means of this, I shall explain all the sciences in detail;
O fair-eyed one, this is the syllable of power (Śakti), the fourth letter, situated in the middle of *kala*.
The Vāgbhava [bīja] consists of five syllables; then the Kāmarāja is spoken of, O fish-eyed one, beginning with Śiva and the Moon and ending with Śiva.
O blessed lady, this six-syllabled Kāmarāja is the deluder of all;
O lady of excellent limbs, it begins with the seed-syllable of Śakti and the Moon, and bestows all supernatural powers.
She whose form consists of four syllables is indeed the three-syllabled Tripurā, the Supreme (Parā).
O Goddess, you are composed of all sacred fords and possess the essential nature of all the gods. (11–11)
She is the supreme knowledge consisting of all scriptures, the supreme consciousness consisting of all yoga,
consisting of all sacrifices, and having the nature of all-knowing wisdom.
She is the embodiment of all the gods, visibly beautiful with every form of auspiciousness; O Goddess of Gods, by worshipping her, Kāma became beautiful in all his limbs.
O Goddess, Kāmarāja is she who is eternally of the nature of Brahman.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the glorious Jñānārṇava, the Nityātantra. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the gods, O handsome one, tell me the divisions of this [Tantra]."
By what means and by whom is this [nature] to be worshipped? Clarify this according to the truth.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the excellent one named Lopāmudrā, who is the fourth power (śakti) of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, O beautiful one. (12-2)
Having abandoned [the previous form], Lopāmudrā is revealed at the beginning, enriched by Śiva and the Moon;
this is the knowledge (vidyā) worshipped by Agastya, which causes the agitation of the three worlds. 12-3.
This vidyā is indeed worshipped by Kāmarāja; of this there is no doubt.
O auspicious lady, these two vidyās are difficult to obtain within the three worlds. (12.4)
O fair-faced one, I shall now declare the extraction of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, which resides between Śakti and Mādana, by means of the Vāgbhava [syllable]. (12.5)
The first part, Vāgbhava, should begin with Śiva; the second, Kāmarāja, should begin with Śivā;
and the third should begin with Candra—this is the Vidyā honored by Manu.
The first is Vāgbhava, O Goddess; the first is Candra, situated in the middle of Śiva.
Mādana is in Kāmarāja, while the Seed of Power (Śaktibīja) is accompanied by Ānana. (12.7)
This vidyā, propitiated by Candra, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
know that it begins with *vāgbhava* (HĀSA) and has *śiva* (KHPHREM) in its middle. (12.8)
Mādana is in Kāmarāja; now hear the third, O Pārvatī. It begins with Hasa and is the seed-syllable of Śakti, worshipped by Kubera. || 12-9 ||
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the third seed-syllable of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, preceded by the Śakti-bīja, is the Vidyā honored by Agastya. (12.10)
By the power of Lopāmudrā, she is the manifest embodiment of Brahman itself. Obeisance to the Vāgbhava syllable of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja; abandon Mādana. (12-11)
Having joined the Moon (candra) in that very place, and thereafter [placing it] in Kāmarāja, one should abandon the Moon and place it at the beginning; this is the Vidyā worshipped by Nandin.
O Goddess, having abandoned the third earth of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, place it there below the moon, situated at the throat of Śakti.
O Maheśvarī, this Vidyā, known as Lopāmudrā—the second [Vidyā]—is the one propitiated by Indra and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (12–14)
In the Kāmarāja [bīja], having omitted Bhṛgu, Śiva goes to the third [bīja] of Śakra;
this is the Vidyā, O Varārohe, known as Tripurā, worshipped by the Sun. (12–15)
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the Śāṅkarī [vidyā] consisting of four kūṭas;
having written the second [form], Lopāmudrā, O you who are worshipped by the gods. (12–16)
Having written that same [syllable] again, situated in the fourth and fifth [positions],
one should worship Bhuvaneśānī by uttering her name once.
The great vidyā of four peaks was worshipped by Śaṅkara;
O Goddess, having written Lopāmudrā immediately after that, || 12–18 ||
The Nandikeśvara-vidyā is indeed the six-peaked Vaiṣṇavī;
formerly, O Goddess, the supreme Niṣkūṭā was worshipped by Durvāsas.
O fair-faced one, O Maheśvarī, divide into two parts that Vidyā known as Kāmarāja which resides within the *srikūṭas* in the worlds, O Mistress of the Worlds. (12-20)
Devoid of the *bindu* and devoid of the *nāda*, she is worshipped by Durvāsas;
O Goddess praised by the gods, [she is worshipped] with these twelve mantras. || 12-21 ||
O Goddess, she who abides at the *dvādaśānta* is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman; she is the Queen of all sciences, served by all the sacred traditions (*āmnāyas*). (12-22)
She is praised by all the great mantras of the scriptures, worshipped by the gods, eternally bowed to by all yogas, and is exclusively of the nature of Brahman. (12.23)
Thus, the Great Vidyā is threefold; this very Vidyā is Tripurasundarī, the Great Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign of the Three Peaks. (12.24)
It cannot be described at all by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others,
nor can that fourth state ever be expressed by speech, mind, or intellect.
The Goddess, who is directly composed of Brahman and whose nature consists of sixteen syllables—by remembering her with the mind alone, O Great Sovereign, I am indeed Sadāśiva. (12.26)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Vidyā of Tripurasundarī," in the glorious Jñānārṇava, the Nityā Tantra. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
The venerable Goddess said:
"The sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā is directly the Supreme Brahman itself."
Speak, O Mahādeva, if I am dear to you.
All [the others] are said to have three peaks, while Śāṅkarī has four;
Vaiṣṇavī indeed has six peaks—thus the Mantras have been described, O All-pervading Lord. (13-2)
All these sciences have been heard by me in their threefold form;
now I desire to hear the Śrīvidyā consisting of sixteen syllables.
Īśvara said:
O lady of excellent hips, O beloved, by virtue of deceit, one who knows the mantra of Śrīvidyā becomes food for the Yoginīs, according to the command of the venerable Guru. (13.4)
O Dear One, one should not give this sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā to anyone—not even to a king who bestows his kingdom, nor to a son who gives up his own life. || 13-5 ||
O auspicious Pārvatī, everything may indeed be given—even universal sovereignty—and even one's own head along with one's life; yet the sixteen-syllable mantra must never be given away.
O Dear One, all those mantras that are being uttered are vocal;
the reality devoid of utterance is the sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā.
O Varārohā, even though she is of the same caste, the reality is directly without syllables;
O Śivā, it is just as a flower enjoyed by a bee becomes fit for use. || 13-8 ||
Likewise, although the reality is indeed beyond syllables, it is joined with syllables;
the utterance of mantras is just like writing upon water. (13.9)
The sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā is the knowledge that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
without the instruction of a guru, it certainly results in a curse. (13-10)
The end of Candra and the end of Vāruṇa, together with Śakra and the others, are distinct;
[the syllable] Vāmākṣi is enriched by Bindu and Nāda, consisting of the digits (kalā) of Viśvamātṛ. || 13-11 ||
Listen, O Goddess, it is being declared in four ways: because you are captivating, you are said to be difficult to find on earth. (13.12)
O Goddess, one should join [the mantra] at the beginning of the Vidyā; she is manifest as the very nature of the waking state.
Arising is the waking state, which is constant awareness and the turning away of the mind. (13.13)
The four *kalās* are established in the waking state;
the waking state is said to consist of the quality of *sattva*, being solely of the nature of *śakti*.
The *Sakalā* consists of three peaks (*trikūṭā*), while the *Bhedās* indeed consist of five peaks (*pañcakūṭā*).
The *Vaiṣṇavī* should have eight peaks (*vasukūṭā*), and the *Śāṅkarī* should have six peaks (*ṣaṭkūṭā*). (13–15)
This second type would be difficult to find in the three worlds;
for she alone, O Queen of the Gods, is the form of Śiva due to her all-pervasiveness. (13–16)
She is motionless among all beings, eternally consisting of Śiva, and supreme;
for she is directly the form of deep sleep and the very form of Brahman, O beloved. (13–17)
Death, forgetfulness, fainting, and sleep shrouded by darkness—these are to be known as the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), which is the very form of Śiva. (13–18)
In its state of absolute isolation, the waking state is Śāmbhavī, consisting of five peaks;
at the end of deep sleep and the beginning of waking, the dream state consists of passion (rajas). (13–19)
Longing, delusion, anxiety, and recollection regarding sense objects—these four constituent parts (kalās) are prescribed for the state of dream. || 13–20 ||
She whose form is Śiva, whose form is Śakti, the Great Goddess of Tripura;
O Goddess, adorned by the beginning of the Vedas, she is eternally composed of Śiva and Śakti. || 13-21 ||
O Supreme Goddess, the seven divisions are complete with six peaks;
Vaiṣṇavī consists of nine peaks, and Śāṅkarī consists of seven peaks.
Merely by remembering this, a hundred elephant-gifts are accomplished.
The threefold division has been told; now hear, O beloved, about the fourth Vidyā. (13–23)
By the mere realization of which Brahman is directly perceived, without a doubt;
she whose characteristic is pure luminosity, manifesting from deep sleep until the end of the waking state.
Having reached the state where all conditions have ceased, the Fourth (turyā) is indeed the supreme digit;
it is declared to be liberated from both existence and non-existence, and transcending the qualities (guṇa). || 13-25 ||

Dispassion, the desire for liberation, tranquility and the like, and a pure mind—these are the qualities of the fourth state (turyā), which consists in the discernment between the real and the unreal. || 13-26 ||
O Bhadrā, having indeed written the first two seed-syllables in reverse order, O Supreme Goddess, one should then extract the others. (13-27)
O lady of excellent hips, one should worship her as Antarmukhā, Kumārī, and Tripureśvarī,
enshrined within these five seed-syllables.
O Supreme Goddess, this sixteen-syllable Vidyā consists of six peaks;
indeed, O Auspicious One, it comprises all three peaks and possesses sixteen phonemes. (13–29)
The mantra of Viṣṇu consists of nineteen syllables, while that of Śiva consists of seventeen syllables;
even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues, [one could not fully describe its power].
This sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā cannot be described at all;
who is capable of praising the fifth [mantra] of Viṣṇu? || 13-31 ||
Since the supreme reality is beyond syllables, it is the ultimate cause therein;
for those who have become silent behold it, and thus the Middle Way becomes the Middle. (13.32)
In the form of the knowledge of Brahman, she bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O Goddess of gods, by a single utterance, [she grants] ten million Vājapeya sacrifices.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and circumambulations of the earth, as well as pilgrimages to holy sites such as Kāśī, numbering three and a half crores; || 13-34 ||
They do not equal it, O Goddess of the gods; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Girijā, what more need be said? By a single utterance, one attains even absolute Brahman. || 13-35 ||
This sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā must never be disclosed;
it should be guarded by you, O auspicious Pārvatī, like your own private parts.
Whatever action arises from the union of Śiva and Śakti, that is not an object of knowledge; likewise is the venerable sixteen-syllabled Vidyā.
He who, having seen the sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā, recites it without the instruction of a guru, shall be devoured by the hosts of Yoginīs. (13.38)
Obtained through the grace of the glorious Guru, she bestows universal sovereignty;
she grants the good fortune of the three worlds and abundant prosperity. (13.39)
This is the manifest beauty of Love himself, capable of attracting the three worlds;
it is like a river of nectar that bestows skill in the art of language.
Bestowing a multitude of arts endowed with good fortune and prosperity,
she grants absorption in the Supreme Brahman and supreme renown.
O Goddess, by whose power the fourteen worlds exist, may that Veda-mother rescue those who are submerged in the ocean of conceptual proliferation.
O Supreme Goddess, you existed as their causal form;
through your compassionate glance, the power of the four oceans may arise. || 13-43 ||
The mother of ten million cosmic eggs, the bestower of great liberation;
from her, O beloved, the great mantras issue forth like sparks of fire. (13.44)
From the presence of Vahni (Fire), many sciences indeed arose;
likewise, they were produced from Vāgbhava, and therefore it is called Vāgbhava.
Likewise, O auspicious one, the letters of the Mātṛkā have issued forth in sequence from the Vāgbhava [bīja].
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, O Beloved, she consists of the Śabdabrahman. || 13-46 ||
Protecting the entire world, she is likewise the Enchantress of the Three Worlds;
she is the Art of Love who deludes [all], and she is the progenitress of sons and grandsons.
Everything is strung together as male and female in the Kāmasūtra;
at that time, she is endowed with good fortune and dwells in the abode of Brahmā. || 13-48 ||
She is said to be the source of the universe, profound with the pride of her own auspiciousness;
she is established in the fourfold corpus of speech and is the subduer of the three worlds.
She is directly composed of consciousness, embodied as knowledge, the bestower of enjoyment,
the eternal giver of great prosperity, and directly the embodiment of the imperishable.
O auspicious one, I have declared to you this supreme Śrīvidyā consisting of sixteen syllables;
O beloved, it must be guarded like a treasure from thieves. (13-51)
It should not be given to just anyone; it should be given to one who has bestowed life, who is pure, who is a true devotee, and who is dearer than one's own life.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Sixteenfold Vidyā," in the illustrious Jñānārṇava, the Nityā Tantra.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
The venerable Goddess said:
"The wheel-mandala has been described, but no worship was mentioned for that mandala."
O Supreme Lord, you have spoken; I wish to hear this according to its true nature.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed procedure for worship;
first, there should be the installation of its constituent parts, the ritual jars, and so forth. (14.2)
O wise one, listen to the procedure for that in brief, according to the rules:
having first drawn a square mandala with water on the left side.
O Goddess of gods, with her broad hands she should worship there the beautiful support (ādhāra) made of gold, silver, copper, or other materials, O Beloved. (14.4)
One should worship the ten *kalās* in the form of a circle of fire:
Dhūmra, Nīlavarṇā, Kapilā, and Visphuliṅginī. (14–5)
Jvālā, Haimavatī, Kavyavāhinī, Havyavāhinī, Raudrī, Saṃkaṣiṇī, and Vaiśvānarakalā—these are the ten. (14.6)
One should worship the Fire-god there together with these digits (kalās).
O beautiful one, one should place a pitcher made of gold or some other material there.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the form of the Sun with its digits:
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Vibudhā, and likewise Bodhinī. (14–8)
Kalinī, Śoṣaṇī, Vāruṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, as well as Māyā, Viśvāvatī, Hemā, Prabhā, and Saurakalā—these are they. || 14-9 ||
Having filled the jar with water, O lotus-eyed one, one should contemplate the nectar situated therein as being manifest in the form of the moon. (14.10)
Having worshipped the lunar disc with its digits, O Goddess adored by the gods:
Amṛtā, Mānasī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Prīti, and likewise Rati. (14.11)
Śrī, Hrī, Svadhā, Rātri, Jyotsnā, and likewise Haimavatī;
Chāyā, Pūrṇimā, Nityā, and Amāvāsyā as the sixteenth.
Having worshipped with these mantras, one should sacrifice to Ānandabhairava.
Śiva, Candra, and Mātṛkānta; Kalā, Indra, Ambu, and Vahni. (14–13)
The wind (ya) joined with the left ear (u) and marked with a dot (bindu)—having uttered this seed-syllable, one likewise [worships] Ānandabhairava. (14–14)
One should again write the seed-syllable joined with the *śikhā-mantra*;
omitting the first [letter], one should place the moon and join the left eye to the ear. (14–15)
To Surādevī, then *vauṣaṭ*; this is Ānandabhairavī.
Having worshipped the Moon with this, the jar becomes worthy of worship. (14–16)
Having prepared a square mandala on the left side,
one should place a tripod there and set a conch shell upon it.
Having filled [the vessel] with pure water, one should worship it together with the causal [mantras].
Having worshipped the six limbs there, O Dear One, this is the general *arghya*.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the characteristics of the special arghya (offering water).
[One should draw] a square mandala between oneself and the Śrīcakra. || 14–19 ||
With water from the general *arghya* vessel, the preceptor,
kneeling on the ground with his hands held upward and joined in a hollow, should place the *yantrikā* there.
The mandala consists of a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and a square; having visualized the fire there, one should then worship that which consists of the yantra.
O Supreme Goddess, as before, one should worship Trikūṭā situated in the center;
O Supreme Sovereign, one should worship her there within the triangle with each of the kūṭas individually.
Repeating [the mantra] twice, one should worship the six limbs within the six triangles;
O Dear One, one should also place a vessel made of gold or silver.
Then, having worshipped the form of the Sun, one should draw the yantra as before;
one should worship it according to the sequence as before, using all the syllables both individually and collectively.
Having especially filled the moon with liquid, O beloved, one should draw the yantra as before, with Trikūṭā situated in the center of the yantra. (14–25)

O Dear One, one should contemplate that triangle, which is worshipped by the three peaks (Trikūṭas), enriched with the three lines beginning with 'A', 'Ka', and 'Tha', and supreme, with 'Ha' and 'Kṣa' within it. (14–26)
One should worship the six limbs by repeating [the mantra] twice within the six triangles; one should worship oneself with the Haṃsa-mantra and with bliss. (14–27)
There, one should worship the root-vidyā consisting of sixteen syllables and then recite it.
Having offered incense and a lamp, the wise practitioner should then pay homage and present the arghya offering.
One should display the mudrās therein; one becomes manifest as the embodiment of Brahman.
One should then sprinkle oneself and the materials for worship with that [water].
One should perform sprinkling everywhere so that everything becomes permeated with Brahman;
having worshipped oneself, one should then cause all beings to tremble with awe.
Having recited the root-mantra weapon (*mūlavidyāstra*) and performed the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with the *sphoṭana* sounds and so forth, one should,
O Goddess, bow down facing that [mantra] and perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) as before.

Then one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth, as well as the armor (*saṃnāha*) upon the body; [one should recite] the mantra that purifies the hands from the middle fingers to the palms.
O beloved, this purification of the hands is performed by repeating [the mantra] twice over the fingers;
thereafter, O beloved, one should offer the seat for oneself and then the seat for the Cakra.
One should bestow the seat of all mantras and worship the seat of the sādhya and the siddha;
having placed the four [seats] upon the feet, the calves, the knees, and the private parts. || 14-34 ||
And the six limbs of the maiden Īśānī of Asripura are as before.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the supreme nyāsa of Śrīvidyā.
One should contemplate the complete Vidyā, possessing a ruddy luster, within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
one should remember that sixteen-syllabled mantra as it drips with nectar, bestowing great good fortune. (14.36)
Then, O beloved, one should rotate the Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī [mudrā] at the region of the left shoulder,
and place the Ripujihvāgrahā mudrā at the base of the foot.

Thinking, "I am the creator of the three worlds," one should place [the seed-syllable] upon the forehead mark (tilaka); having meditated thus, one should place it in its entirety within the mouth as a surrounding encirclement.
Then, once again, one should perform the placement upon the entire body with the complete [mantra], extending it pervasively throughout the body. (14.39)
At the conclusion of the pervasive [deities], having placed the *yonimudrā* in the mouth and paid homage, this placement (*nyāsa*), which is the full form of Śrīvidyā, increases good fortune. (14.40)
O Beloved, having rotated the ring finger around the crown of the head,
O Goddess, one should cast it into the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and then place it upon the wrist.
On the forehead, the wise one should place the ring finger while recollecting the sixteen-syllable mantra;
O Goddess of the Gods, this placement is called "Enchantment" (saṃmohana) and it causes agitation.
One should meditate on the three worlds as crimson and remember Śrīvidyā within the mind;
[one should contemplate her] at the feet, the calves, the knees, the hips, the navel, and the back.
At the navel, on both sides, as well as at the two breasts, the two shoulders, O Pārvatī, at the two ears, the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the mouth, and the eyes. || 14.44 ||
Then, at the region of the throat, by means of the two hands in succession,
this great placement (mahānyāsa) of withdrawal is performed with the sixteen seed-syllables in order.
By means of the sixteen-syllable nyāsa of Śrīvidyā, one becomes the Lord of the Universe (Īśvara).
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should perform the nyāsa of the Mātṛkā up to the end of the creation, as previously described.
One should perform the placement of Vaśinī Mātṛkā, whose nature consists of the letters of the alphabet, who is endowed with the eight groups of consonants,
and who is accompanied by the eight seed-syllables.

At the end of the vowels, one should write the seed-syllable consisting of the letter after *va* (the letter *śa*) joined with the letter after *pha* (the letter *ha*), accompanied by the earth (*la*), adorned with the ornament of the left ear (*u*), and marked with the bindu and nāda, O Dear One. (14.48)
O Goddess of virtuous vows, one should worship Vaśinī, the deity of speech.
O Maheśānī, at the end of the *ka*-group [consonants] is the supreme seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Kāmeśī. (14.49)
Having uttered "Merūddhata," one should then worship Vāgdevī.
Furthermore, at the end of the consonant groups (varga), there is the letter *dhā* followed by *lā*, conjoined with the fourth vowel (*ū*) and the syllable *kṣmā*. || 14-50 ||
Immediately after that, one should worship Modinī, the deity of speech.
O Maheśvarī, at the end of the ṭa-group [of consonants], air and water are situated in the mouth. || 14-51 ||
[The mantra] enriched with the moon (bindu) on the left ear (the letter *i*), [is] Vimalā, the sovereign of speech.
[The mantra] ending with the *tavarga* (the letter *j*), preceded by the earth (the letter *la*), adorned with the left eye (the letter *ī*). || 14-52 ||
One should worship the seed-syllable marked with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and the goddess of speech (Sarasvatī) who is reddish in hue;
[and] at the end of the labial class (*pavarga*), one should worship the sky, moon, earth, water, fire, and so forth.
Joined with the vowel *u* and marked by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, one should worship Jayinī, the goddess of speech, O you who are honored by heroes. (14.54)

At the end of the *ya*-group, one should worship the goddess who is the sovereign of all speech, joined with the letter *ja*, the time of destruction (*kāla*), the letter *ra*, and the wind (*vāyu*), and enriched by the syllable *ūm*.
One should worship Kaulinī Speech, which is the fourth [vowel] situated in the letter *kṣa*, adorned with the seed-syllable, and pervaded by the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā.

O Maheśānī, one should place [the letters] at the end of the *śa*-group for the sake of accomplishing all aims, in the locations of the head, forehead, between the eyebrows, throat, heart, and navel. (14.57)
O Dear One, one should place the goddesses in sequence upon the support up to the Vyūhaka;
thereafter, one should perform the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) by which [the body] becomes the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 14-58 ||
Śiva himself, in the form of Virāṭ and consisting of the phonemes, is manifestly present; of this there is no doubt.
Gaṇeśa is the first assignment (nyāsa), the destroyer of all obstacles. (14–59)
Resembling the rising sun, with the faces of elephants and three eyes,
they hold nooses, goads, gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in their hands, and are endowed with spears.
Having meditated thus, O Goddess, one should then perform the placement [of the mantras] according to the *mātṛkā*-nyāsa.
Likewise, Vighneśvara and Śrī, as well as Vighnarāja with Hrī. (14.61)
Vināyaka, as well as Tuṣṭi, Śāntiyukta, and Śivottama; Vighnakṛt accompanied by Puṣṭi, Vighnahṛt, and Sarasvatī. (14.62)
Vighnarāja, endowed with delight, the wise leader of the Gaṇas; Ekadanta, Kānti, Dvidanta, and he who is joined with Kāminī. || 14-63 ||
Gajavaktra, Mohinī, and Nirañjanajaṭa; then Kapardin, Tīvrā, and Dīrghavaktra, O beloved. || 14-64 ||
Then Jvālinī, followed by Nandā and Saṃkarṣaṇī; then Vṛṣadhvaja, together with Śubhagā and Gaṇanātha. || 14.65 ||
Kāmarūpiṇikā is followed by Gajendra, who is joined with Śubhrā;
Śūrpakarṇa is accompanied by Jayinī, and the three-eyed one is conjoined with Satyā. (14.66)
Then Lambodara, Vighneśī, she whose nature is the Great Sound (Mahānāda), the fourfold form, the bestower of desires, and thereafter she who is united with Sadāśiva. || 14-67 ||
Then there was one named Madavihvala, followed by Āma and Dāvikaṭa; likewise Durmukha, Ghūrṇa, Sumukha, and Bhūtimat. || 14.68 ||
Pramoda, likewise Bhūmi, Ekapāda, as well as Satī; Dvijihva conjoined with Ramā, and Śūra, and also Mānuṣī. || 14-69 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, Makaradhvaja was followed by Vīra, as well as Ṣaṇmukha, Vikarṇā, Varada, and Bhṛkuṭī. || 14.70 ||
Vāmadeva, as well as Lajjā, and likewise Vakratuṇḍa;
followed by Dīrghaghoṇā, and then Viraṇḍaka, the wielder of the bow.
Senānī is joined with Yāminī; Grāmaṇī is conjoined with Rātri. Matta is joined with Caṇḍikā, and Vimatta with Śaśiprabhā. (14.72)
One intoxicated by his mount and fickle, and one with matted hair and tremulous eyes;
one with a trunk and joined with a straight woman, followed by one with a sword and accompanied by an unfortunate woman. (14.73)
Vareṇya and Subhagā, Vṛṣaketu and Śivā; Bhakṣyapriya and Durgā, Meghanāda and Kālikā. || 14-74 ||
One should assign Gaṇeśa and Kālakubjā, O Goddess, as Gaṇapa and Vighnahāriṇī using the colors of the Mothers; thereafter, one should perform the assignment of the planets (grahanyāsa). || 14-75 ||
One should contemplate the ruby as white, red, dark blue, yellow, and pale; likewise as smoky-black, blackish-smoky, and smoke-colored.
[He saw] those whose forms were at will, led by Ravi, adorned with all ornaments,
with their left hands resting upon their thighs and their right hands granting the gesture of fearlessness.
Having placed the Sun in the heart with the vowels, one should then place the Moon with the *ya*-group;
next, one should place Mars between the eyebrows with the *ka*-group, and [Mars] in the three eyes.
The wise one [Mercury] is located in the heart with the *ca*-group; Jupiter is in the *ṭa*-group.
O Goddess of the Gods, Venus is at the throat with the *ta*-group above the heart. (14.79)
One should place Saturn with the *pa*-group in the navel, Rāhu with the *śa*-group in the mouth, and Ketu with two *la*s in the anus; thus one should install them, O fair-faced one.
Then, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the host of constellations, which bestows happiness;
[they are] like the blazing fire of time (kālāgni), adorned with all ornaments.
The Aśvini-mukhyās have beautiful hands, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
likewise, they are in pairs, pair after pair, surrounding Rohiṇī.
Each single [letter], as well as each pair, is said to end with Puṣya.
[They are placed] on the forehead, on the two eyes, and subsequently on the left and right ears. (14.83)
O Goddess of the gods, one should likewise place [the mantras] on the two nostrils and the throat in sequence;
having properly placed [them] up to Puṣya, one should then assign Sārpaka by means of the two letters Kha and Ga.
Maghā is on the right shoulder by means of the letters gha and ṅa; Pūrvā-phālgunī is on the second shoulder, joined with the letters ca, cha, ja, and sa on the right elbow.
O beloved, one should place Uttaraphalgunī on the left elbow;
then, the hand situated at the right wrist consists of the letters Jha and Ña.
O beloved, one should place Citrā, joined with the letter ṭha, on the left at the wrist;
and Svātī, joined with the letter ḍa, one should place on the right hand. (14.87)
One should place Viśākhā, conjoined with the letter *ḍha*, upon the left hand;
likewise, O Pārvatī, one should place Anurādhā, conjoined with the letters *tha* and *da*, upon the navel.
O Dear One, one should place Jyeṣṭhā, joined with the syllable *dhakāra*, on the right hip;
likewise, O Dear One, one should place Mūla, situated in *napapha*, on the left hip.
O Dear One, one should place Pūrvāṣāḍhā on the right thigh with the syllable *va*, and immediately thereafter, Uttarāṣāḍhā on the left thigh with the syllable *bha*. || 14.90 ||
One should place Śravaṇa, conjoined with the letter Ma, on the right knee;
one should place Dhaniṣṭhā, situated in Ya, on the left knee.
Then, O Goddess, one should place Śatabhiṣaj with the letter *la*; thereafter, O Beloved, one should place Pūrvābhādrapadā on the right calf. || 14.92 ||
Having sequentially placed [the syllables] situated in the *vaśa* and *varṇa* [groups] upon the left shank,
one should place Uttarābhādrapadā, consisting of the syllables *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, on the right foot.
Then, having assigned Revatī to the left foot by means of the letter *kṣa*, as well as the *bindu* and *visarga*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Yoginīs. (14.94)
One should contemplate them as white, black, reddish, tawny, variegated, and yellow;
they have four arms, symmetrical faces, and are adorned with all ornaments.

Having uttered the two seed-syllables of Ḍāṃ and Ḍīṃ, O Dear One, [one says] "Ḍamalāvarayā," enriched with the left ear (va), the moon (u), and the resonance (nāda), as well as "Ḍākinyai namaḥ. || 14.96 ||
At the end of the vowels, one should utter the two protective words at the end of "mā";
for the sake of purification, one should place [the mantra] for the self of the skin in the region of the throat. (14.97)
One should address Rākiṇī with the throat-syllables beginning with the letter *ra* in sequence, joined with the seed-syllables as before; here, one whose nature is blood should converse. (14.98)
Thereafter, one should place [the letters] beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha* in the Anāhata [cakra];
and likewise, O Goddess, Lākinī, whose essence is flesh, resides in the Maṇipūraka.
Having likewise placed Kākinī, whose nature is that of differentiation, in the Svādhiṣṭhāna with the syllables BAṂ LAṂ VAṂ, one should place Sākinī with the syllables VA SA VA RAṂ. || 14.100 ||
And one should place Asthirūpā upon the support with the previously mentioned seed-syllable;
likewise, one should worship Majjārūpiṇikā, who resides in the syllables Ha and Kṣa. || 14.101 ||
O Maheśānī, one should place Hākinī upon two petals in the middle of the eyebrows;
one should worship her, joined with the seed-syllable as before, and likewise consisting of the nature of semen. || 14.102 ||

O Great Goddess, this is the placement [of the goddesses] together with the Yoginīs: the goddess Yākinī, white in color and residing in all the elements, is placed in the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head). || 14.103 ||
Then one should perform the placement of the zodiac signs (rāśinyāsa), which always brings about complete protection;
one should visualize them as red, white, yellow, pale, variegated, black, and ash-colored.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should perform the placement of the colors tawny, reddish-brown, brown, variegated, black, and smoke-colored using the four letters beginning with 'a'.
One should place a ram at the right ankle; then, by means of pairs, a bull at the knees through the Vedas, and thereafter a pair upon the testicles.
With two [syllables] one forms Karkātaka in the belly, and with two [more], Siṃhaka on the shoulder;
with the anusvāra and visarga, and with the *śa*-group, one forms Kanyakā.
O you who are honored by heroes, one should place [the letter] with the *ka*-group on the right side of the head;
likewise, on the left side of the head, one should place the bearer of the scales (the letter *ta*) with the *ca*-group.
Likewise, O beloved, one should place Scorpio on the shoulder with the *ca*-group;
and likewise, O beloved, one should place Sagittarius on the belly with the *ṭa*-group.
One should place the Makara with the *tavarga* on the testicles in sequence;
likewise, one should place the Kumbha with the *pavarga* on the left knee.
With the *ya*-group and the letter *kṣa*, one should place the Fish (Mīna) at the left ankle;
then, one should indeed install the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*), which consist of all the holy fords (*tīrthas*). || 14.111 ||
White, black, red, dark, green, and yellow, in sequence;
again and again in order, O Goddess, is the collection of the fifty seats (pīṭhas).
The wise one should recollect the sacred seats (pīṭhas) as being joined with the entire Mātṛkā;
the wise one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the letters of the Mātṛkā for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. || 113 ||
Kāmarūpa is a great pīṭha; then there is the pīṭha of Vārāṇasī, as well as Nepāla and Pauṇḍravardhana.
Purasthira, likewise Pīṭha, and Candrasthira after that; then Pūrṇaśaila, the great Pīṭha, and Arbuda thereafter. (14.115)
Then follows the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Āmrātakeśvara and Ekāmra;
after that, the sinless Visrotaḥpīṭha and Kāmakoṭa.
Kailāsa, Bhṛgu, Kedāra, the seat (pīṭha) of Candrapura, then Śrīpīṭha, likewise Oṃkāra, and after that Jālandhara. (14.117)
Then there is the Mālava seat, Kulānta, and Devakoṭaka; Gokarṇa is a great seat, as is Māruteśvara.
Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, Rājagṛha, Mahāpatha, Pīṭha, Kollagiri, and beyond that, Elāpura is proclaimed. || 14.119 ||
Kāmeśvara is a great pīṭha; Jayantikā is a great pīṭha; Ujjayanī is indeed a pīṭha; and Caritra is named Kṣīraka. || 14.120 ||
Hastināpura-pīṭha, Uḍḍīśa, and Prayāgaka;
Ṣaṣṭhīśa, the pīṭha Śrīśaila, Māyāpūra, and Jaleśvara;
Malaya as a great pīṭha, Śrīśaila, and the Meruka mountain.
Mahendra, Vāmana, and Hiraṇyapura as well.
The seat of Uḍḍīyāna is composed of Mahālakṣmī;
beyond that, O Supreme Goddess, is the seat of Chāyācchatrapura.
One should always perform the placement of the fifty seats and the placement of the Mātṛkās;
O Great Goddess, by performing this sixfold placement, one becomes Śiva himself in manifest form.
Then one should assign the goddesses of the desires, who have the luster of pomegranate flowers,
accompanied by the Śaktis on their left laps, and holding flower-arrows and sugarcane bows.
The Śaktis, resembling saffron in hue and adorned with all ornaments,
should be meditated upon as holding blue lotuses in their hands, capable of attracting the three worlds.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should subsequently assign Kāmarati and Kāmaprīti;
[then] Kānta joined with Kāminī, and Bhrānta joined with Mohinī.
Like that, she is a part of desire (*kāmāṅga*) in the lotus; likewise, she is a wanton woman (*vilāsinī*) who moves at will (*kāmacāra*).
She is like the wish-fulfilling vine (*kalpalatā*) for the ears, and similarly, she is soft and dark-blue (*komalaśyāmalā*). (14.128)
One joined with Kāmavardhana is to be known as Śucismitā;
Kāma joined with Vismitā is Rama, who is joined with Viśālākṣī. || 14-129 ||
Ramaṇa, Lelihāna, Ratirnātha, Digambara; Ratipriya, Vāmā, Rātrinātha, and Kubjikā. (14.130)
The beloved is joined with Smara, and the lover is joined with Satyā;
likewise, the night-stalker is joined with Kalyāṇī, and the son is joined with Bhoginī. (14.131)
Nandaka is joined with Kāmadā, and Madana with Sulocanā; O Goddess, he who is called Nandasuta is likewise joined with Sulāvaṇyā. (14.132)
Niśācara, Madinī, Rati, and Haṃsa; thereafter Kalaha joined with Priyā, and Puṣpadhanvan with Kāṅkṣiṇī. || 14.133 ||
Mahādhanus with Sumukhā, Grāmaṇī with Nalinī;
Bhīma with Jaṭinī, and Bhrāmaṇa with Pālinī. || 14.134 ||
Bhrāmaṇa is joined with Śikhinī; thereafter is Śānta; after that, Mugdha; then Bhṛgu; and after that, Bhūmā. || 14.135 ||
Bhrāntā, Amaralolā, Bhramāvahā, Sucañcalā, Mohanī, Dīrghajihvā, Mocakā, and likewise Satī. || 14-136 ||
Likewise, Mugdha and Lolākṣī, Moha and Mardanabhṛṅgiṇī, Mohaka and Capeṭā, and Manmatha joined with his Mistress. || 14.137 ||
The pair Mātaṅgamālinī and Bhṛṅgā, Kalahaṃsinī, together with Gāyaka, as well as Viśvatomukhī. || 14.138 ||
Gaja is joined with Nandikā, and after that is Gīti; then there is Nartaka with Rañjinī, and Khela accompanied by Kānti. (14.139)
Unmatta, Kalakaṇṭha, Mattaka, Vṛkodara, Megha, Śyāmānvita, and Devī Vimalaśrī—these are the [names] in sequence, O beloved. (14.140)
O Goddess, O sinless one, one should always perform the placement [of mantras] with the letters of the Mātṛkā, just like the Mātṛkā itself.
By means of this application of placement, one becomes a shaker of the three worlds.
One should place [the syllable] of Bālā, belonging to the northeast of the City of Blood (Asripura), marked with nine yonis;
[furthermore, one should place them] on the two ears, the chin, the temples, the mouth, the two eyes, and the nose. || 14.142 ||
One should place [the mantras] on the two shoulders and the heart, on the elbows and the flanks, on the knees, the groin, and the feet, and on the sides, the heart, and the two breasts. || 14.143 ||
And on the throat, one should place the [mantra] known as the Nine Yonis, consisting of three seed-syllables;
then, having again uttered the Bālā [mantra], one should duly install the sixteen-syllable [mantra].
Having again uttered the *bālā* [mantra], one should contemplate a square;
by means of the application of placement (*nyāsa*), one should contemplate the *golaka* as the *śrīcakra*.
Having conceived of nine locations—the six cakras, the forehead, the parting of the hair, and the aperture of the head—one should thereafter perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), O Goddess. (14.146)
One should place Śrīvidyā at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), and then, O Goddess, the Tithinityās, followed by the Gurus in sequence, joined with the vowels of the Mātṛkā.
One should perform the nyāsa on the face as with the Mātṛkā; these bestow all good fortune.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of Śrīvidyā," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the Nityā Tantra. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme Nityā-maṇḍala.
Kāmeśvarī is the great vidyā who brings all the worlds under her control.
One should write the syllables BĀLĀM and TĀRAM at the edge of the heart, followed by the word KĀMEŚVARĪ.
At the end of ICCHĀKĀMAPHALA, one should write the word PRADARŚAYA SARVA. (15.2)
Then one should utter "Sattvavaśam," followed by "Kari Sarvajagatpadam.
At the end of the *kṣobhaṇa* mantra, one should utter "Kari" and write three *huṃ* syllables. (15.3)
Having drawn the five arrows with the withdrawal [mudrā], [one worships] Kumārikā;
this Nityā Kāmeśvarī has been described incidentally, O Daughter of the Mountain. (15.4)
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable at the end of the word *bhaga*, followed by *bhuge* and *bhagini*.
At the end of the syllables [of the mantra] ending with *bhagodarī*, one should write *bhagamāle* and *bhagāvahe*. (15.5)
In the secret place of the vulva, at the edge of the vulva, at the edge of the womb, and near the vulva; falling down at the very end, and then, O Bhagavashankari! (15.6)
Then, one should draw the form of the vulva (*bhaga*), O lady with large, lotus-like eyes;
one should draw everything in its true form, with the region of the vulva perpetually moist. (15.7)
One should write: "O Giver of Boons, bring my vulvas to me," followed by "retas, suretas, bhaga, klinne, klinnadrave. (15.8)
Moisten and dissolve all sentient beings, O Mistress of the Bhaga! O Amoghe, O Bhagavice, agitate and cause all to be agitated! || 15-9 ||
O Bhageśvarī, one should address the beings with the Vāgbhava mantra, beginning with *blūṃ*;
then *bhe blūṃ*, *bho blūṃ*, *heṃ blūṃ*, and thereafter *heṃ klinne*. (15.10)
And [the mantra] "Bring all vulvas under my control," followed by the seed-syllable of women (*strībīja*) and the syllable consisting of *bala* at the end. (15.11)
Having written Bhuvaneśī, this Vidyā Bhagamālinī, consisting of one hundred and forty-five syllables, has been recounted here incidentally. || 15-12 ||
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Parā, followed by *nityaklinne madadrave*, this mantra, joined with the wife of Agni (svāhā), is declared to be *Nityaklinnā*. (15.13)
She is the bestower of all good fortune and the giver of all sovereignty.
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should likewise draw a pair of goads.
In the center of that, O Goddess, one should write the syllable consisting of the letter *bha* and *ra*;
one should write the *ca*-group, excluding its final letter, situated within the fire.
The mantra of Bheruṇḍā, endowed with the fourteen vowels, marked by the bindu and nāda, and joined individually with the wife of fire (svāhā), bestows the fruit [of practice]. || 15-16 ||
Having uttered "Bhuvaneśī," [followed by] "Vahnivāsinī" in the dative case—this mantra, O Goddess, ending with the heart [syllable], is the eternal Vahnivāsinī. (15–17)
O Bhuvaneśānī, [one should utter] the Praṇava, the syllable consisting of the letter *pha* with a *repha*, followed by the Moon (*śaśī*) with the *visarga*, and then "nityaklinne madadrave. (15–18)
This Vidyā, conjoined with the wife of Fire (Svāhā), bestows all sovereignty;
it is the eternal Mahāvidyeśvarī, which has been taught by me in this context.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Parā and Śivadūtī with the suffix -ṅī, this mantra, O Goddess, ending with the heart-mantra, is the Dūtī who grants all desires. (15–20)
Having uttered the seed-syllable Oṃ, one should write the supreme armor (kavaca);
having written khe, cha, and kṣaḥ, one should also write the female seed-syllable (strībīja).
The syllable *hūṃ*, *kṣe*, *parā*, and *astra*—this twelve-syllable vidyā is named Tvaritā; she is eternal and difficult to obtain in the three worlds. (15–22)
Consisting of all lion-thrones, like a young girl, she is the Kulasundarī;
one should likewise enclose her with the Bālayā, for she is indeed Nityabhairavī. (15–23)
The five arrows, O Goddess of gods, become the eternal Śakrākṣarī;
she is the Trailokyavimalā Vidyā, known as Nityā, the Supreme Sovereign. (15–24)
O Dear One, this five-syllabled mantra, beginning with the seed-syllable of the arrow (Bāṇa), is another [form];
it consists of the Praṇava, Bhuvaneśvarī, and the syllable whose essence is Pha-re-ma. || 15-25 ||
Then [one should utter] the second [syllable], which consists of the *srū* [mantra], followed by the *aṅkuśa* of Bhuvaneśī;
having extracted the word "nitya" with the vocative case, [one utters] "madadravām. (15–26)
The armor and the goad [are formed] with fifteen [syllables]; then follows the blue-bannered one (*nīlapatākinī*), which is emitted together with *kāla* and situated within fire and wind. || 15-27 ||

Combined with the five separate [vowels], and then endowed with the sound of Śakra (the letter *i*), marked with the Bindu and Nāda—this is the seed-syllable Vijayā, O Dear One, which is eternal. (15–28)
One should write the seed-syllable *tāra* conjoined with *candra* (the moon) and *vāruṇa* (Varuṇa).
Then, O Goddess, on the fourth [day], one should draw Sarvamaṅgalā.
O Goddess, this mantra ends with the heart [syllable]; she is eternally all-auspicious.
O Goddess, [the mantra] consists of the Tāra, the heart, and the word "Bhagavatī" at the end, followed by Jvālāmālinī.

Having recited [the mantra] twice, and at the very end having written "O you who effect the withdrawal of all beings" (bhūtasaṃhārakārike), one should write the pair of words "O Jātavedas, O Blazing One" (jvalanti). || 15-31 ||
One should write the pair "jvaleta" blazing, followed by a pair of "huṃ" syllables;
the mantra is composed of the three fire-seeds, "huṃ," and the weapon-mantra ending in "svāhā. (15-32)
This is the eternal Great Goddess, the supreme Jvālāmālinikā;
she is adorned with the final letter of the *ka*-group and the final vowel, embellished by the vowel of Indra (the letter *e*).
Overcome by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, the Supreme Goddess is manifold;
one should place her sequentially upon all the vowels beginning with 'a'. (15.34)
O Supreme Goddess, O Lotus-eyed One, one should eternally install Śrīvidyā, the Mother of the Universe, together with the vowels in the vowel-sounds.
Thereafter, the knower of mantras should place Prakaṭā and the others upon the Ādhāra and the other centers;
then, he should perform the *sthitinyāsa* with the sixteen syllables of the Śrīvidyā. || 15-36 ||

Having placed three [syllables] on the five fingers of the two hands, at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), the mouth, and the heart, one should place one [syllable], O Daughter of the Mountain, from the navel down to the ends of the feet. || 15-37 ||
One [should place it] from the throat down to the navel; another indeed beyond that;
and one from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) down to the throat, having placed [the remaining part] on the two feet. || 15-38 ||
Having placed [the mantras] upon the fingers, this placement (nyāsa) brings about stability;
thereafter, one should perform the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa), which bestows all accomplishments.

O Goddess, [the letters] are located in the aperture of Brahmā, the forehead, the eyes, the ears, the nose, the lips, the interior of the teeth, the upper palate, the tongue, and the hollow of the throat. || 15-40 ||

O Goddess, for the sake of all prosperity, one should install the mantra with the syllables of the Śrīvidyā upon the back, all the limbs, the heart, the breasts, the belly, and the genitals. || 15-41 ||
Afterwards, O beautiful one, one should place [the mantra] upon all the limbs by way of pervasion;
having restrained the vital breaths according to the rule, with the body armored by the mudrās.
Agitation, driving away, attracting, subjugation, intoxication, and the great goad;
Khecarī, the seed-form, and the yoni-mudrā—these follow in sequence.
O Supreme Goddess, I shall now declare in due order the seed-syllables (bīja) of the mudrās;
the five mudrās consist of the five arrows, and the syllable composed of the essence of *krom*. (15.44)
First is the seed-syllable of Rudrabhairavī, followed by that of Sadāśiva;
then, O Goddess, is Vāgbhava—thus indeed the fourfold sequence.
The seed-syllables for the four mudrās and the nine mudrās are given in sequence; now I shall explain the exposition of the mudrās of Maheśvarī in order. (15–46)
Having formed a fist with the left hand at the region of the ear, the best of tantric practitioners should extend the index finger straight and whirl it around. || 15-47 ||
The Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī mudrā is indicated at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa),
having restrained this world with a fist whose thumb is held within.
The mudrā known as Ripujihvāgrahā is indicated at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa);
O Maheśānī, it is formed by the turning of both hands. || 15.49 ||

Having joined them, O dear one, one should hold the two ring fingers with the two index fingers; one should join the two middle fingers together in the center, and likewise place the two little fingers below them. || 15-50 ||
Having joined even the two thumbs in a triple manner by means of a pair-by-pair sequence,
this is the mudrā named Trikhaṇḍā, for the rite of summoning Tripurā.
Having formed the two hands into the *viralita* (separated) gesture, place the middle fingers together;
then, having pressed the two little fingers with the two thumbs, [hold them] straight. (15.52)
One should form the two index fingers like a staff, with the ring fingers resting upon the middle fingers;
this is the *Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* mudrā, which causes the agitation of the three worlds. (15.53)
When the middle finger is joined with the index finger and kept straight, then it becomes the *sarvavidrāviṇī* mudrā; it deludes all things, both moving and unmoving. (15.54)
O Sulocanā, one should bend the pair of index fingers toward the middle finger;
this very mudrā is then the attractor.
Having turned the palms over and directed the fingers toward the heart and face, one should worship; then, by way of reversal, they should be closely joined in sequence.

When the tips of the two index fingers are shaped like hooks at the base of the thumbs, and all [fingers] are joined together as one, it becomes the mudrā that brings everything under control. (15.57)

Having formed the hollowed cupped hands (puṭāñjali), with the two middle fingers placed within the hollow and the two index fingers then positioned at the tips of the little fingers facing each other.
O Supreme Goddess, when the two ring fingers are straight and the two thumbs are positioned facing the tips of the middle fingers, this is the mudrā that causes universal intoxication. (15.59)
From this very same mudrā, by means of the sequence of the ring finger and the index finger, this mudrā in the form of a hook is the Great Hook (Mahāṅkuśā). || 15-60 ||
Having placed the left arm upon the right arm and the right [arm] from the left side, one should subsequently join them by turning them in due order. || 15-61 ||
One should restrain the pair of the little fingers and ring fingers with the two index fingers;
then, having made the two middle fingers straight, they should likewise be straight like a vulva.
The two thumbs constitute the *khecarī-mudrā*, which unites the state of the *pāthīva*;
this beloved [mudrā] bestows the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) upon all the gods. (15.63)
Then, having formed a *añjali* and turned it over, one should place the two middle fingers at the tips of the little fingers, O Goddess, and hold them there.
O Dear One, the pair of index and middle fingers should be firmly joined by the two ring fingers,
and the two thumbs should be brought together in the shape of a half-moon.
This is declared to be the Seed-seal (bījamudrā), which bestows all bliss in the Pīṭha.
Having properly crossed the two hands, the two index fingers are placed equally at the base. || 15.66 ||
One should join them in the middle of the *kuru*s; immediately thereafter, O Goddess, the ring fingers are interlaced while the little fingers remain as they were. || 15.67 ||
By joining the two thumbs so as to form the shape of a womb, this is declared to be the supreme Yonimudrā, the Mother of the Three Worlds. (15.68)
Having thus disposed his body and having his form armored with mudrās,
he should perform the rite of internal sacrifice by which the All-pervading Lord himself becomes manifest.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Nyāsa of Śrīvidyā," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the Nityā Tantra. 15.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, [tell me] the procedure for the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) as well as the procedure for the external sacrifice (bahiryāga)."
O Īśāna, tell me everything, if I am dear to you.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the great internal sacrifice (yajana),
which extends from the root-center (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and is subtler than a fiber of a lotus stalk.
Consisting of the brilliance of millions of lightning flashes from the mass of light of the rising sun, she causes the brilliance of millions of moons to melt away;
she is the singular radiance of the three worlds.
One should meditate upon the Goddess who effects the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the entire world in its entirety, in such a way that the mind becomes motionless. (16.4)
The mind attains immobility in an instant through the power of Śiva and Śakti, becoming an abode for the mass of innate bliss. (16.5)
There, concentration arises, manifested by two types of perception:
one indeed named "self-awareness," and the other bearing the name "non-awareness."

One who possesses the consciousness of self-awareness (saṃprajñāta) arises through the predominance of power (śakti), while that which is called non-cognitive (asaṃprajñāta) indeed comes into being through the predominance of Śiva. || 16-7 ||
The distinction between self-aware [samādhi] is intense or even more intense;
whereas the distinction between non-self-aware [samādhi] is dull or even more dull. (16.8)
Where there is such ideation and discernment, one is called "self-discerning"; however, one who is beyond such discernment is established as a man of steady wisdom. || 16-9 ||
"This very wisdom is the realization of wisdom, which is beyond thought. O Goddess, these two designations indeed become the Śiva-tattva. (16.10)
O Goddess, intense and even more intense samādhi is characterized by such signs as laughter, weeping, horripilation, trembling, and perspiration. (16.11)
The eyes are conquered like a closed lotus, and that body is steady in its characteristics; O Goddess, this is proclaimed as the slowest and most gentle form of samādhi.
And by means of the Śāmbhava state, which is the object of knowledge, may he be continuously blissful.
Having performed the rite of the internal sacrifice, one should perform the external worship. (16.13)
Having thus disposed his body, the supreme practitioner, being the self of all, should meditate upon the stainless reality that deludes the three worlds. (16.14)
The supreme consciousness, the mistress of all worldly transactions without exception,
possessing the luster of a thousand rising suns and the radiance of the pomegranate flower.
Resembling the hibiscus flower, with the luster of a ruby gem;
resembling a blooming lotus, with the brilliance of molten gold—[thus is] the Sovereign of the Gods.
Adorned with sprouts on her feet that have the appearance of red lotus petals, her two feet were graced with anklets inlaid with priceless jewels. || 16-17 ||
Resplendent with the brilliance of jewels set in her toe-rings,
she possessed thighs as delicate and soft as the graceful trunks of plantain trees.
Adorned with a shimmering red garment upon her orb-like hips,
she was graced by the playful tinkling of the ruby bells fastened to her girdle.
She possessed a waist that could not be discerned, a deep navel, and a slender belly;
she was supreme, endowed with great breasts that were elevated by the line of hair between them.
Adorned with the beauty of her well-rounded, firm, and lofty breasts,
she shone with the weight of vast necklaces of priceless pearls.
Adorned with necklaces shining with the luster of the nine gems,
she was beautiful with the charming surface of her cheeks, which were lovely with the ornaments of her ears.
The radiance of her beautiful face was like that of the rising sun, with earrings [shining alongside it];
she had a face like the full moon, a lotus-like countenance, and an excellent nose.
She possessed beautiful eyebrows like the quivering bow of the God of Love, lotus-like eyes,
and was marked by a rich tilaka made of gems shining upon her forehead.
She whose forehead is adorned with a crest-jewel set with pearls and rubies and tiny bells, who wears a crown shining with the crescent moon, and who possesses three eyes. || 16-25 ||
Her four arms, which are like creeper-vines of coral, shine with beauty;
her four hands hold a sugarcane bow, a flowery arrow, a noose, and a goad. || 16-26 ||
The Mother who embodies all the gods, beautiful with every form of auspiciousness,
who consists of all sacred fords, divine, and the fulfiller of all desires.
The Goddess who consists of all mantras, eternal, proficient in all scriptures, who embodies all sacred fields, auspicious, and composed of all vidyās. || 16–28 ||
She who consists of all sacrifices, whose nature is that of all the gods, who embodies all the scriptures, who is eternal, and who is saluted by all the Agamas.
The Goddess who consists of all sacred traditions, who is served by all abodes,
who is composed of all bliss, the supreme consciousness that is the abyss of knowledge.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Mother, one should gradually draw her into the nostril and,
having invoked her into the center of the wheel with the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā, [one should worship her].
One should meditate upon her as being established there, residing within the Śrīpīṭha;
one should display the mudrās, O Goddess, and worship her thrice with libations.
O Supreme Goddess, one should arrange the limbs of absorption within the body of the Goddess;
one should properly present perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and other offerings to the Goddess.
Having worshipped the Supreme Deity with the sixteen types of offerings,
one should again offer libations three times with the root mantra.
At this time, O Goddess, one should worship the Tithinityā; O Supreme Sovereign, these are the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Vicitrā. (16–35)

One should worship [the goddesses] who take the form of the lunar days (tithis) ending with the new moon and the full moon; and having visualized a great triangle in the order from the east, south, and north. || 16-36 ||
One should indeed draw five lines each there in sequence;
one should contemplate the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'u' on the southern side.
Then, having written the five [vowels] beginning with Ū on the eastern line,
one should thereafter write [the five] beginning with Śakti on the northern line.
The mantra ending in an *anusvāra* [is used for the sixteenth]; one should worship the sixteenth [vowel] at the *visarga*.
O Goddess of Gods, the sixteen *Nityās* have been described in counter-clockwise order. (16–39)
O Daughter of the Mountain, beginning from the first lunar day and ending with the full moon,
one should worship each Nityā daily and shall attain great good fortune.
O Maheśānī, during the dark fortnight, one should worship the circle of lunar days (tithi-maṇḍala), beginning with Vicitrā, O Varārohā, until one reaches Kāmeśvarī. (16.41)
O Supreme Goddess, these sixteen digits of the moon, O Mistress of the Gods, which are to be worshipped with devotion in reverse order, [should be worshipped] sequentially. (16.42)
O Goddess, one should worship the Tithinityā in three ways for the sake of good fortune;
furthermore, one should worship Śrī Tripurānityā for the sake of auspiciousness.
O Great Goddess, by following the instruction of the Guru, he attains good fortune after having worshipped the eternal goddesses, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, in their proper sequence.
At this time, O Goddess, the wise man should worship the Guru;
I shall explain to you, O sinless one, by means of the yoga of the closing of the flowers. (16.45)
The mass of rays is measured in petals, while the gurus are more than a hundred;
therefore, one should contract the flower, for [an excess] is infinite and causes the loss of accomplishment.
Those known as having lost their lineage are limited [in number], yet they bestow all prosperity.
If one does not cause the flower to close, then in the twelfth [month] there will be a loss of lineage.
If one's form were lost through continuity, one would not be dear to the deity;
for this very reason, O beloved, I have properly closed the flower.
The gurus of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja are indeed bestowers of prosperity;
one should worship the lineage of gurus three times within the center of the three eastern squares. (16.49)
First, one should worship those initiated by Parā who are distinguished as Parāpara;
thereafter, O Goddess, beloved, one should worship the Aparā gurus in three ways.
Know, O fair-faced one, that in the divine current there are seven supreme gurus; they are males, O beloved, whose names end with the word Ānandanātha.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, women are to be known as ending with the word *parāmbā*;
O Mistress of the Gods, beyond that is considered *paraśiva*, the supreme light. (16.52)
Likewise, O Goddess, Parāśakti is Kauleśvarī, O Dear One;
[the others are] Śuklā, Devī, Kuleśānā, Kāmeśvarī, and Ambikā, in due order. (16.53)
The Gurus, numbering as many as the Munis, are known as Parā and possess divine forms; the Samayas are Bhogaklinna, Vedākhya, and likewise Sahaja. (16.54)
Listen, O beloved, regarding the lineage of the Siddhas known as Parāpara and the lineage of the Mānavas:
Gagana, Viśvavimala, Madana, and likewise Bhuvana. (16.55)
Līlā is dearer than her own self; thereafter, there are men numbering as many as the Nāgas.
These others, O Supreme Goddess, are fixed and imperishable. (16.56)
These three are fixed for the benefit of the teachers;
O Maheśānī, O beloved, I have extracted this "contracted flower."
Subsequently, at the conclusion of the flood of human beings, one should worship the triad of one's own gurus:
the Parameṣṭhin Guru, the Guru, and the one known as the Parama Guru.
O Maheśānī, one should worship one's own guru and the triad of gurus;
or else, one may worship a single guru, beginning from the Mānavaugha. || 16-59 ||
This method has been explained; now another method is stated:
[the worship] of that which is to be venerated in all its forms, beginning with the eight groups of human beings. || 16.60 ||
For as many as there are nine gurus here, so many flowers should one offer to the Nine Goddesses of the Wheels (Navacakreśvarī). || 16.61 ||
Then, O Goddess, among the multitude of men, there are indeed seventeen;
afterwards, one should contract the flower and worship the ninth, the Śrī-guru. || 16.62 ||
O fair-faced one, I shall explain [the procedure] for those who do not know the teacher and the disciple:
having uttered "Salutation to the Gurus," one should write "Salutation to the Pādukās. (16.63)
At the end of *guru* and at the end of *parama*, one should likewise say "Obeisance to the Gurus" (*gurubhyo namaḥ*).
Similarly, one should utter "Obeisance to the Teachers" (*ācāryebhyo namaḥ*) for their sandals. (16.64)
Likewise, the sandals of the Ācāryas and the sandals of those previously perfected;
this shall be the lineage of gurus for all ordinary teachers and disciples. (16.65)
Having worshipped the lineage of gurus, one then becomes Śrī Tripurā herself;
however, a person devoid of the lineage of gurus is like a man excluded from the row at a meal.
Because it belongs to the common lineage of gurus, it would not be devoid of the lineage;
this path of the "closing of the flower" has been accomplished and established by me, O beloved. (16.67)
Out of compassion, O Supreme Goddess, for the benefit of practitioners, the Gurus known as Kāmarāja have [expounded] the sequence regarding the Śrīvidyā. (16–68)
O fair-faced one, hear also from me the supreme primordial Śiva and the primordial Ambikā Kāmeśvarī, as well as the vidyā known as Lopāmudrā. || 16-69 ||
The Divine Current (divyaugha) and the Great Current (mahaugha), and beyond that, the All-Blessed (sarvānanda);
thereafter follows the Goddess Ambikā Prajñā, and the seventh shall be the Light (prakāśa).
The divine Parākhyaguru, Lopāmudrā, Prabhāmaya, Divya, Citra, Kaivalyadevī, Ambā, and Mahodaya. || 16-71 ||
O beloved, listen: the Siddhas are to be known as *parāpara* within the human stream (*mānavaugha*).
Vidyā, Śakti, Viśva, and the fourth is Komala. (16–72)
The fifth, however, is Supreme Bliss (parānanda), which is called "Captivating" (manohara), O Dear One;
the seventh is Self-bliss (svātmānanda), and the eighth is said to be the "Manifest" (pratibha). || 16.73 ||
O Goddess, these are proclaimed as the gurus known as Aparā; one should employ them as before, followed immediately by the eight [gurus] of Anantā. (16.74)
Or the triad, or one's own guru, or even up to nine, O lotus-eyed one;
this is declared to be the lineage of gurus for the disciples of Dakṣiṇāmūrti. (16.75)
The various lineages of tradition should be understood according to the succession of one's own guru.
One should not grant the supreme assembly to one who is devoid of the traditional lineage.
The common gurus, however, are indeed equal across all divisions.
Having worshipped the lineage of gurus, one should then worship the deities of the tradition.
O Goddess who deludes the three worlds, O fulfiller of all hopes,
one should worship the Eastern Tradition within the wheel that agitates all.
In the wheel that bestows all good fortune, as well as in the wheel that accomplishes all aims,
one should worship the Dakṣa-āmnāya in the wheel that provides all protection.
O Goddess, one should worship the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya) within the three middle wheels;
O Mistress of the Gods, one should worship the Kubera Tradition (kauberāmnāya) within the nine wheels.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the central throne at the Bindu;
in this very manner, one should worship the five pentads.
Śrīvidyā, Parāprajyotis, Parā Niṣkalaśāmbhavī, Ajayā, and Mātṛkā—these are proclaimed as the five sheaths (kośas). || 16-82 ||
Śrīvidyā, as well as Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Triśakti, and Sarvasāmrājyā—these are proclaimed as the five Lakṣmīs. (16.83)
Śrīvidyā, Tvaritā, and likewise Pārijāteśvarī, as well as Tripuṭā and Pañcabāṇeśī—these five are remembered as the Kalpalatās. (16.84)
Śrīvidyā, Mūlapīṭheśī, Sudhā, Śrī Amṛteśvarī, and the one renowned as Annapūrṇā—these five are the wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus). || 16-85 ||
Śrīvidyā, Siddhalakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, Bhuvaneśvarī, and Vārāhī—these are declared to be the five celebrated jewels. (16.86)
O Maheśānī, the Mūlavidyā is proclaimed as Śrīvidyā;
it consists of the letter at the end of Vāruṇa (va) situated in Vahni (ra), endowed with Bindu and Nāda. || 16-87 ||
The seed-syllable of Lakṣmī is declared to be joined with the left eye (the letter *i*).
The seed-syllable of Śrī, the supreme seed-syllable, is declared to be the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī.
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then recite that which consists of the syllable Hrīṃ;
"O Śrīpuṭā, O Kamale, O Kamalāgre, may you be gracious! (16.89).
One should place the central *bhūmi* within the position of Rudra;
one should bestow the pair [of syllables] "prasīda" and the seed-syllable of Śrī, Bhuvaneśvarī.
