Then one should give the seed-syllable of Śrī; "Mahālakṣmī" is the heart-mantra. This Mahālakṣmī mantra is considered to consist of twenty-seven syllables.
One should inscribe the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Parā, and Kāmarāja;
this is the triple power (triśakti), O Goddess, which is difficult to attain in the three worlds.
Mādana with Candra, the goddess Lakṣmī adorned with long eyes, joined with Viṣṇukrūreśvarī, and this [one] joined with Vaiṣṇavī. || 16-93 ||
One should form the enclosure with the seed-syllable Śrī, which bestows all scriptures;
having first uttered the Praṇava, one should extract the Parā-Ahaṃsa. (16.94)
Therefore, O Goddess, I am this head, declared as Vasuvarṇa;
the Goddess is the absolute source of the Vedas, the supreme, partless Śāmbhavī. (16.95)
The *haṃsa* is that which ends with the letter *ja* and *pārṇa*; therein, it is proclaimed as the *mātṛkā*. [The sequence is:
the *praṇava*, *bhuvaneśānī*, space (*viyat*), moon (*candra*), fire (*agni*), and wind (*vāyu*). (16.96)
One should write "Bhuvaneśī" and "Dhruva," and then "Salutation to Sarasvatī.
This [deity] is indeed Pārijāteśī, who is comparable to the delight of the Pārijāta tree. || 16-97 ||
The Kāṇḍavānīśvarī-vidyā has been recounted by me in this context;
it consists of three seeds and the seed of Parā, and when accompanied by desire, it is declared to be "tripartite" (tripuṭā). || 16-98 ||
The mantra of Pañcakāmeśvarī is proclaimed for placement upon the child (bālanyāsa):
the Vāgbhava syllable, the left eye, ending with the fixed vowel (O), and conjoined with the bindu. (16.99)
The Vidya of the Mistress of the Root-Pitha has been told by me as a well-guarded secret;
it consists of the supreme seed-syllable (Parā-bīja), which is the glorious seed-syllable (Śrī-bīja), the first syllable of Bālā.
*Rājyada*, *rājalakṣmī*, *candra*, and *sargavibhūṣita*—these are proclaimed as the reverse seeds (*biloma*), the initial seeds (*ādibīja*), nectar (*sudhā*), and Śrī. (16.101)

O Bhuvaneśānī, one should first write the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, and immediately after that, the Śrī-bīja; then one should inscribe the letter 'A' (viyat), followed by 'Ta', 'Ā', 'Di', 'Kha', and 'Pha'. (16.102)
That [mantra] beginning with *viyat* (the letter *i*) and so forth is considered by Manu to be *Phrāṇiti*.
The third letter of the *ca*-group (*ja*), joined with *māyā* (the vowel *ī*), the letter *ra*, and the moon (*bindu*). (16.103)
Having extracted Mahācaṇḍa, one should write "Saṃkarṣaṇī";
having uttered "Kālamahāna," it is conjoined with Viyat and Indu. (16.104)
The seed-syllable of Māyā is indeed declared to be the great mantra of Siddhalakṣmī; and Annapūrṇā, O Goddess of Gods, is proclaimed in the Uttarāmnāya. (16.105)
One should write the portion "mātaṅginyai," encased within the *vāṅmāyāśrī* mantra.
This twelve-syllable *vidyā* of Mātaṅginī is thus proclaimed. (16.106)
Joined with the ether and fire, adorned by the moon of the left eye;
O Maheśānī, Mistress of the World, you are difficult to attain within the three worlds. (16.107)
Having first extracted the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], [one should utter] "O Blessed Lady" (bhagavati) with the [vocative] perfective suffix (saṃbuddhyā).
Then [come] "Vārtālī," the two [forms of] "Vārāhī," and "She who has the principal face of a boar" (yugmavārāhamukhī). || 16-108 ||

Salutations again and again to Andhā and Andhinyā; salutations again and again to the supreme Rundhinī. Salutations joined with Jambhā and Jambhinyā; salutations joined with Mohā and Mohinyā. (16.109)
In the pillar [mantra], one should utter "to the Paralyzer" (*stambhinyai*) joined with the heart [seed-syllable], followed by the name of the person, in both instances of paralyzing;
then one should recite "of all the wicked and the malicious," "of all," and "everything. (16.110)
Paralyze the tongue; perform the pair; quickly bring the two under control.
Vāgkūṭa is the triad of speech, the beloved of the fire of mantra. || 16-111 ||
This great vidyā has been proclaimed, hidden within all tantras.
The Śrī Devī said: "O Lord, the mantras have indeed been declared, yet they remain hidden within all tantras. (16.112)
"Having propitiated them, how are those worlds produced that are so difficult to attain on earth?
O Mahādeva, tell me all of this in great detail."
Īśvara said:
"Well asked by you, O blessed lady, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds—[as one who has not realized the truth of the mind resorts [to practice], like a woman with a wicked son]. (16.114)
O Goddess, it is thus declared here that which is concealed in all the tantras:
one should perform the purification of mantras for the sake of the purity of mantras. (16.115)
Having divided the square ground and drawn three lines each way,
one should then draw a circle within the sixteen [squares] and inscribe the syllables.
In the directions, there are fourteen, sixteen, and eighteen [squares] for Indra, Agni, and Rudra;
in the elemental [spheres], fifteen, three, and one [square] for Pātāla, Vahni, and Himāṃśu.
The wise one should then sequentially produce the letters, the lines, and the script.
For those who do not accomplish the mantra and so forth, the syllable of their name certainly falls;
and the second place of accomplishment should be known as that which bears the name of the object to be accomplished. (16.118)
The third is "well-accomplished" (susiddha), while the fourth is designated as "enemy" (arisaṃjñaka).
The accomplished (siddha) succeeds in due time; the one to be accomplished (sādhya) may or may not succeed. (16.119)
An *ari* (enemy) mantra would devour the practitioner at that very moment;
a *siddhasiddha* mantra grants success through recitation, while a *siddhasādhya* mantra grants success through double the amount of recitation.
*Siddhasusiddha* brings success through gathering [disciples]; *Siddhāri* indeed kills the twice-born (*dvija*).
*Sādhya* succeeds through great effort; *Sādhyasādhya* causes extreme suffering.
*Sādhya* becomes *Susiddha* through devotion; *Sādhyāri* destroys one's own refuge.
Through study, those who have attained perfection and those whose perfections are well-established shall bestow the desired fruit.
Because success through recitation and other means is easily achieved with a *susiddha* mantra, whereas it is otherwise with others;
however, a *susiddha* mantra is indeed easily mastered due to the effort exerted in previous lives.
Therefore, a practitioner who recites this mantra will achieve all the accomplishments of the Siddhas;
even in the case of malevolent sorcery against an enemy, if it should occur on the earth, there shall be no misfortune for the two [parties]. (16.124)
If perfected by means of an enemy [mantra], it will certainly destroy one's own family;
but if perfected by an enemy, it will strike down those who are to be accomplished as enemies, as well as women.
And having attained one's own mantra through the secrets of concealing the *kula*, one becomes firmly established by means of the noble, supreme, and great mantra. (16.126)

This has been said, O Maheśānī: having abandoned other doctrines, [one should practice] the supreme Māla-mantra consisting of three seed-syllables, which was obtained in a dream and given by a woman. (16.127)
O Goddess, for those [who have not been purified], the purification of the Siddhas and so forth does not exist at all, O Maheśvarī, in the Cakrarāja, the place of worship of the Śrīvidyā. (16.128)
Adorned by a multitude of great lords of the treasury, she dwells within the mind.
"I worship the sandal that generates all auspiciousness"—having uttered this, the wise one should worship [the goddess] beginning with Para-jyotiḥkośā. || 16-130 ||
In this very manner, one should worship the five pentads;
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should worship the Śaiva vision within the Bindu.
The vision of the Śākta [wheel] is all-pervading, O Supreme Goddess;
however, the vision of the Brāhma [wheel], which is to be worshipped, is located on the first circle of the earth, O Beloved. (16.132)
O Goddess, one should worship the Vaiṣṇava doctrine to the left of Śiva;
O lotus-eyed one, the solar doctrine occurs in the wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra).
In the wheel of stability (sthiticakra), however, the supreme Buddhist philosophy is to be worshipped.
Having thus worshipped everything, one should satisfy Śrīvidyā.
One should again offer libations three times with the *tattvamudrā*;
this *tattvamudrā* is said to be formed by the thumb and the ring finger. (16.135)
O Goddess, one should offer the flower with the mudrā known as Jñāna;
the Jñāna-mudrā is established through the union of the thumb and the forefinger. (16.136)
Having propitiated [the deity] with all ritual services, one should display the mudrās in sequence;
then, one should perform the limb-enclosure (*aṅgāvaraṇa*) arising from the Śrīvidyā mantra. (16.137)
The worship of the limbs is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center;
the pair of seed-syllables consisting of Māyā and Lakṣmī, however, follows the previous sequence.

O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, it has been taught that one should join [the mantras] as a triad, or else by means of the method of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*), O you who are worshipped by heroes. (16.139)
Having joined them together, O fair-faced one, one should worship all of them in due order;
in the Trailokyamohana-cakra, one should worship the manifest Yoginīs.
In a square [mandala] with four doors, adorned and bestowing success, one should worship Aṇimā on the right side of the western door. (16.141)
One should worship Laghimā on the right side at the northern gate;
O Dear One, one should worship Mahimā at the eastern gate, on the left side. || 16.142 ||
O Goddess of the gods, the attainment of lordship [is performed] at the southern gate as before.
Or, by that same sequence of yoga, one attains mastery over the wind element in the northwest.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Icchāsiddhi in the eastern quarter and Prāptisiddhi, Sarvakāmā, and Siddhi in the south-western quarter.
O beautiful goddess, they are to be known in the form of the downward and upward sequences:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Aindrī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī. (16.146)
Vārāhī, as well as Ṣaṣṭhī and Cāmuṇḍā, are the seven Mothers;
Mahālakṣmī is the eighth, according to the sequence starting from the west.
On the left side, however, they should be worshipped starting from the northwest (vāyavya) as before:
Saṃkṣobhaṇī, Drāvaṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśyā, Unmādinī, and Mahāṅkuśā. || 16.148 ||
One should worship Khecarī, Bījā, and the one called Yonī, as well as Trikhaṇḍā;
having worshipped these, one should worship the supreme Cakreśī Tripurā. (16.149)
O lotus-faced one, one should display the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā, which accomplishes all purposes and goals, in front of the siddhi of aṇimā.
The wheel that fulfills all hopes is presided over by the secret Yoginīs;
therefore, O Goddess, one should worship it with sixteen spokes for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose. (16.151)
O Goddess, [I praise] Kāmākarṣiṇī, as well as Buddhyākarṣiṇī, Ahaṃkārākarṣiṇī, and the one whose form is the attraction of sound.
She who draws in touch and is formless, and she who is formless yet draws in forms; she who attracts tastes and who performs the attraction of scents.
Likewise, O beloved, [there are] Cittākaṣīṇikā and Dhairyākaṣīṇikā,
as well as Nāmākaṣīṇikā and Bīṇākaṣīṇikā.
O Dear One, [she is] Amṛtākarṣiṇī, Bījākarṣiṇī, Śarīrākarṣiṇī, and she whose form is the attraction of the self (Ātmākarṣaṇarūpiṇī). || 16-155 ||

In the sixteen-spoked [cakra], starting from the west and proceeding in reverse order, these sixteen digits (kalās) accompanied by the vowels are to be worshipped; they are the eternal ones, whose mandalas drip with nectar. || 16-156 ||
One should worship the goddess Cakreśvarī, the Mistress of Tripura, who bestows prosperity;
O Dear One, one should worship her in front of the form of Kāmākarṣaṇī.
Having displayed the mudrā that causes all to flee, one should offer [the oblation].
In the wheel of universal agitation, one should worship those whose names are most secret. (16.158)
One should worship Anaṅgakusumā in the east with the *ka*-group, and likewise Anaṅgamekhalā in the south with the *ca*-group. (16.159)
One should worship Anaṅgamadanā with the retrograde *ṭa*-group; then, one should worship Anaṅgamadanāturā with the *ta*-group in the north. || 16-160 ||
One should worship Anaṅgarekhā in the southeast with the *pa*-group;
one should worship Anaṅgavegā in the southwest with the *ya*-group. || 16.161 ||
In the northwest, one should worship Anaṅgāṅkuśā with the *śa*-group;
in the northeast, Anaṅgādimālinī is to be worshipped with the *la*-group. (16–162)
One should worship the goddess Cakreśvarī, and then Tripurasundarī,
who bestows universal sovereignty at the tip of Anaṅgakusumā.
And one should display the mudrā of universal attraction, O Goddess praised by the gods;
having offered the worship of the wheel, one should then worship the fourth wheel.
The power that agitates all, as well as the power that subdues all;
the power that attracts all, and the power that causes delight to all.
The power that deludes all, the power that causes the paralysis of all,
the power that causes everyone to yawn, and likewise the power that brings all under control.
The ninth power is the Supreme Goddess Sarvārtharañjinī;
she is the power that intoxicates all and the power that accomplishes all aims. (16.167)
She is filled with all perfections and likewise consists of all mantras;
she possesses the power of the fourteen spokes and brings about the destruction of all dualities. || 16.168 ||

O Goddess of the gods, in the wheel that bestows all good fortune, they should be worshipped in reverse order starting from the west, following the left-hand path; thus they grant all accomplishments. || 16-169 ||
Then, one should worship in front the power Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, the supreme Cakreśvarī, the bestower of accomplishments, who dwells in Tripura. || 16-170 ||
Then, having displayed the mudrā of subjugation and immediately thereafter having made the offering, [one worships] the Kula-yoginīs in the ten-spoked wheel that accomplishes all aims. || 16–171 ||
One should worship [these goddesses] in sequence during the fifth [period], for they grant the accomplishment of all purposes:
the Goddess who bestows all siddhis, and likewise she who bestows all prosperity.
The Goddess who brings about everything dear, who effects all auspiciousness, who fulfills all desires, and who liberates from all suffering. || 16-173 ||
She who pacifies all death, she who wards off all obstacles, the goddess beautiful in every limb, the bestower of all prosperity. (16–174)
One should worship these [goddesses] in the ten-spoked [cakra] in reverse order, starting from the west;
O Goddess, one should worship the Mistress of the Cakra (Cakranāyikā) in front, who bestows all accomplishments.
O Goddess, one should worship Tripurāśrī, the bestower of all accomplishments; and having displayed the Sarvonmādana mudrā, one should present the offering.
In the wheel that produces all protection, one should worship the Yoginīs, beginning with Nāgabuddhā;
thereafter [one worships] Sarvajñā, Sarvaśakti, and Sarvaiśvaryapradā.
The Goddess who consists of all-knowledge, the destroyer of all diseases,
whose nature is the support of all, and likewise the remover of all sins.
The Goddess consists of all bliss, her very nature being the protection of all;
she bestows the fruits of all desired objects and grants all prosperity.
One should worship in the lineage of the womb-vulva (paṅktayoni) by way of reverse order, starting from the west;
O Goddess, one should worship Mālinī, the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśī), in front of Sarvajñā.
Having displayed the great hook and the great mudrā, and having made the offering, O beloved Maheśānī, one should worship the yoginīs in the central wheel.
O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, within the eight-cornered wheel that removes all diseases,
reside the secret yoginīs, Vaśinī and the others, who bestow spiritual accomplishments.
One should worship the previously mentioned [deities] in sequence according to the reverse order starting from the west;
Siddhāmbā, the mistress of the wheel, is to be worshipped in front of Vaśinī.
Thereafter, one should present the Khecarī mudrā;
then, [worship] in the triangle of the wheel that bestows all siddhis and grants all desires. || 16-184 ||
One should worship the yoginīs known as Parā, Aparā, and Rahasyā,
having fully uttered the five arrows consisting of Kāma and Kāmeśvarī.
O Great Goddess, one should worship the deity Bāṇa from the one called Jambhana;
the first is of the nature of *dha*, while the second is of the nature of *tha*.
One should worship the deity of the bow called Mohanā belonging to Kāmeśvarī;
the second is the pair of nooses belonging to Bhuvaneśānī, which brings others under control. || 16-187 ||
O Dear One, the attraction of the three worlds belongs to Kāmeśa and Kāmeśī;
that which is called the goad (aṅkuśa) is my own seed-syllable, known as the paralyzer (stambhana).
O Dear One, one should worship the goad of Kāmeśa and Kāmeśī outside the enclosure of the six limbs, worshipping them in sequence nearby.
One should worship in the four directions according to the sequence starting from the west;
and one should worship Kāmeśvarī, the power of Rudra, in front with the first *kūṭa*.
Having worshipped the Vaiṣṇavī [śakti] in the southeast corner with the second peak-syllable, Kāmākhyā, one should worship her with the third.
One should worship Bhagamālā, the power of Brahmā, in the north; Viśvamātṛkā, the mistress of the wheel (cakreśvarī), known as Ambikā, in front of Kāmeśī.
Then, having worshipped the seed-syllable mudrā,
one should present the worship of the wheel (cakrapūjā) within the sovereign wheel consisting of universal bliss, known as the Bindu.
O beloved, listen: one should worship Tripurā, the Yoginī known as the supreme and secret [essence], whose form is Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, and who is the object of pure awareness.
Having uttered the three peaks (kūṭatraya), one should worship that which is the nature of all vidyās,
the form of all deities, and composed of all things.
One should also [worship] that very Cakreśī, Mahātripurasundarī,
who is the Śrīvidyā of sixteen syllables and bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The sovereign of all the circles of the mandala, honored by all the scriptures,
the mistress of all traditions, adorned with knowledge, and whose form is Brahman.
Having worshipped thoroughly with ritual services such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should again offer libations three times with the root mantra. || 16-198 ||
Having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should then display the other mudrās in their proper sequence.
[With] purifiers produced from the essence of trees, possessing a beautiful fragrance... || 16-199 ||
One should incense the Supreme Goddess with excellent incenses consisting of ten ingredients and so forth—
namely, musk, saffron, olibanum, and that which originates from the Śāla tree, O Goddess.
The preceptor should constantly burn incense composed of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, white sugar, clarified butter, and honey, for the sake of attaining all auspicious success.
O Goddess, by means of the incense mantra, even that which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds [is attained]. Around the circle of the altar, there should be rows of lamps soaked in ghee.
One should worship with [lamps] made of camphor or filled with oil;
then, having offered incense and lamps, one should perform the libation as before, O Dear One.
O Goddess who is worshipped by the gods, one should perform the rite of *ārātīka* as previously described.
I shall now describe another *ārātīka* that fulfills all desires.
The wise one should draw a wheel in the center of a vessel fashioned from gold or other materials;
having filled it with rice, he should then divide it into nine parts.
Immediately after that, having fashioned nine globes in the form of the moon,
[he should prepare] pairs of *maṇḍaka* cakes filled with a core of sugar.
Having fashioned the *ghaṭikās*, one should join them by means of the sevenfold [set] seven times;
thus, one should apply nine *ghaṭikās* in the manner of seven times seven.
Having placed them within the eight corners, one should cast the balls on top.
Then, having scattered the *caṇa*-mudrā, one should offer lamps cooked in ghee.
One should place fist-shaped objects and fists here and there;
having lit lamps thereafter, one should worship them with the five jewels.
One should worship the vidyās seated upon the five lion-thrones there, having raised them up from the head nine times again and again. (16–210)
O Goddess, having circumambulated [the mandala] again and again like the nine enclosures, one should then emerge and establish the great splendor consisting of a garland of lamps. || 16-211 ||
O Dear One, one should meditate with steady eyes upon the procedure for the enemy;
[one should offer] an oblation of food endowed with six flavors and combined with white cakes and other sweets.
Filled with maṇḍakas stuffed with sugar and honey, accompanied by milk-rice (pāyasa), and filled with pure boiled rice as white as pearls and camphor. || 16-213 ||
Abundantly beautified by ghee and camphor, adorned with a full offering of ghee,
and enriched with the splendor of various side-dishes and *vaṭaka* cakes glowing like saffron.
Filled with black gram rice and adorned with various flavorful drinks;
filled with ghee and milk, and adorned with the four mudrās.
Having made a formal resolve for the Supreme Goddess, one should perform the rite of the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).
With the root mantra, one should offer five oblations accompanied by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Six oblations for the six limbs are proclaimed as the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma).
Then, having sat upon a pleasant seat, thereafter on the left side... [16-217]
The practitioner, with his knees touching the ground, should draw a square mandala in its center from the upward-turned palms joined together, O Dear One. (16–218)
Then, one should worship the mandala called Vyoma (Space) in the center of the triangle;
[the mantra] is the supreme Vāgbhava ending with "to the Mandala" (maṇḍalāya), followed by the heart-mantra (hṛt). || 16-219 ||
O Dear One, having placed the mandala to be worshipped in the mouth,
one should worship this fourfold mandala with the mantra.
Having placed mandalas in the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest corners as before, one should then worship them as before, O Dear One. (16–221)
One should offer the bali-oblation as before for the sake of all prosperity, O Maheśānī, to Baṭuka, to the Yoginīs, and to Vallabha. || 16-222 ||
One should offer the bali-oblation to Kṣetrapāla and Gaṇeśa as before;
then, one should cast it upon the maṇḍala prepared on the left side.

There, one should worship the support (ādhāra) and the vessel provided with food and water; having consecrated it with the mantra along with its causal syllable, one should offer the bali-oblation to all beings.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, [one should recite] the mantra of sixteen syllables three times;
then, O Bhuvaneśānī, [one should utter] the Tāra (Om), followed by the word "sarvavighna" (all obstacles). || 16-225 ||

Uttering the syllable *huṃ* and the consort of Fire (*vahnivallabhā*) for all beings, including those who perform ritual acts (*kṛt*), one should offer the bali-oblation with the mudrā known as Tattva.
The five-fold offering (balipañcaka) has been declared to be the provider of all protection for the virtuous;
one should offer the five offerings together within the pervasive maṇḍala.
O Goddess, standing on the left side, he shall become the remover of all obstacles;
having worshipped the entire wheel according to the rule, O Supreme Goddess,
by the grace of the venerable Guru, O Goddess, he becomes omniscient and a knower of all principles.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of Śrīvidyā," in the glorious Jñānārṇava, the Tantra of the Nityās, within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, [I have] not heard this meaning."
The supreme ritual procedure for the Śrīcakra of the sixteen-syllable vidyā.
And whatever [practice] such as recitation there is, which is the means for accomplishing each individual syllable—tell me that, O Maheśāna, if I am dear to you. (17.2)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O you who are auspicious in all your limbs, to the supreme procedure of Śrīvidyā, by the mere knowledge of which the omnipresent Lord himself becomes the creator and the destroyer. (17.3)
Wherever the Śrīcakra, joined with the sequence, is worshipped according to this method, one shall bring everything under control; of this there is no doubt.
The city, the entire region, and the circle of the country come under one's control, O Adrijā; all women become submissive, tormented by the blazing fire of desire. (17.5)
With hearts deluded by ignorance, yet with their minds fixed upon the practitioner—by the sight of him, O Mistress of the Gods, all women become [enamored]. (17.6)
Relying upon the rosary, which takes the form of the letters of the Mātṛkā,
[one attains] speech made of pearls, which bestows the fruit of liberation.
She eternally bestows all accomplishments and brings all kings under her control;
as she is fashioned from pearls, so too is she made of crystal. (17.8)
A rosary of rudrākṣa beads bestows liberation and the abundance of all prosperity; a coral rosary, however, is for subjugation and accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings. (17.9)
A rosary of rubies bestows fruits [of worldly success], while one that grants the fruit of sovereignty;
however, a rosary of putrajīvaka beads bestows knowledge and prosperity upon the virtuous.
Through a rosary of lotus seeds, supreme and great prosperity is born;
a garland of red sandalwood, moreover, bestows all enjoyments. (17.11)
Then, having worshipped the rosary and anointed it with sandalwood paste,
the wise one should resort to it and recite the vidyā exactly one hundred thousand times.
Women indeed cause his mind, though it be perfectly steady, to wander;
at that time, the best of practitioners should recite a second hundred thousand [mantras]. (17.13)
The daughters of the lordly nāgas from the depths of Pātāla agitate him;
yet, by means of the nets of their sidelong glances, the practitioner does not fall into delusion. (17.14)
Then the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform three hundred thousand [recitations].
When the third hundred thousand has been reached, the celestial maidens cause [the disciple] to melt.
Through pride born of beauty, which causes intoxication with good fortune, they surely cause the practitioner to melt; therefore, his mind becomes unstable.
Then, having performed the recitation three hundred thousand times—which is effective for destroying all sins—one who stands firm in the vow with a composed mind [attains success]. || 17-17 ||
O beloved, he brings under his control men and women, as well as all that is moving and stationary, including those dwelling on the earth, in heaven, and in the netherworld.
One should draw the sovereign wheel with substances such as gorocanā and other materials; in its center, one should depict an excellent image that is exceedingly beautiful and delightful. (17–19)
Then, O Goddess, one should meditate upon her as blazing, accompanied by her name, and fearless due to the knowledge of the great seed-syllable, extending for thousands of yojanas.
O Goddess, never seen before, she is difficult to find even when merely heard of; she may be a beautiful princess, entirely devoid of fear and shame. (17–21)
O beloved, when the practitioner, having become situated in the center of the wheel, contemplates while being fully absorbed in the mantra, she, being deluded by the mantra, comes to him.
Having likewise visualized himself as ruddy, with the brilliance of a thousand rising suns,
and having likewise rendered the deity to be accomplished (sādhya) ruddy, the wise one should mutter the mantra.
By this sequential yoga, one becomes personally endowed with the form of Kandarpa, possessing all beauty and charm, and beloved by women. (17–24)
He is the fortunate one in all worlds, the subduer of all worlds;
his body is bound with mudrās and adorned with all red offerings.
O Goddess, whoever fulfills the wheel whose name is proclaimed,
he shall become like a servant, O wealthy lady, or even a sovereign king.
One should place the name of whichever woman [is intended] in the center of the wheel;
O Maheśānī, while remaining unseen, the wise man should assume the *yonimudrā*. (17–27)
By force, one quickly brings forth a yakṣiṇī,
a princess, a nāga maiden, an apsarā, a sky-farer, or a celestial woman.
A Vidyādharī of divine form, the daughter of a seer, the beauty of her enemies,
tormented by the fever of love, with her circular hips quivering.

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, through the yoga of meditating upon the great art of passion (mahākāmakalā), [one attains the state of] those whose inner hearts are pierced by the arrows of desire and whose eyes are restless.
It would agitate the women of the heavens, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld.
One part of gorocanā and one part of saffron—‖ 17-31 ‖
Then, O Goddess, one should grind two equal parts of sandalwood;
with this, one should apply a *tilaka* on one side, which brings the three worlds under one's control.
Having consecrated [the object] one hundred and eight times with the mantra, one shall bring it under control—the king, the city, or the village—whatever is shown by that [practice]. (17.33)
O Supreme Goddess, by means of the mantra, all of that—betel, incense, water, leaves, flowers, fruit, and curd—comes under his control. || 17-34 ||
Milk, clarified butter, powdered food, clothing, and camphor; musk, saffron, sandalwood, cloves, and nutmeg.
O Supreme Goddess, whatever fruit or object there may be in its entirety,
if one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and gives it to anyone whatsoever— || 17-36 ||
O Goddess, he becomes submissive; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Indeed, all women become submissive and become like female servants. (17.37)
This method for attracting the world has been taught; it shall not be otherwise.
The practitioner of mantra should write it on the ground with yellow pigment (rocanā) at a secret location. || 17-38 ||
Having depicted the beautiful and highly enchanting image, richly adorned with elegant ornaments and arrayed in all manner of jewelry.
She is joined with the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the circle of the birth-place;
she is the Great Vidyā of one's birth-name, ending with the syllable *aṅkuśa* (the goad) and the syllable *vīta* (the fearless).
One should write the syllable *mada* at all the joints of the body;
one should contemplate it as dissolved within the joints of the body, with the luster of a pomegranate flower. (17.41)
Then, having become oriented toward that hope, one should oneself assume the form of the Goddess, bind the Kṣobhiṇī mudrā, and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. (17.42)
Having directed her into the temple of passion, which consists of the digits of the moon and the sun,
she then had all her limbs impaired and was tormented by the arrows of Kāma.
With a mind focused on no other, wandering in the delusion of love, and languid with passion—
one should thus attract a woman even from a distance of a hundred yojanas.
O beloved, one should write the entire *mātṛkā* on the outside of the wheel,
either on birch bark, a golden plate, a silver plate, or a copper plate.
He shall be invulnerable to all living beings, especially to tigers and the like;

likewise, adorned with the wheel of his own secret signs joined with the *mātṛkā*, and by means of camphor, saffron, and other such substances, he shall attain freedom from old age and immortality. (17–46)
By this method, O Goddess, with yellow pigment, aloe-wood, and saffron, || 17-47 ||
O fair-faced one, while drawing the name of the person to be accomplished by means of the wheel-yoga,
it should be placed within any [part] of one's own name, surrounded on all sides.
O Maheśānī, one shall bring under control the entire circle of living beings, both stationary and moving, by treading upon them with one's feet; of this there is no doubt. (17.49)
By means of the radiant *Kāmakūṭa* of Mahātripurasundarī, one should seize each individual syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished. || 17-50 ||
One should cause [the disciple] to enter even outside with all the letters of the Mātṛkā;
one should place it in the middle of gold on the crest or on the left arm.
Wherever one should maintain this [mantra] which brings the three worlds under control, O Goddess of the Gods, it indeed makes even a lord of kings become a servant. (17.52)
Kings, horses, serpents, and elephants fierce and intoxicated with rut—
even tigers and maned lions in their madness— indeed become submissive to him.

Having announced the name of the city according to the previous sequence, O Daughter of the Mountain, one should cause it to be deposited either in the center, at a crossroads, or in the four directions. (17.54)
A great agitation arises among women, even among great people;
likewise, it arises before all wicked ones who stand in front. || 17-55 ||
Within this [palace] was the earth, complete with its mountains, forests, and thickets,
blazing and adorned by the circle of all the lords of kings, clothed in the oceans.
He who meditates for six months becomes like Kāma himself in person; O beloved, by the mere casting of a sidelong glance, women come under his control.
O Goddess, having seen you, one may draw toward oneself kings, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, animals, and the entire world with all its moving and non-moving beings. (17.58)
Upon seeing it, one shall destroy one's rivals; there is no need for deliberation in this matter.
[It likewise destroys] bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and fevers such as those beginning with the *cāturthika*.
Having seen diseases such as colic and abdominal tumors, it destroys them in an instant;
O Dear One, this [mantra], beautiful with vermilion, when worshipped at night— || 17-60 ||
O beautiful one, when one thus correctly draws Śrī even from a hundred yojanas away—in all directions and intermediate points, and even those dwelling in heaven—[she comes]. (17.61)
Having written [the name] on birch bark with yellow orpiment, agallochum, and saffron, one swiftly brings under control [the person], along with their children, cattle, and kinsmen. (17.62)
In the midst of that, having duly worshipped his own city, country, mandala, and even the district, by name as Vidarbha; || 17-63 ||
Having placed it within the earth, one shall bring the three worlds under control;
alternatively, one may wear it on the neck, on the crest-lock, or at the base of the arm.
O auspicious lady, wherever it may be situated, it will agitate even a great city.
Likewise, the juice of *dhattūra* combined with the milk of the sun (*arka*) [is used]. (17.65)
Then, having combined rocanā and kuṅkuma together with lākṣā and laktaka, and further adding musk and camphor, one should mix them all into a single substance. || 17-66 ||
O Maheśvarī, having drawn this wheel with the name of whomever [it is written],
for that person there shall be no fear from tigers, elephants, disease, enemies, serpents, and so forth.
O Goddess, there is no fear of thieves, planetary afflictions, water-dangers, misfortunes, śākinīs, or ḍākinīs,
nor any fear arising from the malevolent spells of others.
O Goddess, one should constantly maintain this; it shall destroy untimely death.
Alternatively, one should [worship] the Goddess situated in the center, located between the two triangles, joined with her own name and marked with yellow pigment and saffron. (17–70)
And having caused [the mantra] to be deposited, within seven days one shall become a slave or a servant;
having drawn [the figure] with yellow substances, one should worship it with yellow flowers. (17.71)
Facing the eastern direction, one shall paralyze all disputants;
O Goddess, the thousand-faced one becomes bewildered at that very moment.
O Goddess of the Gods, having drawn a wheel with the juice of great indigo, he who is eloquent by name indeed becomes like a stone.
Having joined the name [of the victim] according to the ritual rules, the wise man, facing south, O Maheśānī, should burn it in the fire; this, O beloved, is the slaying of enemies. || 17-74 ||
Having thoroughly mixed [the powder] with buffalo dung and horse dung on a stone slab, and having scraped it with cow urine, one should inscribe the name as before. (17.75)
Having cast [the substance] into the midst of fermented gruel (āranāla), it becomes a means for inciting hatred;
having written the name with yellow pigment (rocanā) in the middle of a crow's wing feather. || 17.76 ||
Hanging in the sky, it causes the eradication of enemies;
indeed, [it is prepared] with great indigo, yellow pigment (rocanā), milk, and the juice of lac. || 17-77 ||
Having drawn [the diagram], the practitioner should wear it; by this he shall bring all castes under his control.
By this very procedure, one should install [the deity] within the midst of water.
Bathed with that water and having drunk it, it brings everything under one's control;
through that water, good fortune arises—of this there is no doubt.
O fair-eyed one, one should correctly visualize the earth or a city situated in the midst of this as blazing intensely, and after seven days, it shall be thoroughly shaken.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe that which destroys great sins;
one should worship Śivā with fragrant flowers, O beloved Goddess.
One whose soul is burdened with great sins shall become free from sin at that very moment.
[This is achieved] by means of *śamī*, *dūrvā* sprouts, *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, or even leaves born from the *arka* tree. (17.82)
By doing so for one month, a person destroys the impurity created over seven lifetimes;
facing the eastern direction, he should worship with yellow substances.
Having drawn [the diagram] in the yellow place, one should paralyze all disputants;
facing the northern direction, one should draw it with vermilion powder.
The wise one should worship according to the rules and bring all the world under his control;
facing westward, he should draw [the mandala] with sandalwood paste.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the wise man shall captivate the minds of all women; he becomes beloved, O Goddess, and brings them under his control like a servant girl.
If one faces the direction of Yama and worships Kṛṣṇa, the loss of the mantra occurs for that person whose name is inscribed [upon it]. (17.87)
O Supreme Goddess, it is worshipped in due order, as before, in the corners of Agni, Rākṣasa, Vāyu, and Śambhu. || 17-88 ||
It shall bring about paralysis, enmity, disease, and the eradication of enemies;
the wise man should cast the wheel drawn with yellow pigment (rocanā) into the midst of milk.
O Goddess, it certainly brings everything under one's control; of this there is no doubt.
When properly placed in the midst of cow urine, it becomes a means for the eradication of enemies. (17.90)
The King of Wheels situated within a triangle causes enmity;
situated in the midst of a blazing fire, it causes the destruction of enemies.
O Maheśvarī, one should draw [the design] with vermilion powder in a secluded place at a crossroads, starting from the outermost edge and proceeding toward the center. || 17.92 ||
One should place the Mātṛkā, beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Kṣa', there;
and one should worship it at night according to the sequence of the Kula practice.
O Goddess, the practitioner becomes a sky-walker; of this there is no doubt.
In the same way, one should worship the Kula path on either of the two mountains.
Having attained freedom from old age and death, the master of mantras becomes happy. On a day presided over by the great elements, the wise one should worship the wheel in the cremation ground.
Following the previous sequence and according to the ritual rules, the practitioner with a steady mind [attains] the perfection of the sword, the perfection of the mind, and even the pill.
The power of sandals, the accomplishment of the vetāla, the accomplishment of the mind, and the bestowing of minerals;
the accomplishment of great caverns, and that which arises from yakṣiṇīs and servants.
The practitioner of mantra obtains all that; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the great worship of Śrīvidyā.
For sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, this is the supreme *puraścaraṇa*;
O Great Goddess, one should worship the supreme wheel with red lotuses.
Accompanied by all the rays of light and preceded by the eternal tradition (nityāmnāya),
O Goddess, it is adorned with camphor powder according to the sequence of the Kula practice.
O Goddess of gods, within just a single month, one shall destroy all the millions of great sins committed in previous lives; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, auspiciousness remains beautiful and very firm in his house.
O Maheśānī, one should worship Śivā with hibiscus flowers as before.
O Supreme Goddess, for one month exactly, in the same manner as before;
O Beloved, [one is freed from] the sins such as the killing of a Brahmin committed in previous births.
One shall destroy [all obstacles] here; of this there is no doubt. The wise man becomes wealthy.
O Dear One, one should worship as before with young *ketaka* leaves. || 17-104 ||
One shall destroy even the multitudes of minor sins (upapātaka) within a single month;
incomparable good fortune arises for him—of this there is no doubt. (17.105)
One should worship for the duration of one month with delightful lotuses;
O Supreme Goddess, as before, this destroys former sins. (17.106)
One should worship Śivā as before with Campaka flowers, which are most delightful;
by doing so for just one month, one surely destroys the sins accumulated over hundreds of births.
By the grace of Tripurā, the practitioner of mantra shall become possessed of good fortune.
O Great Goddess, one should worship Parā with large white lotuses. (17.108)
O Dear One, as before, one shall destroy the sins accumulated over twenty lifetimes;
by merely a month [of practice], liberation stands within his grasp. (17.109)
O Goddess, one should worship for exactly one month with Bandhūka flowers;
the wise man shall bring the three worlds under his control and burn away his former sins.
One should worship with bilva leaves together with aquatic flowers, O Supreme Goddess, for the duration of one month with a serene mind, as before. || 17-111 ||
O Goddess, he shall always be prosperous and the remover of all sins,
[worshipping] with *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *kunda*, and *śatapatraka* flowers.
One should worship for the duration of a single month with white lotuses mixed [with other offerings];
by this very sequence of the Kula practice, the sin accumulated over a hundred births is destroyed.
It destroys the sin produced by the killing of a Brahmin and other such acts; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Goddess, liberation is in his hand, and by his word he becomes equal to the Lord of Life (Brahmā). || 17-114 ||
O beloved, having worshipped for exactly one month with agasti, bāṇa, bandhūka, and red lotuses according to the previous sequence, one becomes clear-minded. || 17-115 ||
The practitioner of mantra shall destroy all sins and become manifest as equal to Kāma himself.
[17.116] (With *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *bakula*, and *nāgakeśara* flowers, O Goddess... [17.116]
One should worship, in sequence as before, with beautiful white water-lilies and red sindūra;
within a single month, incomparable good fortune arises for him. (17.117)
O Goddess, it shall destroy even the evil born of a thousand lifetimes.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for Śrīvidyā," in the venerable Jñānārṇava, the Nityā Tantra.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
The Lord said: "O sinless one, I shall now describe to you the ritual procedure for the worship with jewels."
O Goddess, one should indeed fashion flowers made of rubies.
They should perform the worship of the King of Mandalas as before,
with various fragrant flowers, camphor powder, and sandalwood.
Within twenty-one nights, she indeed makes twenty rulers of the earth her female slaves and destroys great diseases. (18.3)
The mantra-practitioner becomes as radiant as the sun; of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful one, one should fashion golden flowers with pearls and gems. (18.4)
They should perform worship with various flowers as before;
within twenty-one nights, O beloved, the wives of kings will be brought under one's control.
O Goddess, one endowed with artistic grace becomes fortunate on earth;
one should worship with many golden flowers fashioned from coral. || 18-6 ||
As before, O Supreme Goddess, according to the sequence of the Kula practice,
with various flowers, O Goddess, O Mistress of the Gods, within three weeks— || 18-7 ||
All cruel beings become subject to him; he shall destroy the hosts of his enemies.
Likewise, one should worship with golden flowers set within emeralds. (18.8)
For twenty-one nights, one should worship the sequence with various flowers;
the gods will grant him boons and his enemy shall perish—there is no other way. (18.9)
O Goddess of the Suras, one should worship the Cakra with flowers fashioned from gold and set with great rubies for twenty-one days. || 18-10 ||
O Goddess, by the power of that liquor, one shall become equal to Bṛhaspati.
|| 18-11 || [Adorned] with flowers fashioned of gold and resplendent with vajra armlets. || 18-11 ||
Within twenty-one nights, he shall delude this world;
gods and demons alike will come under his control—of this there is no doubt.
One should worship the discus with golden flowers made of sapphire;
likewise, with blue lotuses for twenty-one nights. (18.13)
Enemies go to their destruction, and indeed the rest become submissive;
the wise one should worship with gold using flowers fashioned from *gomedaka* gems.
And with *kiṃśuka* flowers, O Supreme Goddess, as before;
within seven days the enemies become submissive, and their destruction occurs among them. (18.15)
O beloved, within three weeks it destroys the accumulation of great sins;
indeed, those who live by eating raw flesh become submissive, without a doubt. (18.16)
One should worship the sequence with golden flowers set in lapis lazuli;
having worshipped with campaka and other such flowers, one may paralyze the three worlds in an instant.
By twenty-one recitations, one becomes a remover of all sins.
O Goddess, one should not worship with flowers that have been stale, even if they are made of gold.
O Supreme Goddess, if one should worship Śivā with flowers that have become *nirmālya* (already offered) or with remnants, or even with golden flowers made of the nine gems— || 18–19 ||
At that time, gods, humans, serpents, rākṣasas, and the like—all of them certainly become submissive within three weeks; of this there is no doubt. (18–20)
One shall destroy the sins accumulated over ten million births; of this there is no doubt.
One should worship with flowers made of gold and jewels, and with the nine precious gems.
Then, O Daughter of the Mountain, it is as if ten horse-sacrifices have been performed.
Now listen to what happens when there is no abundance of gold, jewels, and other such wealth. (18–22)
The worship should be performed with those very flowers by the most excellent practitioners;
O Goddess of the Gods, whatever flower is offered wherever, that [is the appropriate offering]. (18–23)
In each respective case, it should be offered; one should not give according to one's own whim.
One should worship the Lord of the Mandala with the very form of the ornament. || 18-24 ||
O Śivā, by means of golden flowers alone, one may paralyze the three worlds;
within a single month, even the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes are destroyed.
He would destroy and delude the entire earth encircled by the ocean.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Detailed Exposition of the Ritual for the Worship of the Golden Jewel of Śrīvidyā," in the venerable Jñānārṇava, the Tantra of the Nityās.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
The Goddess said: Tripurā is the supreme Śakti, the one who brings the three worlds under her control.
O Lord, tell me the means for attaining this supreme bliss.
"O Lord of Gods, if I am dear to you, [tell me] of the three seeds.
Īśvara said:
"O lady of excellent limbs, this Vidyā has come down through the lineage of succession. (19-2)
When remembered, she destroys the bonds of existence and removes all sins; O Īśānī, when meditated upon, she accomplishes all goals through the recitation of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra. (19.3)
When worshipped, she destroys suffering, misfortune, poverty, and fear;
there is no doubt that she pacifies the multitude of obstacles through the performance of fire offerings.
I shall describe to you the accomplishment of each of the three separate seeds.
[Clad in white garments, adorned with perfumes and camphor. (19.5)
Adorned with ornaments of shimmering pearls, wearing a pure white garland,
seated in a bright palace, he was fully endowed with the practice of celibacy.
One should worship with white flowers and offer a very radiant food-oblation consisting of milk-rice enriched with ghee,
as well as rice mixed with the fruit of immortality (amṛtaphala).
O Queen of the Gods, one should present to the Goddess Vāgīśvarī an offering (naivedya) consisting of ghee and sweetmeats, and filled with various kinds of pure food. || 19-8 ||
With most auspicious ritual services, one should accomplish the speech of liberation;
the wise man, while recollecting Vāgīśī, should mutter the Vidyā known as Vāgbhava.
White as camphor, adorned with ornaments of pure flowers,
wearing exceedingly bright garments, and decorated with diamonds and pearls.
Her hands are radiant with a rosary made of pure pearls and stainless gems; she holds a book, displays the gesture of granting boons, and bestows fearlessness. || 19.11 ||
O Great Goddess, by meditating in this way, one becomes the sovereign of all vidyās;
[one should visualize her] raining down a shower of nectar flowing from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Therefore, one should meditate upon the tongue as consisting of light, having the nature of a lamp;
otherwise, a fool may become like a stone or equal to a living corpse.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, the practitioner of the power of Kāmakalā, beautiful with red ornaments and anointed with red perfumes and unguents, [should proceed]. (19.14)
Properly clothed in red garments, one should worship in the center with the essence of the Kāmakalā, using various red flowers, saffron, and other such substances.
From the base (mūlādhāra) up to the Brahma-randhra, she has the nature of a shimmering lamp;
she is adorned with ornaments possessing the luster of the bandhūka flower.
Holding in her hands the sugarcane, the bow, the flower-arrows, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
she fills the three worlds with the vermilion of her body.
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate [upon this]; it can delude the three worlds in an instant.
Kings, serpents, rākṣasas, and gods all come under one's control. (19-18)
O Goddess, like Kandarpa, he takes away the pride of women;
and a woman conceived of in the mind shall become submissive to him like a maidservant.
One who meditates upon her, who resembles the shimmering moon and possesses a body as red as the rising sun, shall agitate even the celestial beauties within the womb of women.
How much more so, O Goddess, would a human woman delude even the three worlds?
This very goddess, with the luster of vermilion, was contemplated in my heart for a moment. (19–21)
Then one should quickly summon Rambhā or even Tilottamā, having meditated upon a woman of red complexion who possesses his very essence. (19–22)
One should visualize seed-syllables upon her head, raining down flowing nectar;
meditating thus, O Goddess, one should delude her whose mind is inflamed with passion.
In a mere instant, one enters and brings the three worlds under control.
O fair-faced one, through meditation on this Kāmakalā, the five desires [are attained]. (19–24)
They delude the entire world; listen to the ritual application, O Pārvatī.
O Goddess of the gods, the previously mentioned desires should be known as having five designations. (19–25)
Having pierced it with the first desire, place it within the mind-born one;
then, having formed the casket of Kandarpa, place it within the interior of the corner.
All this, O fair-faced one, is known as Makaradhvaja;
when it has entered the Fish-bannered [deity], it deludes this entire world.
This yoga, named Trailokyamohana, has been fully described.
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall now explain the practice of the seed-syllable of Śakti. (19–28)
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess within the body from the beginning of creation until its dissolution—
she who rains down streams of flowing nectar and destroys all poison.

Shining with golden luster, possessing the beautiful radiance of a mass of lightning, she holds a jar filled with the shimmering crescent moon, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 19-30 ||
Meditating upon her who holds the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā) and who is the very embodiment of nectar, the practitioner of mantra shall remove poison existing in various forms. (19.31)
O Goddess, by remembering her, I attained the state of having a blue throat;
having become the Conqueror of Death, I wander upon both land and water.
A minister equal to Vainateya (Garuḍa) destroys thousands of loads of poison;
he shall destroy bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and the multitude of diseases.
It shall destroy all quartan fevers and epileptic seizures.
Now, Trikūṭā is the complete Mahātripurasundarī. || 19-34 ||
When meditated upon, she swiftly brings the three worlds under the control of the practitioner;
residing in the circles of the navel, heart, and mouth, she possesses a ruddy radiance.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, through meditation upon her who is as clear as a ruby, the eightfold sovereignty and good fortune arise for him. (19.36)
By constantly recollecting that name, the practitioner of mantra becomes dear to the yoginīs;
the wheel of mothers resides within his body, and through them, he shall be happy. (19.37)

O Goddess of the lords of gods, there is no doubt that the practitioner of mantra becomes possessed of sons through meditation, when Khecarī, established in the wheel and full, bestows spiritual perfection. (19–38)
Since sixty-four million yoginīs of great splendor abide here, having propitiated this wheel, O you who are honored by heroes! (19.39)
First, having meditated upon the eight seed-syllables on the external relative word, one becomes like another Kāmarāja in union with a woman. || 19-40 ||
O Dear One, he shall delude even the goddess Trailokyasundarī with his intoxicating noose, goad, bow, and arrows; how much more so, then, mortal women?

In that very way, with weapons consisting of the connection of powers (śakti-sambandha) and having a body composed of that, one shall bring under control the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Devas; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess of gods, by propitiating her, Kāma became beautiful with good fortune; and Hari also, O Supreme Sovereign, O beloved, [attained his state] through the practice of Tripurā. || 19-43 ||
Having become the deluder of the three worlds, he became the eternal sustainer.
By propitiating him, Brahmā became the creator;
O lady of beautiful hips, the moon and sun are the agents of creation and destruction. (19-44)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Practice of the Three Seed-Syllables of Tripurā," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"Tell me the procedure for recitation and fire-offerings (japa-homa) by which one may destroy obstacles."
O Śaṅkara of noble vows, speak for the benefit of practitioners.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, beloved; I shall explain the procedure for recitation and fire-offerings.
O Goddess, one who is firm in his vows should worship the entire wheel.
One should worship the wheel—whether it is external, situated within, or the central one—having propitiated it with ritual offerings; being pure, one should recite the mantra a thousand times.
If the practitioner stands before that [image], the fruit shall be infinite;
or else, having meditated upon the King of Wheels here, accompanied by worship. (20.4)
The wise person should begin the recitation; it shall become the destroyer of great sins.
One should recite either aloud, in a whisper, or mentally. (20.5)
O Supreme Sovereign, *nigada* is clearly articulated with distinct speech;
however, that which is indistinct, with a quivering mouth, is proclaimed as *upāṃśu*. (20.6)
But the mental recitation, O lady of excellent hips, consists of the form of the syllables of contemplation.
O lady of beautiful countenance, that which is muttered a hundred thousand times by means of verbal recitation— || 20-7 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, it becomes equal to mere whispered recitation;
O Lotus-eyed One, that which is muttered as a mere hundred thousand times in a whisper— || 20-8 ||
O Supreme Goddess, it is equal to one [recitation] through mental utterance;
with the body bound by mudrās, by means of the yoga of meditation previously described. (20–9)
He who recites it one hundred thousand times is liberated from great sins; with two hundred thousand recitations, even the sins arising from seven lifetimes are destroyed. (20.10)
It shall destroy the foremost of the great sins; of this there is no doubt.
Then, O Mistress of the Kula, he who recites the mantra three hundred thousand times— || 20-11 ||
It shall destroy ten million great sins; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, by reciting it four hundred thousand times, one indeed becomes a master of speech. (20-12)
O Goddess of the gods, there is no doubt that by merely reciting five hundred thousand times, one becomes Kubera himself;
by merely reciting six hundred thousand times, one becomes a great Vidyādhara. (20.13)
By reciting the mantra seven hundred thousand times, the practitioner of mantras attains union with the Khecarīs;
by reciting it eight hundred thousand times, the man becomes worthy of worship even by the gods.
O Dear One, he becomes the master of the eight siddhis, beginning with aṇimā;
kings come under his control, and women especially so. (20.15)
One should recite the mantra of Tripurasundarī one million times;
he himself becomes the creator and destroyer of the forms of Rudra—of this there is no doubt. (20.16)
He shall become worthy of universal reverence, always established in well-being, and a possessor of good fortune;
wherever in any region there is a Linga facing the west.
Whether it be a self-manifested (svayambhū) or a Bāṇa-liṅga, one devoid of a bull, situated in water, or even a western shrine, O lady of excellent vows, or any other [shrine], || 20.18 ||
O Goddess, with a serene mind, one should recite the Vidyā in sacred fields, at the Ganges, by a river, on a mountain peak, or in any pure and auspicious place. (20.19)
Abiding there, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; then this vidyā, which brings the three worlds under control, becomes manifest in the very form of the Goddess herself. (20–20)
One should recite the mantra thus according to one's capacity and then commence the rite of fire-oblation (*homakarma*).
O fair-faced one, one should perform the oblation with *kiṃśuka* flowers, using a tenth part [of the recitation count]. (20–21)
O Goddess, by means of safflower blossoms mixed with the three kinds of honey,
one shall destroy the flood of obstacles in an instant according to the method prescribed by the rules.
Bestowing all desires, she grants the fruits of sovereignty, enjoyment, and liberation;
having constructed a sacrificial pit according to the rules and endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
The *yoni*-shaped pit bestows eloquence, while the vulva-shaped (*bhaga*) one effects attraction;
the circular one bestows fortune (*lakṣmī*), and indeed these three may be combined in the form of a half-moon.
The nine-cornered triangular pit (navatrikoṇakuṇḍa) bestows the accomplishment of the Khecarī [power];
the square pit is the cause of peace, prosperity, nourishment, growth, and water.
The six-cornered [maṇḍala] increases all prosperity, wealth, and good fortune;
the lotus-marked [maṇḍala], O goddess worshipped by the gods, is the cause of all success. (20–26)
O lady of excellent hips, it has eight petals and bestows the fruits of one's desires;
indeed, all these rites are performed within the square.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the characteristics of the square:
the wise one should construct a square, equal on all sides, measuring one cubit.
O Goddess, listen to the supreme characteristics regarding the girdle (mekhalā).
The excavation should be fifteen finger-breadths in depth and made as beautiful as possible. (20–29)
Leaving one finger-breadth at the region of the neck, the first girdle should be nine finger-breadths in height and six finger-breadths in width. (20–30)
O Goddess, the second girdle should have a width of four finger-breadths;
then, the third girdle should be made seven finger-breadths high.

O Goddess of the Gods, it should be five finger-breadths high and two finger-breadths in width; O Beloved, the girdle (mekhalā) should be made with a width of four or three finger-breadths. || 20-32 ||
Alternatively, O Goddess, one should cause a pit to be dug measuring twelve finger-breadths in depth,
and construct three girdles measuring twelve, eight, and half of that [four] finger-breadths respectively.
The length and likewise the height of the *kuṇḍa* should be four finger-breadths;
one should fashion a well-characterized *yoni* in the western part of the *kuṇḍa*.
The wise one [should fashion it] twelve finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in width, having the form of an *aśvattha* leaf or triangular.
Now, listen to one of the two positions; for I shall indeed state its characteristics:
a wise man should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is eighteen finger-breadths deep.
The girdle should be four finger-breadths in width and six finger-breadths in height; it should be fashioned as before, and the vulva should likewise be so formed.
The triangular pit should be twenty-four finger-breadths in size all around;
one should dig it as before, leaving one finger-breadth for the neck.
The girdles should be made as before, and there may even be just one; likewise, O Maheśānī, the yoni is proclaimed to be a triangle. (20–39)
O Daughter of the Mountain, one should construct the triangular and other fire-pits (kuṇḍas) so that they are equal in measurement to the square pit.
The *yonikuṇḍa* has the form of a womb; it is marked with the *bhaga* and takes the shape of the *bhaga*.
O Goddess, one should fashion it like a triangle according to the proportions of a square.
One should prepare a circular cord measuring four cubits;
with that, one should fashion a circle, and the excavation should be performed as previously described.
The girdle (*mekhalā*) is described as before, and the womb (*yoni*) likewise;
indeed, the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) is shaped like a half-moon according to the sequence of its circumference.
One should make it four cubits in measure so that it takes the form of a half-moon; O Supreme Goddess, it should be provided with a girdle and a womb as before.
O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the nine-triangle fire-pit (*navatrikoṇakuṇḍa*);
the wise practitioner should construct a pit that resembles the central wheel.
O Goddess of gods, the central triangle is like the [outer] triangle as before; it should be without girdles so that there are nine corners. (20–46)
Then, by the very sequence of breaking the joints, there shall be an octagon of corners; one should dig it in that specific manner according to the calculation and in due order.
The girdles should be fashioned as before, leaving one finger-breadth [of space] around the neck in sequence;
likewise, one should fashion the yoni, which increases all good fortune. (20.48)
O Maheśānī, an eight-petaled lotus-shape should arise according to the measurement of the square, so that it becomes eight-petaled. (20.49)
One should perform its excavation in a single spot, which bestows comfort to the eyes; the girdle should be made as before, in the shape of a lotus, bringing happiness. (20.50)
O Goddess of the gods, one should likewise fashion the *yoni* for the sake of all prosperity;
having thus constructed the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Having relied upon the location of the lamp, the construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should take place;
one should fashion it as circular, O Goddess, or in the shape of a tortoise, O fair-eyed one.
Having divided that space into nine compartments, one should write the syllables;
the name of the field should be written in the central compartment, and the others should be written elsewhere.
One should apply the pair of vowels in sequence to the eight directions;
thus, O Goddess, the *avarga* has been described, as well as the seven beginning with *kavarga*.
O Goddess, one should then write [the syllables] starting from the east in sequence up to Kubera;
one should write two hundred thousand syllables in the northeast corner known as Kūrma.
O Pārvatī, know that the name of the field in whichever square it resides indicates its face;
O Pārvatī, know that on both sides of the face are the two hands.
Then, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, know that the two sides are the location of the belly;
finally, the two feet and the tail are proclaimed.
Indeed, hundreds of desires are fulfilled when [the moon] is in the mouth;
however, when it is in the hand, there is great suffering that brings about the destruction of all undertakings. (20.58)
In the belly, there is excessive suffering; in the feet, loss is said to occur;
and in the tail, the loss of wealth arises—this shall not be otherwise.
I have proclaimed this site for the lamp, which is difficult to find in the three worlds;
one should seek such a place for the lamp in a city, a village, or even a district.
O Dear One, wherever one may see [this], success in one's purpose will occur;
for one should determine the location of the lamp by means of the name of the field-lord.
One should perform the recitation (japa) and the fire-oblation (homa) at the location of the lamp; these always yield fruit.
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with excellent characteristics in the northeast of the pavilion.
Make a sand mandala one thumb-joint high on ground smeared with cow dung, forming a level surface.
Therein, one should perform the outlining: first, one should draw three lines toward the west in sequence, and afterwards, three lines toward the east, proceeding clockwise.
Then, O Goddess, one should withdraw the pen at the northern end;
having performed the sprinkling thereafter, one should subsequently [mark] with vermilion.
Or else with saffron, O Goddess, or with camphor powder;
or with the powder of turmeric, or with grain-ground flour, O Beloved. (20.66)
One should draw a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-petaled lotus;
likewise, one should draw a square mandala with four gates.
O fair-faced one, having cast a flower into the center of Tripureśī,
one should then worship the purification of the vessels, such as the *sruva* ladle and others.
O fair-faced one, having divided the fuel-sticks, the *dūrvā* grass, and the *darbha* grass into two parts,
one should place the vessel for the clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) and the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (*carusthālī*) according to the distinction of pairs.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should place the *sruva* ladle and the *sruk* ladle, followed by the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* waters, in pairs and with their openings facing downwards.
Having taken the water contained in the arghya vessel, one should worship the *prokṣaṇī*;
having performed the threefold purification (*utpavana*), one should sprinkle with that water. (20–71)
All those vessels shall become purified;
having then turned them face upward, one should consecrate them with the *bālā* mantra.
And having strewn *dūrvā* grass all around the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), O beloved,
the strewing is said to be with the tips pointing eastward and northward.
Then, having taken the *sruva* ladle with the left hand, one should [wipe] that mouth with a blade of *dūrvā* grass, starting from the western direction and proceeding toward the east. (20.74)
Having wiped it three times, one should then bring the instrument below;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should recite the mantra over it as far as the opening.
Then, O lady of excellent hips, by means of a young girl, the purificatory rites are indeed performed;
having recited the root-mantra, one should write "Salutation to the sacrificial pit" (kuṇḍāya namaḥ). || 20-76 ||
O Goddess, with this mantra the wise one should worship the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), [placing] Kāmeśvarī in the middle of the pit, together with Kāma and during her season. || 20-77 ||
Having invoked and fully worshipped [the deity], one should bring the fire into its interior;
one should gaze [upon it] with two syllables of the Netra-mantra of the root-vidyā.
Having protected it with the Astra-mantra, one should then rotate it three times clockwise around the perimeter of the sacrificial pit, keeping it enclosed within the palms.

One should cast forth a portion of fire from the *saṃpuṭa* [mudrā] with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, O Goddess praised by heroes, toward the corner of the southwest, which is the portion of the flesh-eaters and belongs to the Rākṣasas. (20.80)
Having worshipped with the *kavaca* mantra and knelt upon the ground,
he established both the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) and the fire within the center of the sacrificial pit.
Having drawn the form with the mantra, one should worship Śivā;
[this is done] by means of the sequence of the openings of the fire-channel (vahannāḍī) located in the region of the navel-mandala.
Having unified the fire of knowledge with the external fire, one should worship;
having uttered the root mantra, one should also utter "Āṃ So'haṃ."

Having uttered the fire-consciousness (vahnicaitanya) ending in the letter *ṅ*, conjoined with the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), one should meditate upon Kāmeśvarī within the womb by means of this mantra. (20.84)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should apply the six limbs to the body of Varāha:
*sahasrākṣi*, *svastipūrṇe*, and likewise *uttiṣṭha puruṣa*. (20.85)
Pervading the smoke, the seven-tongued one is proclaimed as the wielder of the bow;
O lotus-eyed one, one should join those ending in the dative case to the six limbs.
*Tāram*, at the end of *vaiśvānara*, [is] *jātaveda*; "bring [the deity] here" (*ihāvaha*).
Then, *lohitākṣa*, and "accomplish all rites" (*sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya*). || 20-87 ||
The mantra, joined with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), should properly worship Vahni;
one should meditate upon Vahni as gold-colored, bearing a spear and a svastika.
Abounding in the splendor of the Bestower of Boons, adorned with excellent ornaments of gold;
having thus worshipped Agni, O lotus-eyed one, [place it] in his mouth. || 20-89 ||
One should contemplate a hexagon there and worship the seven tongues of flame,
adorned with the fire-syllable (ra), the wind-syllable (ya), and the left ear (u), embellished by the *nāda* and *bindu*.
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should join the tongues in this sequence;
indeed, there are seven tongues beginning with the letter *ya* and ending with the letter *sa*. (20.91)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should worship those called Hiraṇya, who have the color of gold heated by rubies, in the corner of Śambhu. || 20.92 ||
Vaidūryābhā, Suvarṇā, and thereafter Kanakā;
having worshipped them in the eastern corner, one should worship Rudralohitā.
One should worship the goddess named Rakta, who resembles the rising sun, in the southeast corner;
and the goddess named Kṛṣṇā, O Goddess, who is blue and has a blue radiance, one should worship in the southwest.
O Goddess, one should worship Śubhrā, who is white with the luster of pearls, in the west;
one should worship Dhūminī, who has the hue of a ruby and is intensely red, in the northwest.

One should worship Karālī, who possesses the luster of ten million moons and manifold forms, situated in the center and occupying the southern and northern portions, the bestower of all accomplishments.
One should worship the names in sequence at the end of the seed-syllable of the tongue:
Agni, Hutavāhana, Hutāśana, and Vartman.
One should worship there in sequence these eight names in their proper order: Devamukha, Saptajihva, Vaiśvānara, and Jātavedas.
Having thus worshipped the fire born from the womb of Kāmeśī,
O fair-eyed one, take the darbha-bracelet and perform the binding of the hand.
One should perform the oblation with the root mantra, the arrow-mantra, and the fourth mantra;
having thus performed the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), one should likewise perform the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) and the subsequent rites.
Having contemplated the rites such as the tonsure ceremony for the Fire born from the womb of Kāmeśī with the root mantra, one should worship the external wheel.
One should contemplate the six limbs in the six corners, the Mothers in the eight corners, and the world-protectors on the square of the earth, as well as the mature fire. || 20-102 ||
Having worshipped Brahmā on the right, one should worship the vessel of clarified butter;
having duly worshipped the fire produced from stone, one should [offer it] into its mouth.
Having invoked the Wheel-King together with all its rays,
one should worship it— which is served by all lion-thrones— with ritual offerings.
The practitioner of mantras should properly diffuse incense that fills the sacrificial pit and the pavilion; then, O Beloved, he should display a lamp and many other lamps.

O Daughter of the Mountain, having wrapped it with a garland and three girdles, one should subsequently spread out the sacrificial pap (caruka) in all directions for the attainment of happiness. || 20-106 ||
Then, having performed the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), one should perform the fire-oblation for specific desires (kāmanāhoma) with jasmine,
jātī, and mallikā flowers mixed with honey.
O Goddess, by offering oblations filled with clarified butter, the state of Vāgīśvara arises—even for one who is mute, deluded, or like a stone; it is not otherwise.
By performing oblations with hibiscus flowers mixed with clarified butter, as well as with similar karavīra flowers,
the mantra-practitioner shall delude the inhabitants of the three worlds.
O Goddess, by offering camphor and saffron mixed with musk into the fire, Madana shall be conquered by the practitioner through this mantra. || 20-110 ||
O lady of virtuous vows, by means of good fortune, charm, and even power,
having offered *campaka* and *pāṭala* flowers, one attains Śrī, whose garments are brilliantly radiant.
The practitioner attains great power and may paralyze this very world;
then, by offering oblations of sandalwood, guggulu, camphor, and agallochum,
he shall bring under his control the wives of kings, lords of serpents, and gods.
All the worlds indeed come under his control; of this there is no doubt.
For one afflicted by the fear of poverty, sovereignty is attained through a homa of lac.
The pacification of difficulties and calamities results from a homa of three parts of meat and honey. || 20-114 ||

O Goddess of gods, those who are situated at a distance should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the path taught by the Guru; otherwise, for those desiring subjugation, it will be fruitless. (20.115)
By means of goat's meat smeared with blood, offered in a fire-oblation at night,
combined with the three sweets, according to the procedure taught by the Guru.
One should bring the entire great fortress of a foreign kingdom under one's own control;
by means of the Great Palāśa, O Goddess of Gods, one shall destroy the enemy's army. (20.117)
Having performed a fire sacrifice at a crossroads at night, O fair-faced one, by offering milk, honey, curd, and clarified butter separately, one becomes a sky-walker (khecara).
Longevity, wealth, health, and prosperity arise for men;
O Daughter of the Mountain, by means of milk and honey [offered] in sequence, death itself is destroyed. (20.119)
Through an oblation of curd and honey, one shall obtain good fortune and wealth;
an oblation with sugar alone causes the paralysis of enemies.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, a person [who consumes] curd, honey, milk, and parched grain is undoubtedly a destroyer of diseases, a destroyer of time, and a destroyer of death. (20.121)
An oblation with red lotuses bestows complete prosperity;
with red water-lilies, the world is brought under control and kings become submissive in an instant.
By means of blue lotuses, even the most wicked are brought under control; it cannot be otherwise.
By offering white lotuses, O Dear One, one obtains prosperity and eloquence through the fire-sacrifice.
By offering white Brahma-lotuses, one shall obtain prosperity and good fortune;
by offering Kahlāra lilies, the practitioner of mantras shall likewise acquire good fortune and wealth.
By means of a full oblation of pomegranates, one shall bring even the great asuras under control;
by means of an oblation produced from citron fruits, the kṣatriyas are brought under control.
Indeed, by means of an offering of orange fruits, Vaiśyas become submissive;
likewise, by an offering of pumpkin fruits, Śūdras and others become submissive. (20.126)
Through the offering of one hundred thousand *kadalī* fruits, there is no doubt that the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are attained by means of the fire-oblation (*homān*). || 20-127 ||
There is no doubt that ten [kings] will indeed become submissive by means of one hundred thousand oblations of date fruits. || 20-128 ||
The command of the Supreme Lord is that there are twenty [types of] women who are subject to one's will;
O Dear One, through oblations of coconut fruits, prosperity arises. (20.129)
O beloved, by means of a hundred thousand oblations of ripe mango fruits, O beautiful one, the knower of mantras becomes like another king. (20.130)
By performing one hundred thousand oblations with jackfruit (*panasa*), one may bring the earth bounded by the four oceans under one's control, along with its hundreds of kings. (20.131)
O Goddess of gods, they become submissive; there is no need for deliberation here.
