O beloved Goddess of gods, through the oblation of sesame and clarified butter, the accomplishment of the task occurs. (20.132)
One should bring wicked people under one's control by means of black mustard seeds and salt;
and by the oblation of guggulu resin, one shall destroy all sufferings.
O Goddess, by offering oblations with saffron, one brings the three worlds under control;
likewise, through the offering of sandalwood, enemies are swiftly brought into subjection.
By means of a fire offering of red sandalwood, men and women are indeed brought under control;
and by means of a fire offering of camphor, the power to subjugate the speech of men arises.
O Goddess, O Beloved, through the homa of musk, all kings and royal ministers, together with their retinues, become submissive.
Through the oblation of sesame seeds and rice, peace prevails in the temple;
through the oblation of sugar and molasses, it accomplishes all desires and goals.
By means of an oblation of ghee and milk-rice mixed with sugar, the practitioner brings the three worlds under his control; the attainment of grain will certainly occur. (20.138)
And with *vaṭaka* sweets accompanied by their ingredients, one should destroy the *upasargas*.
An oblation with *bandhūka* flowers shall destroy all enemies;
with *japā* flowers, the world is brought under control, and with wild forest flowers, there is enchantment.
By offering oblations with Bakula flowers, great good fortune arises;
by the offering of ten-ingredient incense, incomparable good fortune shall come to pass.
By means of *jambū* fruits, women are brought under control; by means of *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruits, the daughters of the Daityas;
and by means of *bilva* fruits or their leaves, incomparable prosperity is attained, O Goddess worshipped by the gods. (20.142)
O Goddess of the Gods, the attainment of happiness comes from pieces of sugarcane, and princesses become submissive through its juice, or even by means of coconut water.
By the mere offering of oblations of clarified butter, all the powers become bestowers of boons.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the measurement that grants success in the fire-sacrifice.
One should offer a complete lotus flower, or even a profusion of them;
O beloved, one may offer as many flowers from the saffron grove as one desires.
O Goddess, there are one hundred sesame seeds, and one hundred grains of black mustard; the parched grain is the measure of a handful, and the clarified butter is the measure of a gadyāṇa.
A handful of water or milk, and food in the measure of a single morsel;
O Maheśānī, the fruit should be large, such as the pumpkin or the citron. (20.147)
The fruit becomes pleasing to the mind when divided into four pieces;
indeed, the plantain fruit must certainly be cut into four pieces, for it should not be eaten otherwise.
Indeed, a piece of coconut or a plantain fruit, O beloved, [should be placed] at the joint;
or else a piece of sugarcane that brings satisfaction to the mind. (20.149)
There should be a whole grape, as well as an orange and a date;
likewise there should be bdellium, half a betel nut, and saffron.
O Goddess, camphor should be equal in measure to guñjā, as should musk and saffron; likewise, sandalwood and agallochum should be equal in measure to kramuka.
All fruits that are pleasing to the mind are dear for the oblation; lac and guggulu are to be counted [among them], as well as whatever object is captivating to the heart. (20.152)
O Sulocanā, having offered oblations dear to the mind, one should perform the fire sacrifice;
this measure of oblations has been told to you, which removes all obstacles. (20.153)
O lady of excellent limbs, one should satisfy Śrīvidyā according to one's desire;
having performed the recitation according to one's capacity, one should offer oblations (homa) with a tenth part of that amount. || 20-154 ||
Or else, O beloved, with *kiṃśuka* flowers which destroy the mass of sins;
or with various substances, whether used individually or combined together, O fair-faced one. (20.155)
The wise practitioner should perform the homa with those who have gathered together according to their capacity.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme special procedure.
First, having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with all the required characteristics—
square, richly adorned, and measuring half a cubit for a hundredfold oblation.
For a thousand [units], it is one cubit square;
for ten thousand, two cubits; and for a hundred thousand, four cubits.
For a *koṭi-homa*, having made the characteristic of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) eight cubits in size;
for pacification (*śāntika*), it should be square, and for subjugation (*vaśya*), it should be crescent-shaped.
A hexagon is indeed for paralyzing and likewise for killing; a triangle is for attracting, and a circle is for driving away. (20–160)

The lotus-corner grants success for the sake of various accomplishments and benefits; in the north is the rite of pacification (śāntika), and for paralyzing (stambhana) one uses the western direction.
Killing is indeed in the south, and the rite of subjugation in the west; the rite of incineration is in the southeast, and likewise, the rite of causing enmity in the southwest. (20.162)
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the northwest or northeast directions grant all accomplishments;
Kṛttikā is declared for attraction (*karṣaṇa*), and likewise Bharaṇī for killing (*māraṇa*).
Svātī is for subjugation as well as eradication; Jyeṣṭhā is for immobilization; Śatabhiṣaj is for causing enmity; and Abhijit is for pacification.
Some [rites] are for summoning all things (*sarvākarṣaṇa*), as well as for killing (*māraṇa*) and for auspicious purposes (*maṅgala*).
Under Mercury (*budha*), the rite of immobilization (*stambha*) should be performed; on Thursday (*guruvāra*), however, the rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) is to be done. (20.165)

Under Venus, all desires are fulfilled; under the Sun, however, there are inauspicious results. In the forenoon, rites for subjugation are effective; at midday, they cause the destruction of affection. (20.166)
Uccāṭana is performed in the afternoon, and likewise, māraṇa at twilight;
śāntika at midnight, and pauṣṭika indeed in the morning. (20.167)
For the rite of immobilization, elephant skins; likewise, for killing, buffalo skins; for expulsion, deer skins; and for the rite of subjugation, goat skins. (20.168)
For inciting enmity, the jackal skin is prescribed; likewise, for rites of pacification, the ox-hide is taught.
For the sake of attaining various siddhis, the tiger skin is declared.
White [powder] on a tiger-skin serves for pacification; yellow brings about immobilization;
red is for subjugation and attraction, while that which is pleasing is for the purpose of agitation.
The color black is prescribed for rites of killing, while smoke-colored [oblations] are for rites such as expulsion;
for the rite of immobilization, fuel-sticks of the rājavṛkṣa tree should be offered into the fire. || 20-171 ||
Combined with buffalo ghee, it always bestows success;
for the rite of killing, one should perform the fire-oblation without delay using fuel-sticks made from pomegranate wood.
O Goddess of gods, one should bring the moving and the unmoving under control with goat-ghee;
likewise, for the purpose of inciting enmity, one should offer fuel-sticks of the *unmatta* plant.
Combined with linseed oil, this brings about enmity;
furthermore, it destroys the entire multitude of obstacles—of this there is no doubt.
Then, O Goddess, having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should worship young maidens;
for by him who has worshipped young maidens, the three worlds have been worshipped.
A young girl should worship the Goddess; thereafter, she should worship Śrīvidyā.
O Goddess, one should worship Śrīvidyā there with five lion-thrones. (20.176)
Then the married women (suvāsinīs) are to be honored; there one should worship Śrīvidyā.
Afterward, one should satisfy the Brahmins and worship Śrīvidyā there.
The Yoginīs should likewise be worshipped, and one should satisfy Śrīvidyā; one should worship all the philosophical systems and various [other] forms of worship. (20.178)
There, one should satisfy Śrīvidyā and then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the glorious Jñānārṇava, the Nityātantra. || 20 ||
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
The Lord said: I shall now proclaim another fire-oblation (homa) by which the eternal Brahman is attained.
Having meditated upon the fire-pit called "quadrangular" by means of gnosis, as previously described.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, that [mandala] should be known as square by means of the *ātman*s;
for the *ātman*s, numbering four according to the Vedas, must be understood by the best of teachers. (21.2)
For those for whom rebirth no longer exists through mere consciousness alone, [this] proceeds by way of a common position among all living beings. (21.3)
That Self, O Supreme Goddess, O fair-faced one, takes the form of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The vital breath, O Goddess, is the wind whose abode is the temple of the heart. (21.4)
Pervading the entire body, you move through both the moving and the unmoving;
you are to be known as the very nature of the *haṃsa*, manifesting through the play of inhalation and exhalation. (21.5)
Its name "living being" (jīva) appears through delusion and mere appearance, but not in reality;
the inhalation and exhalation exist only because of the body's state—it is nothing but delusion, without a doubt. (21.6)
Just as the space within a jar is perceived through the breaking of the potter's wheel [and the subsequent shattering of the jar], O Supreme Goddess, so does space remain pervading all. (21.7)
Just as the state of being broken occurs in a jar, but no such brokenness exists in space,
so too, O fair-faced one, the individual soul residing in the body [perishes] upon the destruction of the body.
It exists everywhere pervading all; therefore, the Self is the supreme Great.
Thus, O beloved, the knowledge of the Self has been declared by me; now hear that of the second.
Listen now to that great word, "antarātman" (the inner self);
O Goddess of Gods, by the word "antar," it signifies the secret, subtle form. (21.10)
Pervading everything in the form of atoms, it manifests; by virtue of its being the innermost essence, it moves or remains unmoving.
Because it pervades everything, it is therefore sung of as the "inner self" (antarātman).
Indeed, when that very self becomes the *haṃsa*, it is accessible to yogins. (21.12)
O lady of excellent limbs, he is swift in crossing over, possessing the wings of the Vedas and Agamas;
he is the pair of feet of Śiva and Śakti, with the three points as his eyes. || 21.13 ||
This Supreme Swan, however, remains pervading the creation;
then, O lotus-eyed one, the elements are born in succession.
Space, wind, fire, water, and earth, O fair-faced one—O Goddess of gods, among these five, consciousness is said to be the first. (21.15)
In the midst of the lake called ignorance, filled with the mud of delusion, within the lotus of phenomenal expansion, which has blossomed from the five elements. (21.16)
The abode of this very Haṃsa becomes composed of Māyā through emanation;
O Great Goddess, it is precisely this [Haṃsa] which, when it becomes free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca), [is the ultimate state]. || 21-17 ||
The Haṃsa, whose form is that of withdrawal, then reveals itself;
it has no state as a bird at all—it is I, the Self, firmly established. (21.18)
Know that this triad is proclaimed as the Supreme Self;
O Goddess, it manifests in the form of the wings, the tail, and the head. (21.19)
O blessed lady, he who is the direct witness in the form of a witness is called the self of knowledge;
by him, O fair-faced one, all this is known with equanimity.
Just as the lunar disk, O Goddess, is seen in water and in milk, yet it is not stained by them, O Goddess, because of the distinction between the water and the milk. (21.21)
O Daughter of the Mountain, a reflection cannot appear on a piece of red resin when it is smeared with mud;
likewise, O auspicious lady, the Knower of the Self is proclaimed to be the witness of all. (21–22)
The Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self are proclaimed as the natures of consciousness;
for this form, O fair-faced one, is indeed the square sacrificial pit of consciousness. (21–23)

It is beautiful with the girdle of bliss, marked by the three circles of the *bindu*, the form of the womb (*yoni*) consisting of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), and eternally composed of the bliss of Brahman. || 21–24 ||
O Goddess, one should offer the intense oblation of phenomenal expansion into the fire of consciousness, which consists of supreme *ahantā* and is illuminated by the lamp of all-knowledge.
That which is called sound has the form of the *mātṛkā* and is adorned with the letters of the alphabet;
when the syllables are offered here, the soundless Brahman arises.
O Goddess, merit and sin are the oblation; O Beloved, what is done and what is not done are the oblation. Likewise, intention and deliberation, as well as dharma and adharma, are the oblation.
O Parameśānī, O lady of stainless countenance, one should perform the oblation with the two mantras;
immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon the Root-Vidyā, which is the form of Brahman. (21–28)
At the end of that, the teacher should subsequently utter [the mantra] for the sake of attaining Brahman;
with the mind as the sacrificial ladle, one should offer the oblation of dharma and adharma into the blazing fire of the self. (21–29)
"O Goddess, with the mantra ending in *svāhā*, I offer the entire world—both with parts and without parts—daily through the path of the *suṣumṇā* as the functioning of the senses. (21–30)
O Goddess, the mantra of the internal oblation cuts through all illusion;
holding the hands of light and space, one should grasp with the ladle of *unmanī*.
I offer dharma and adharma into the fire filled with the oil of the *kalā*s;
the mantra joined with the wife of Agni was taught to you at the end of the Vidyā. (21–32)

O Goddess, when the best of mantra-knowers arises in the state free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca), then the practitioner is truly composed of consciousness and is manifest as the absolute Brahman alone. (21–33)
Even one who has drunk poison ten times over shall become happy by reciting "So'ham" while performing the fire-oblation.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Knowledge-Oblation," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now the twenty-second chapter.
The Lord said:
All rites, such as the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth, [are incomplete] without the worship of the maiden (kumārī).
The fruit is not at all fulfilled; it would not become fruitful through worship alone.
O Goddess, from the worship of a maiden, the fruit of ten million worships shall arise;
whatever flower is given to a maiden becomes equal to Mount Meru. (22–2)
By him who has fed a maiden, the three worlds have been fed;
the water given to a maiden is equal to the ocean. (22–3)
O fish-eyed one, the food offered should be as vast as the great mountain ranges;
one should worship auspicious maidens ranging from one year of age up to sixteen. (22.4)
If they remain unmarried, they bestow progressively higher accomplishments;
however, O Goddess of the Gods, once married, they are merely young girls (kumārikās).
O lady of excellent vows, abandon doubt regarding these women mature with intoxication;
O Goddess, in the worship of the maiden, it should be performed with the mantra of the maiden. (22-6)
By that very division of mantras, one should worship Śrīvidyā as well.
I shall now proclaim the occasional (naimittika) rite, by which the wise one becomes composed of Brahman.
O Goddess of gods, O one honored by the deities, this applies to the one free from conceptual construction and to no other;
he is liberated from all doubt, omniscient, and the best of practitioners.
O Dear One, by performing the ritual of the offering to the messenger (dūtīyāga), one becomes a sky-walker (khecara).
O Śivā, [this is done] in the vessel for the guest-offering (arghyapātra) which consists of the nectar of fire, sun, and moon.
Know that Soma-amṛta is always composed of various substances,
O Goddess of Gods, according to the distinctions of the sequence of syllables for one who possesses conceptual thought.
O fair-complexioned ones, the various substances are now described in order:
for indeed, there are the different substances of milk, clarified butter, honey, and maireya wine. || 22-11 ||
O beautiful lady, in the state of omniscience, no fault is found in sacrifice;
how then could there be the killing of a horse in sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha? (22.12)
O beautiful lady, there are many varieties of substances according to their distinctions:
water, milk, ghee, O auspicious one, honey, liquor, and sugarcane juice. (22.13)
O Goddess, it may be made from flowers, from trees, or produced from grain; it is fashioned in many ways and exists in various forms through numerous varieties. || 22-14 ||
O Sulocanā, intoxication was to be avoided because it obstructs the Dharma;
however, when refined by knowledge, it destroys even the greatest sins.
O Goddess, by worshipping [the deity], one destroys the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, and so forth; such a knower of the mantra becomes free from all defects. (22.16)
One should always contemplate everything, O Goddess praised by all-knowing heroes;
know that the water is the aquatic creature, and one should bring the full jar. (22.17)
O Goddess, water containing living beings remains for seven days;
indeed, the milk belongs to that very living being, and its meat follows—of this there is no doubt.
Since a woman who has borne children may become emaciated, while one who is barren remains robust, O beloved,
the delightful juice produced from the fruit of the mango tree should be consumed by the twice-born.
O Goddess of gods, because it does not cause intoxication, sugar-cane juice is consumed by the wise;
O Beloved, there is nothing that is not meat, for everything, such as milk and the like, [is derived from it]. (22.20)
The collection of knowledge hidden within the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas dwells there,
O beautiful one, just as fire resides within the Śamī tree.
O Goddess, consciousness within all beings is to be known by the best of teachers; it is said that fire becomes manifest from the friction of wood.
Just as that wood is consumed by it, so too is the world consisting of Brahman;
this knowledge, O fair-faced one, is entirely free from both sin and merit.
O Goddess of the gods, this sacrificial limb should be grasped only until a slight thrill arises;
for by greedily seizing it, one becomes a sinner, even a slayer of a Brahmin.
One should avoid all intoxicating substances, such as gold and the like;
therefore, one who knows Brahman and is the best among the knowers of Brahman is free from the sin of *kalañja*.
Through the complete knowledge of dharma and adharma, there is purity in everything—even feces, urine, the menses of a woman, or even nails and bones, O Beloved. (22–26)
O observer of excellent vows, the knower of mantras should contemplate the purifiers themselves;
one should understand that food is Brahman, for from it all things arise. (22–27)
Since it is the support for various living beings, by whom could that excrement be censured?
For, O Goddess of the Gods, there are indeed many kinds of deities residing within the water. (22–28)
Why should one defile with that water the urine produced from it?
O Goddess, [there is] the drinking of cow's urine and likewise the eating of cow dung. (22–29)
O beloved, regarding the expiation for such acts as the killing of a Brahmin, it has been stated:
"How can there be any fault in [the consumption of] semen or urine? It is certainly a delusion; of this there is no doubt. (22–30)
O Supreme Goddess, by that very [substance] the female menses arise within the body;
how then can there be any defilement by which the supreme state is attained? || 22-31 ||
The virility of the Puruṣa, however, is designated as the *bindu*;
and this *bindu*, O Supreme Goddess, is this body whose form is Śiva.
There is no defilement by means of the Śiva-principle regarding the bones and so forth in the Bindu; semen is pure, so by whom can it, the cause of the body, be censured? (22–33)
O beautiful one, this entire path of knowledge belongs to the non-conceptual; O Great Goddess, a man who possesses conceptualization becomes a partaker of sin.
Having emerged from the mother’s womb, he is indeed a mere infant; of this there is no doubt.
O beloved, all his sense organs remain situated within his body. (22-35)
Because it is free from conceptual elaboration, it does not become otherwise there, O Beloved;
the union of the bhaga and liṅga should always exist at the time of birth. || 22-36 ||
O Goddess, when that which is desired arises, one becomes a violator of the Guru’s bed;
for this very reason, when his latent impression (vāsanā) becomes contemptible.
Everything else, when joined with its respective ornaments, shall be auspicious;
it is entirely pure, O blessed one, though the latent impression (vāsanā) is considered defiled.
Therefore, immediately after the consecration of the arghya vessel, [one should place] a small couch made of elephant ivory or fashioned from gold, silver, and so forth. (22–39)
One should place there a mattress made of pure linen cloth;
having scattered flowers in its center, one should likewise [place] the powder of camphor.
Then, O Goddess born of the mountain, one should worship the frog and the others in successive order;
first, one should worship the frog, followed by Rudra conjoined with the Fire of Time (Kālāgni). || 22-41 ||
[He should worship] the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), the tortoise (kūrma), likewise Ananta and Varāha;
as well as the earth, the bulb (kanda), the stalk (nāla), the lotus, and the petals.
Having worshipped the filaments, one should then worship the pericarp;
having likewise honored the pedestal, [one should worship] there at its four legs.
One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in succession;
one should worship these [deities] who are not previously present in the vicinity of their feet.

One should worship, in sequence, the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self, who are of the nature of knowledge; having worshipped them at the front of the couches, one should then worship the three qualities.
[He should choose] a messenger who possesses auspicious marks, is beautiful, endowed with all the [ideal] characteristics,
made lovely by various ornaments, omniscient, and like the goddess Śaradā.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship with the five objects of desire and likewise with arrows;
one should worship Baṭuka and the others in the four directions for the sake of attaining siddhi.
One should place the Mātṛkā, conjoined with the arrows of Kāma, upon her body;
one should contemplate a triangle on the head and worship there in due order.
In the center of the triangle, one should worship the goddess named Bālā, who is Kāmeśvarī; likewise, one should worship Gaṇeśa, the presiding lord of the Kula, as well as Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī.
Having worshipped Vāsanta and Madana in the triangles, O Dear One, one should thereafter worship Kalādhara on her breasts and in her mouth.
O beautiful one, one should worship all the digits (kalās) of both Kāma and Soma, starting from the right foot up to the head, and on the left side, from the head down to the feet.
Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Dhṛti, and the charming Kānti; Manoharā, Manoramā, and Madanonmādinī—these are my beloveds. || 22-52 ||
Mohinī, Dīpanī, Śoṣaṇī, Vaśaṅkarī, Rañjanī, Subhagā, the Goddess Ṣoḍaśī, and Priyadarśanā. || 22-53 ||
One should worship these Kāmakalās, conjoined with the sixteen vowels:
Pūṣā, Vaśā, Sumanā, Rati, Prīti, and likewise Dhṛti.
Ṛddhi, Saumyā, and Marīci are on Śailaja; Aṃśumālinī, Aṅgirā, Śaśinī, Chāyā, and Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā [are on the others]. (22.55)

Likewise, the sixteen digits (kalās) of the Moon, including Tuṣṭi and Amṛtā, should indeed be worshipped with the musical notes (svaras); for they grant the accomplishment of all purposes and goals. || 22-56 ||
Having worshipped her head according to the procedure for the uninitiated,
one should thereafter worship her "abode of passion" (the vulva) with a garland of bhagas.
Having recognized that triangle as her bhaga, which is known as the bestower of all siddhis, one should worship the pair of wheels consisting of universal bliss in its center. (22–58)
Following the sequential method as before, one should worship Śrīvidyā there; then, having offered incense and other articles, one should [worship] her within one's own *liṅga*. (22–59)
*Tāram* and *Bhuvaneśāni*, *Mahātripurasundarī*;
*Namaḥ Śivāya*—this is proclaimed as the ten-syllable *vidyā*. (22.60)
O Goddess, by means of this vidyā, one should worship Śiva within one's own liṅga;
one should sacrifice [to him] under the names Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Īśāna.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti, as well as Śāntyatītā—these should be worshipped; one should sacrifice to the enclosure of the six limbs.
Having recited the complete vidyā, O Goddess, one should worship Nandikeśa in the middle between the testicles with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, with his senses and mind conquered,
he should bind the Sarvakṣobhiṇī mudrā and cause the vulva (yoni) to vibrate.
Or else, O Goddess, [one should recite] with the Kṣobhiṇī or with that called Gajatuṇḍa;
while uttering the Bhagamālā, one should utter the Drāviṇī seed-syllable.
O beautiful woman, as long as one remains unagitated until the semen flows—that which consists of passion—is passion itself, manifest as pure consciousness; of this there is no doubt.
O Supreme Goddess, Prakṛti is called Vīrya and Puruṣa;
therefore, everything is directly the state of equilibrium (sāmarasya), consisting of Śiva and Śakti.
O Maheśānī, the union of those two is indeed Yoga; of this there is no doubt.
The sound *sītkāra* is the form of the mantra, while speech becomes hymn of praise.
In this [practice], nail-marks and tooth-bites are the various flowers;
cooing, singing, and praise constitute the striking and the fire-oblation.
O Daughter of the Mountain, know that embracing consists of musk, saffron, and so forth; rubbing is *tarpaṇa*, and the emission of semen is *visarjana*. (22.70)

O beloved, having purified it with the substance of the family (*kuladravya*), O beautiful one, one should deposit the seed-nectar (*bījāmṛta*), which consists of Śiva and Śakti and is the form of the Supreme Brahman. (22.71)
Having abandoned the nectar of the *arghya* vessel, always free from conceptualization and sinless,
one becomes identical with the Supreme Brahman after worshipping the sequence of the *Śrīvidyā*.
This knowledge of equanimity has been told to you, O fair-faced one;
however, O Mistress of the Gods, a man who possesses conceptual thought becomes a partaker of sin.
A practitioner who harbors doubt becomes one who violates the preceptor’s bed;
for this very reason, O lady of excellent hips, one should always remain free from conceptual construction.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Second Invocation of the Śrīvidyā Messenger," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
The Lord said:
I shall now proclaim another messenger by whom the eternal Brahman is attained.
Having entered the sacrificial hall known as the *praṇava*, O goddess worshipped by the gods!
O Supreme Goddess, O Śivā, who consists of the knowledge of reality, [this temple] is fashioned from will, knowledge, action, and substance, and is joined with nectar by Ambā. || 23-2 ||
Adorned with the goals of human endeavor as its legs, it is further embellished by the limbs of the knowledge of the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self. (23.3)
O beautiful one, the meaning of "That," the meaning of "Thou," and the meaning of "Art"—these three meanings reveal the thread of knowledge. (23.4)

In that place, which is adorned with garments woven from strips of this very sūtra and beautified by celestial cloths, and made auspicious by flowers and perfumes, one should perform supreme worship. (23.5)
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the classification of the dūtīs is fourfold:
O Beloved, they are Hastinī, Śaṅkhinī, Citriṇī, and Padminī. (23.6)
Indeed, there are four kinds of messengers (dūtīs), beautiful and with lovely eyes;
O fair-faced one, Vaikharī should be known as Hastinī because she is gross.
By her this entire sphere of the cosmic egg is sustained;
O Goddess of gods, through her eightfold group she gives birth to the assembly of the world-elephants.
Therefore she is called Karinī, while the middle one is Śaṅkhinī. (23–8)
O auspicious lady, Śaṅkhinī is indeed pure and free from evil;
for she is beloved by all the gods and adorned with peace and good fortune. (23.9)
Likewise, O fair-faced goddess, the speech residing in trees is the middling one; it is the variegated creeper, O Goddess, which destroys great defects. (23.10)
O lady of excellent limbs, the fruit of which is always composed of Śiva and Śakti;
O Goddess, the entire triple world of all living beings is composed of Śiva and Śakti. (23.11)
Perceiving that supreme support within all those living beings,
that supreme Speech, O Supreme Goddess, is merged into the Parabrahman.
Having worshipped that messenger there with the flowers of meditative concentration,
O Goddess praised by the gods, the Kalās should be worshipped in sequence upon her limbs.
But the supreme Padminī should be known as one whose lotus blossoms with the purity of a swan;
for, O Daughter of the Mountain, by the rising of the swan, the lotus indeed abandons its contraction.
It causes good fortune to blossom through the splendor of the object;
thus, it attains supreme illumination and thereby becomes a *padminī*. (23.15)
O lady of excellent hips, sixteen kalās are to be worshipped within her body:
Citkalā, Satkalā, Jñānakalā, and likewise Saṃvitkalā; || 23-16 ||
O Supreme Goddess, four portions of the self are to be known:
dispassion, the portion of liberation, and likewise the portion of the atom. (23.17)
The fourfold group of *vidyā* and *kalā* should be known within the inner self:
*vidyā*, contentment, satisfaction, and the radiance of the Supreme Brahman. (23–18)
The supreme self-aspect (paramātmakalā) is to be known as merged within the supreme reality;
[these are] the aspect of dissolution (lupti), the aspect of peace (śāntikalā), the aspect of awakening (bodhakalā), and the supreme aspect of pervasion (vyāptikalā). || 23-19 ||
O Supreme Goddess, the four kalās are to be known as belonging to the nature of knowledge;
O Mistress of the Gods, the sixteen kalās are established within the syllables of the Śrīvidyā. (23–20)
The sixteen-syllabled [mantra] is the form of Brahman, the sixteenth digit (kalā) possessing a sixteenfold nature;
as the Self in the state of waking, it fashions the three worlds.
The inner self consists of the nature of *sattva* and the nature of *tamas*, and is thus a mixture;
for this very reason, the supreme Śiva consists of the nature of *rajas* and the nature of *tamas*. (23–22)
The Supreme Self, whose nature is knowledge and who is joined with the fourth state (turya), is indeed that which is to be known;
O lady of excellent limbs, one should manifest these digits within His body.

Know that the meaning of the word "That" (tatpadārtha) is her face, O fair-faced one; and the meaning of the word "Thou" (tvaṃpadārtha), which is the meaning of the sentence, is indeed her pair of breasts in sequence. (23–24)
But enjoyment, O Supreme Goddess, becomes the Nāda consisting of Brahman; the entire universe arises from the Nāda, O lady of beautiful hips, for it is the source—of this there is no doubt. (23–25)
Having worshipped Śakti in that very place, one should worship Śiva as the Liṅga of one's own self;
through their mutual influence, the essence of the bliss of Brahman arises.
O Goddess, O Beloved, carrying that nectar with the mind through the channels of the body,
one should then unite it with the nectar of the *arghya* offering and worship the Śrīcakra.
O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the knowledge consisting of the bliss of Brahman;
therein, one is not a Brāhmaṇa by birth, nor is a Kṣatriya a Kṣatriya.
O Supreme Goddess, he is no longer a Vaiśya nor a Śūdra;
he is neither a Cāṇḍāla nor a Paulkasa.
One should understand all things as equal through the definitive realization of the Supreme Self;
just as water fallen from the sky flows along the downward path.
Everything within the village was filled with excrement, urine, and the like, and was mixed with the blood of dead cows, dogs, cats, donkeys, and other animals. || 23–31 ||
O Goddess of gods, just as everything is merged in the Gaṅgā, so too,
O Goddess of gods, no turbidity whatsoever remains in the nectar of the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, O Girijā, there is equality toward all living beings in knowledge consisting of pure consciousness;
there is equality toward all objects—of this there is no doubt. (23–33)
Just as this light of the sun proceeds with impartiality, it dispels the darkness of even the highest other being in an instant. (23-34)
Drying up milk, urine, and even sandalwood paste;
for this very reason, O Maheśānī, when the practitioner of mantra is equal toward all things... [23–35]
O beloved, it should be understood that accomplishment is attained at that very moment through the grace of the venerable Guru.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Second Birth of Jñānadūtī," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
The Lord said: I shall proclaim the procedure for initiation, by which the disciple becomes happy.
O Goddess, everything, including one's very life-force, is given to the Guru.
Through that state, the accumulation of wealth, jewels, gold, fine garments, and the like comes to an end, as does the accumulation of various evils. (24.2)
Therefore, O lady of excellent vows, it is called "initiation" (dīkṣā) in all the scriptures;
[it is for one who is] a sinner, a miser, a rogue, and even a hypocrite. (24–3)

To one who is not humble, who is devoid of right conduct, who is intent on hatred toward the mantras, to a slanderer, to a fool, and to one who is intent on hatred toward the sacred fords (tīrtha). || 24.4 ||
O Goddess of gods, it should not be given to one devoid of devotion, nor to one who is impure;
rather, it should be given to one who is charitable, devoted, virtuous, and whose mind is fixed on the sacred ford. || 24.5 ||
To him who follows the true path, who is devoted to the sacred fire, the gods, and the twice-born, who knows the meaning of all the scriptures and the Vedas, and who is firm in his vows. || 24.6 ||
Initiation should be bestowed, O lady of excellent hips; otherwise, one becomes a partaker of calamity.
Now, O lady of excellent hips, I shall describe the supreme performance of initiation.
Having constructed a pavilion with an altar, adorned with a canopy of flowers, made beautiful by rows of lamps, and well-perfumed with various incenses; || 24-8 ||
Adorned with vermilion-colored garlands and variegatedly painted, O beautiful lady, it should be decorated with saffron upon the altar, O beloved. (24.9)
Or else, O beautiful lady, one should draw the supreme wheel with vermilion powder,
its center adorned with nine angles.
Having drawn a square, [one should place] nine golden jars, or those fashioned from silver, copper, and so forth, or even those made of clay. || 24.11 ||
Filled with water, exceptionally rich, replete with gold and jewels,
made auspicious by fruits and flowers, and perfumed with fragrance.
There, one should worship the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī within the eight vases;
O lady of beautiful hips, one should satisfy Śrīvidyā in the central vase. (24–13)
Having worshipped the entire sequence, one should perform the worship of the virgins and others, as well as the married women,
the assembly of Brahmins, and various types of yogis.
Then, for the sake of the satisfaction of all, he should perform the limb-oblation (aṅgahavana).
Having brought the disciple—who is free from blemish and bowed with devotion—the Guru [should proceed]. || 24-15 ||

Having performed the regulation of breath according to the rules and having seated himself upon a pure pedestal, he himself, accompanied by young women, [should worship] with the mantras beginning with "The gods have come to you... (surāstvām etu). || 24.16 ||
And one should consecrate his head with those waters from the jars;
then, having clothed him in fine garments and smeared him with sandalwood paste. || 24.17 ||
O Supreme Goddess, to the left, upon the purified and worshipped seat, one should seat the disciple there, adorned with all the finery of elegant attire. (24–18)
One should contemplate the Śrīcakra, which has the form of the six paths, upon its head;
or, O beautiful one, in its absence, having filled a large conch with water.
Having propitiated the goddess there and worshipped her with all her arts, one should serve her;
one should look at her with one's own gaze, and merge one's gaze with hers. (24.20)
One should perform the transmission of the command until immobility arises;
that which is immovable is to be known as the Śāmbhava state, free from both void and non-void. || 24.21 ||
O Supreme Goddess, the void is the reality consisting of Śiva, the Puruṣa;
the non-void is indeed the primordial Power, the Prakṛti, O Supreme Goddess. (24.22)

When, through the union of Śiva and Śakti, there is an excess of power and a coarsening of the *rajas* quality, that state should be known as the dream state; therefore, the yoga is characterized by the predominance of Śakti. (24.23)
Śakti is known as the waking state, while Śiva is the state of immobility in the void;
that which is motionless is called deep sleep by those who know the mantras.
The three qualities have been described: O Dear One, the waking state possesses the quality of sattva; O Śivā, deep sleep is of the nature of tamas and is motionless.
O beautiful one, know that the reality which transcends the qualities (guṇātīta) exists because of the preeminence of Śiva;
for when the preeminence of Śiva arises from the union of Śiva and Śakti.
Then one should recognize the fourth state, which severs all bonds;
O Goddess of gods, the sixteen digits (kalās) are established within the knowledge of the Self.
One should cause [the goddess] to manifest within the body of the disciple, merged with the seed-syllables of Śrīvidyā;
she is the sixteen-syllabled Mahātripurasundarī, who is fourfold.
From that meditation, the steadiness of the mind is called *unmanī*.
In the knowledge of Brahman, the mind is like a bird characterized by a beak of craving. (24–29)
It is always restless due to conceptualization, discursive thought, and the two wings;
it is also driven by delusion, envy, and desire, as well as by anger, egoism, and arrogance.

O Goddess, he is accompanied by his army with its arrayed banners; he stands upon the two steps of what is to be done and what is not to be done, within the tree of saṃsāra whose roots are wealth, sons, and the like.

Spread wide by ignorance, beautifully adorned with the branches of blame and praise, and laden with the abundance of blossoming flowers of desire, [this tree is nourished] by transgressions and the like. (24–32)
O lady of excellent limbs, it is filled with leaves and endowed with the fruits of both sin and merit;
there, upon two thick branches, stands the one known as Śruta and Dṛṣṭa.
Having seized that bird, one should bind it with the noose of knowledge;
O Beloved, the side-glance of the illustrious Guru is eternally delighted in the play of the bird. (24–34)
When both sides have been decisively severed by him, O Beloved, he then becomes the Transmental (Samunmanī), oriented toward certainty. (24–35)
Free from all conceptual constructions, it becomes the seventeenth digit;
indeed, that which is called *unmanī* is the severer of the bonds of worldly existence.
The yogi accompanied by Unmanī is neither a yogi nor is Unmanī supreme; just as a lamp placed within camphor is neither a lamp nor, again, the moon. (24–37)
Therefore, O Maheśānī, one should perform the transference by means of the gaze;
subsequently, one should indeed apply the meaning through such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi). (24–38)
O fair-eyed one, at the very beginning, that which is to be joined is inexpressible;
it appears as a mere touch, arising from the hand of the illustrious Guru. (24.39)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, by mere touch, all metals such as iron and others immediately attain the state of gold and become endowed with exquisite ornaments.
But the touch of the hand, O Goddess, indeed destroys the impurity of the phenomenal world and the like, and truly brings about the state of gold. (24–41)
Having placed flowers and fruits in his hands, he should cast his hand into the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
From that, the meaning of the statement "you are indeed Brahman" arises from the hand. (24–42)
This is the ineffable instruction: by touching [the breath] at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), which is the thousand-petaled lotus, the Guru—white as camphor—[is realized]. (24.43)
He eternally bestows boons and fearlessness; he is the embodiment of Brahman, forever sinless, O Supreme Goddess, the illuminator of his own abode within the world. (24-44)
Thereafter, one should awaken the disciple to the consciousness of the six wheels;
[one should visualize] the foundation as gold-colored and beautifully adorned with four petals.
O Dear One, know that Svādhiṣṭhāna, together with Gaṇeśa, consists of four vargas ending with *va* and *śa*, possessing a luster like molten gold. (24–46)
Resembling the indragopa insect and shimmering like coral, it is adorned by Brahmā with throbbing letters beginning with *ba* and ending with *la*, O beloved. (24.47)
The third [center], Maṇipūra, is indeed blue in color and has ten spokes;
it is adorned with the letters from Ḍa to Pha, which possess the brilliance of a mass of lightning. (24.48)
O lady of virtuous vows, hear now of the fourth, the mature Gadādhara-Hari;
O fair-eyed one, it is tawny-hued, possesses twelve spokes, and is inscribed with the consonants from 'ka' to 'ṭha'. (24–49)
O beloved Goddess of gods, the Viśuddha-cakra is endowed with colors possessing the brilliance of sparks and is united with Śiva; it is smoke-colored and consists of the Kalās.
O Supreme Goddess, know that it is adorned with vowels resembling rubies and is presided over by the individual soul (jīvātman) at its very end.
O Great Goddess, the wheel of command (ājñācakra) has a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning;
it consists of two petals and is adorned with the two white syllables *ha* and *kṣa*.
Rich in the nature of the Supreme Self, it is indeed the seventh in the form of Nāda;
because Nāda is dissolved therein, it is therefore called Brahman. (24.53)
O Goddess of gods, the syllables reside within the body; herein, Nāda alone is the cause.
When Nāda is joined with the Kuṇḍalinī through its union with the vital breath (pavana), [the syllables arise]. || 24-54 ||
O Supreme Goddess, O you who are worshipped by the gods, he became serene and attained the nature of the fifty phonemes within the petals of the six cakras. (24–55)
Having attained a state of unmanifest form through the vowels beginning with udātta in sequence, the true guru should thus bestow omniscience upon that disciple. (24–56)
Then the disciple should perform an auspicious worship of the venerable Guru,
[offering him] adorned with jewel-ornaments and provided with silk garments and wealth.
O blessed lady, [this land] is endowed with elephants and horses, as well as buffalo-cows;
it is delightful with fields, villages, and great groves, and is accompanied by hundreds of female attendants.
Filled with golden rays, [she is] adorned with musk, moon, and sandalwood;
having duly gratified the Guru, one receives his grace which is endowed with the ultimate reality.
The excellent disciple should receive it, and immediately thereafter the guru should whisper [the mantra] into the right ear of the young girl. || 24–60 ||
One should subsequently reveal the Vidyās residing upon the five lion-thrones;
thereafter, the supreme secret, Mahātripurasundarī.
O Dear One, one should proclaim [this mantra], which consists of the Supreme Brahman,
which generates all auspiciousness, and which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, into the right ear.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, I shall not reveal the Śrīvidyā of sixteen syllables, which is a throbbing digit of the bliss of Brahman, as if it were my very life-force.
O lady of virtuous vows, one should remember this auspicious sixteen-syllable mantra as a treasure-trove, hidden within the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, and even the Yāmalas. || 24-64 ||
Even to a uterine brother who has given one his entire being and life;
even to a king who has bestowed a kingdom; and even to a son who has given one his life. (24.65)
This [mantra] of sixteen syllables must not be given; rather, O Daughter of the Mountain, one’s entire possession should be given.
Even one’s head, together with one’s virtuous son and wife, may be given under any circumstances.
This sixteen-syllable mantra must not be given away, O Pārvatī, even at the cost of one's life; this great vidyā should be guarded like one's own womb.
Just as salt dissolved in water becomes one with it, so too, O beloved, does the mind become absorbed in the feet of the venerable Guru. (24.68)
Then, out of compassion, the Great Vidyā of sixteen syllables should be bestowed—whether accompanied by syllables or abiding in a state beyond syllables. (24.69)
O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, just as blueness is perceived in the sky through delusion, so too do the syllables exist within the Śrīvidyā. (24–70)
O Supreme Goddess, know that the sixteen-syllable mantra is the very form of Brahman;
just as soot is never found within a lamp made of jewels.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, just as the state of being unmanifest and manifest exists within the Śrīvidyā, [so too is this mantra];
one should not give it to just anyone, but should give it only to one who is dearer than life. (24.72)
Having accomplished his purpose, the supreme teacher should speak the words of the child;
he should not, however, bestow the sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā, which is of the nature of Brahman. (24–73)
O Goddess of the gods, by a single utterance, ten million Vājapeya sacrifices [are attained];
a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices, however, can never equal it. (24.74)
O Goddess of the gods, by a single recitation, one performs a circumambulation of the earth;
indeed, it is as if millions upon millions of tawny cows have been gifted by those who do so.
O Goddess of gods, it never attains equality with even a single recitation;
[this is true] at the time of Ardhodaya on a meritorious lunar day, compared to a thousand *bhāras* of gold.
Even ten million *tulāpuruṣa* gifts do not equal a sixteenth part of that which is described;
at whatever time an object is praised, at that time it is entirely free from defect. (24.77)
Likewise, O fair-faced one, this Great Vidyā consisting of sixteen syllables should be known;
she is the very nature of the Supreme Self, whose form is the vibration of the universe. (24.78)
O Goddess, through the process of inhalation and exhalation, the *haṃsa* becomes a recitation of sound consisting of twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths] during day and night. (24.79)
Pervading everything by way of its flowing nature, it abides everywhere;
as the Self, it is to be known as Ajapā, whose essence is both the Sun and the Moon.
She whose nature is stainless and whose nature is free from appearance; O fair-faced one, she is subtle by virtue of being both formless and possessed of form. (24.81)
Adorned by the wife of fire (Svāhā) through the production of awakening, the Goddess is beautified by the six limbs and worshipped by Haṃsa himself. (24.82)

O fair-faced one, [I bow] to the Supreme Goddess, the deity who is manifest as the Unmanifest Gāyatrī, whose meter is the Gāyatrī and whose face is the Veda, appearing in person like a supreme ascetic (paramahaṃsa). || 24.83 ||
Know Śrīvidyā to be all-pervasive, whose nature is the supreme light;
for, O beloved, the liṅga that is the true nature of the Self resides within the house of Māyā. (24.84)
This homage to existence is washed by the waters of the river of faith,
and it is further adorned with flowers, namely the excellent blossoms of meditative concentration.
Upon the embers of gnosis, he presides everywhere, offering incense known as conceptual proliferation and a lamp consisting of pure consciousness, adorned with every kind of food offering.
Free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, absolute, and the complete Brahman; this sixteen-syllable supreme Vidyā is designated as Śrīvidyā. (24.87)
O fair-faced one, on a propitious day of the bright fortnight and under an auspicious weekday,
or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should undertake the commencement of the mantra and other practices.
Indeed, there are no defects regarding the lunar day or the month during an eclipse of the moon or the sun;
O Goddess of all gods, on such an auspicious day, even a gift given is purifying. || 24.89 ||
O lady with large lotus-like eyes, it should be known that [an action] in the month of Caitra is fruitless;
in Vaiśākha there is the acquisition of land, and in Jyeṣṭha death is certain.
In Āṣāḍha there is the loss of kinsmen, and in Śrāvaṇa one attains a lifespan of a hundred years;
in the month of Bhādrapada there is decline, while in Āśvina there is the abundance of jewels.
In Kārttika there will be prosperity, and in Mārgaśīrṣa great wealth;
in Pauṣa there may be distress, but in Māgha there is supreme success.
In Phālguna, all rites [are performed]; such is the fruit of the months.
Having first taken the initial vowel of the disciple, O beautiful one, [one should place it] in the Pira. (24.93)
O Goddess, one should form a mental conception of a beautiful name for the sake of a stable intellect.
One should place the Śrīvidyā, whose form is unmanifest, in his heart.
The series of syllables of the Śrīvidyā is, O Pārvatī, composed of consciousness within the Supreme Brahman, remaining there just as salt is dissolved in water. (24.95)
Therefore, know that which consists of Brahman to be applied throughout all the scriptures.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation," in the glorious Jñānārṇava, the Nityātantra. || 24 ||
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
The Lord said:
I shall describe the ritual of the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for the benefit of practitioners.
A worship performed for even a single year will certainly bear fruit.
Therefore, the worship of the sacred thread must indeed be performed for the sake of attaining accomplishment;
beginning from the month of the sun's entry into Libra, which follows the [month of] Gemini. (25.2)
O Goddess of the Suras, this great worship is exceedingly beautiful and purifying;
it should be performed on the fourth and eighth days of both lunar fortnights.
On the ninth or the fourteenth day, one should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa sacrifice;
one should have fine threads made of gold, silver, or copper.
Those made from cotton, those originating from silk thread, those produced from *trasarī* thread, and those originating from lotus bark. || 25-5 ||
One should prepare the purifier (pavitra) from darba grass, muñja grass, or hemp.
The Praṇava, the Moon, Fire, Brahmā, the Nāga, Guha, and the Sun—[these are the deities]. || 25-6 ||
One should worship Sāmba and Sarvadeva upon the nine threads; having consecrated them with the Śiras-mantra, one should then do so with the Hṛdaya-mantra. (25.7)
Then the preceptor, having sprinkled [the vessel] with water and bound it with the Astra-mantra, should indeed tie it up with the Kavaca-mantra. || 25-8 ||
With *rocanā* and saffron, with red sandalwood and sandalwood, with musk, saffron, and the like, as well as with camphor and *nāgara*.
One should have it painted with red ochre and other pigments so that it is very beautiful;
having sprinkled it with the root mantra, one should place it in the northeast corner.
Having purified the entire collection of sacrificial grass with the six ancillary mantras, O Goddess of the Gods, on the previous day or immediately [on that very day]. || 25-11 ||
With one hundred and eight threads, or with nine threads, it is prepared; that indeed is the supreme *pavitra*, while half of that is remembered as the middling one. (25.12)
Half of that again would be the smallest; thus, O beloved, it is said to be of three kinds.
O virtuous lady, at the time of the preliminary consecration, one should spread out barley grains.
Having placed flowers there upon the four seats, the preceptor [should perform the rite] with the purifiers, which are purified by the collection of the five nectars. || 25-14 ||
Having fashioned [the image] with the five stainless jewels and all collections of medicinal herbs, O lady of excellent vows, one should then properly cover it with a pair of new garments. (25.15)
Having established the vessel for the Goddess, filled it with gold and other precious materials,
and having invoked the Goddess into that vessel, one should worship her with the root mantra.
Then, having worshipped the sequence [of deities], the preceptor should begin the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārpaṇa) with the Śrīvidyā mantra and by means of the Guru’s name. || 25-17 ||
One should give the *pavitra* to the preceptor, and immediately thereafter to all [others];
then one should offer the *pavitra*s to the three kinds of gurus.
Then one should perform the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for the host of Tithinityās;
then for those situated in the nine wheels, and for the nine Cakreśīs.
O Goddess of gods, having offered the purificatory thread (pavitraka) to each of the hosts of rays with devotion, one should then satisfy the gurus, O beloved. (25–20)
With golden ornaments, garments, and a collection of various riches,
one should thereafter wear his pure grace.
Having performed the ancillary oblation (tadaṅgahoma), one should worship with the purifier (pavitra);
then one should perform the worship of the virgins (kumārī) and the assembly of married women (suvāsinī).
O Supreme Goddess, if one desires one's own success, the yoginīs, the yogins, and the various classes of brahmins must indeed be worshipped. (25.23)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Investiture of the Sacred Thread of Śrīvidyā," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, the *Nityātantra*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
The Lord said:
I shall describe the ritual of offering *damanaka* flowers for the benefit of practitioners.
O beloved, by this, the worship performed throughout the year becomes complete.
When Madana sought to disrupt my asceticism while I was born as a mountain, he was reduced to ashes; then his wives, Rati and Prīti, were filled with sorrow. || 26.2 ||
From the tears produced from his eyes, the *damanaka* creeper arose;
and its fragrance and beauty, O fair-eyed one, were exceedingly great. (26–3)
O beloved, being satisfied, that friend granted me a boon; therefore, for the sake of Rati’s pleasure and delight, Madana was manifested by me.
If a practitioner of mantras does not worship with *damanaka* flowers during the course of a year, his annual worship shall accrue to Madana. (26.5)
Thus, O goddess worshipped by the gods, this boon was granted to him by me alone;
therefore, O goddess worshipped by heroes, the worship of Damanaka must indeed be performed. || 26-6 ||
Otherwise, that fruit produced by the year arises for one's desires;
O Goddess, one should place the uprooted *damana* plant in an excellent vessel. (26–7)
One should perform the subduing (*damana*) in nine ways and worship immediately thereafter;
then, O beautiful one, with the seed-syllable of Ānandeśvara, which has been differentiated.
One should worship Damana in due order, his limbs divided into nine parts by means of the seed-syllable of Ānandeśvara together with the Bindu.
Having subsequently consecrated that very person with the Aghora-vidyā, [one should do so] in the southern direction using the previously mentioned lion-throne mantra. || 26-10 ||
One should perform protection with the Astra-mantra, and thereafter with the Kavaca-mantra;
having bound the Triśūla-mudrā, one should whirl it above the Damana.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the offering of *damanaka* flowers should take place;
one should uproot [the plant] with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and smear it with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). || 26-12 ||
One should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) using sandalwood, saffron, indra-puṣpa, and other such substances;
on the first day, one should carry out this most excellent preliminary consecration. (26.13)
Alternatively, for the sake of the swift accomplishment of the year-long worship, one may perform the consecration immediately;
this is done at dawn on the fourteenth day, following the daily ritual worship.
Then, having fashioned a nine-cornered [diagram] of great splendor with vermilion,
one should place nine jars filled with gold, gems, and other precious things.
Or the most excellent of teachers should place a single beautiful water-pot;
having prepared a mandala to the right, adorned with saffron and other pigments.
Having drawn an Aśoka tree, one should draw a triangular mandala;
in its center, one should worship Kāma, youthful and of reddish glow.
Clad in red garments and adorned with red ornaments on the left and right, O beloved, he is enriched by Rati, Prīti, and Viśobhā, wielding the five arrows and the bow. (26.18)
Accompanied by Vasanta, one should worship that Kāma, who dwells in the midst of a Kadamba forest, with this mantra for the sake of attaining siddhi. || 26-19 ||
Having written Vāgbhava, Bhuvaneśānī, Śrī, and Kāmātmaka, followed by "Kāmāya namaḥ," this is the nine-syllabled Vidyā.
Having uttered the three seed-syllables of desire, one should recite that which consists of passion: "Ratyai namaḥ," O fair-faced one; this is the eight-syllabled Ratividyā.
One should utter "prīti" (joy) in the place of "rati" (pleasure); this eight-syllable mantra of joy [is as follows]:
"gauraśyāme ratiprītī maṇibhūṣaṇe. (26–22)
With lotus and betel leaf in hand, resplendent in red garments, adorned with divine ornaments, and graced by garlands of flowers. (26.23)
Immediately after that, one should meditate upon Kāma on the left and right,
and subsequently worship Vasanta situated in the midst of a *kadamba* forest.
Fair-complexioned, with his left hand holding a jar filled with nectar,
and with his right hand bearing a collection of various flowers.
Then, having fully worshipped Kāma along with his limbs (aṅgas), one should present incense, lamps, and other offerings.
When Kāma has been thus worshipped during the *damana* rite, he shall accomplish all undertakings.
Having thus worshipped Mahātripurasundarī perfectly,
the wise practitioner should duly worship the Krama and feed the Kumārīs.
Having fully honored the married women, one should worship the assembly of Yoginīs;
then, having thoroughly honored the Brāhmaṇas who have reached the further shore of various philosophical systems.
After the oblation of the limbs, he should honor the Guru with ornaments such as jewels,
thousands of *bhāra* measures of gold, and delightful divine garments.
Having performed the worship, O Goddess, one should then utter the *pūrṇāhuti* offering.
By this procedure, O Goddess, one should perform the ritual of offering the *damanaka* flower. (26–30)
O you who are born of the mountain, the annual worship performed for him becomes fruitful.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Subduing and Installation of Śrīvidyā," in the *Śrīmajjñānārṇava*, within the *Nityātantra*, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord.
